# Routledge Studies in Fascism and the Far Right

**Series editors: Nigel Copsey,** *Teesside University, UK* and **Graham Macklin**

*Center for Research on Extremism (C-REX), University of Oslo, Norway*

This book series focuses upon national, transnational and global manifestations of fascist, far right and right-wing politics primarily within a historical context but also drawing on insights and approaches from other disciplinary perspectives. Its scope also includes anti-fascism, radical-right populism, extreme-right violence and terrorism, cultural manifestations of the far right, and points of convergence and exchange with the mainstream and traditional right.

# Acknowledgements

This book is a collective effort. It was written over the past eight years in close collaboration with my colleagues in the Department of Online Culture Studies at Tilburg University. Not only did I learn a lot from listening and reading their work on the rapid transformations in culture and the public sphere, many of them have read, reviewed and given feedback to parts of the analyses that I present in this book. I truly have enjoyed their expertise. Several case studies were in some earlier form published on Diggit Magazine (the case studies in [Chapters 3](#C_010_c3.xhtml) and [5](#C_012_c5.xhtml)) and I have benefited from the detailed feedback of my colleagues. I thank Sjaak Kroon, Sander Bax, Odile Heynders, Add Backus and Inge Van De Ven for their time investment in critically reviewing my work. I also wish to honour my colleagues Julian Hanna, Tom van Hout, Inge Beekmans, Mingyi Hou, Saif Shahin and Rob Moore here for their intellectual voice and to have shared their thoughts and given productive feedback on earlier versions and parts of this book. Iris Dumoulin took on the hard job of fixing references and listing the many images, thanks! But I’m especially grateful for my journey with Jan Blommaert and Piia Varis. Jan became my mentor 20 years ago, and gradually we became friends and colleagues. This intellectual giant gave me an analytical perspective, and this perspective resonates throughout this book. Piia Varis helped me take my first steps in academia, and I will never forget her dedication and investment in me and in hundreds of students. Both Jan and Piia have introduced me to so much literature and untapped sources of knowledge, generously shared their ideas and reflections, that they can rightly consider certain parts of this book as their own. Together with Piia and Jan, I had the joy of starting the Digital Culture Studies track in Tilburg University. The programme that we constructed has given birth to many beautiful things, xiiiand I hope that they consider this book as one of those fruits. Without their work I wouldn’t have been able to write this book.

I also thank my fellows at CARR (Centre for the Analysis of the Radical Right) for the opportunity to write a two-monthly contribution dedicated to the study of the Far-Right. Parts of the analysis of The Golden One have been produced for them. I also thank the reviewers of Social Sciences for giving me the opportunity to sharpen my thoughts on the idea of metapolitical influencers and to allow me to use parts of the paper on Brittany Pettibone in this book. I thank Social Media + Society to let me reuse parts of my paper on ‘new right metapolitics and the algorithmic activism of Schild and Vrienden’. Parts of the section on digitalization as context have appeared as part of a post on the blog Ideology, theory and practice. I thank the reviewers of my paper on Guillaume Faye’s Legacy: The alt-right and Generation Identity for the very valuable feedback and the *Journal of Political Ideologies* for allowing me to reproduce some parts of that paper in this book.

Even though several case studies have appeared in print or online before, the book in its entirety is new. This newness is first and foremost the result of bringing these cases together, with new ones and thickening the different cases to make a more elaborate and generalizing point about metapolitics and the far-right in contemporary society and especially in relation to digitalization. In this larger endeavour we see the actual value of the case method. We can connect and see in the infinite small details and the connections between the local and the large changes in societies around the world.

Last, but certainly not least, I thank my family for their endless support, patience and tolerance. Without my wife, kids and my parents I wouldn’t have had the strength to write.xiv

# Introduction

DOI: [10.4324/9781003283379-1](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003283379-1)

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

Brenton Tarrant, the Christchurch terrorist, framed his terrorist attack not as an attack on diversity, but as ‘an attack in the name of diversity’. In his manifesto, Tarrant explains this commitment to diversity in terms that are reminiscent of the ethno-pluralist differentialism of the French far-right school of thought *La Nouvelle Droite.* ‘The attack’, he said, ‘was to ensure a preservation of beauty, art and tradition. In my mind a rainbow is only beautiful to (sic) due its variety of colours, mix the colours together and you destroy them all and they are gone forever and the end result is far from anything beautiful’. This is not the old Nazi speaking about the supremacy of the white race. On the contrary, he, seemingly paradoxically, is legitimating his racist terrorism in the name of diversity and its associated beauty. This may sound strange for the unacquainted reader, as we tend to associate appraising discourses on diversity with the left. The acceptance of diversity was central in the anti-racist discourse after World War II ([Balibar, 1991](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_5); [Vaarakallio, 2015](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_97)), and even today these concepts are almost automatically associated with a left-wing point of view. But it was exactly this anti-racist consensus that *La Nouvelle Droite* integrated into their new theories and stretched to its extremes in order to reinvent ‘the true right’.

Labels like neo-Nazi or fascist are not the sharpest analytical tools to dissect this discourse. Throughout this book, I will argue that we need a more fine-grained approach that lets us understand contemporary far-right violence in relation to the theoretical renewal of *La Nouvelle Droite* in the 20th century, and the contemporary uptake of its metapolitical battle all around the world. *La Nouvelle Droite* was the name given by the French press to a ‘school of thought’ called *Groupement de Recherche et D’études pour la Civilisation Européenne.* The group was created in 1968 by far-right 2intellectuals Alain de Benoist, Dominique Venner, Pierre Vial, Pierre Krebs and many others. Following François (2014: 91), I understand *La Nouvelle Droite*, or the French new right, as ‘a collection of European-wide think tanks led by GRECE, which is ideologically situated between the “Old Right’ and extreme-right and revolutionary right of a pan-European persuasion”. *La Nouvelle Droite* exists as a polycentric pan-European network of journals, think tanks, intellectuals and websites. This school of thought is not producing one homogenous body of positions. Depending on the individual thinkers, but also during the five-decade life span of the group, different positions have been taken. Added to this complexity is also the fact that former members of GRECE like Guillaume Faye, Robert Steuckers and Pierre Vial, even if they are highly critical of Alain de Benoist and *La Nouvelle Droite*, still work in line with *La Nouvelle Droite’s* ideological tradition. Despite all this complexity and diversity within the school of thought, we can still pinpoint foundational ideological positions, *des idées mères*. This network of revolutionary far-right thinkers ([Bar-On, 2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_10): 2) is known for their ‘differentialism’, or ‘ethno-pluralism’, and their ‘metapolitical battle’: a cultural battle or a battle for ideas that should, in the long term, help the true right to rise again. Even though Brenton Tarrant probably has never read the works of intellectuals like Alain de Benoist or Guillaume Faye, he still is echoing their theories. Already in his classic book *View from the Right*, published in 1977, Alain de Benoist – the number one of *La Nouvelle Droite* – defined the essence of the right ‘to view the diversity of the world and by consequence the relative inequalities that are necessarily the product of this, as a positive thing; and the progressive homogenisation of the world, extolled and effect by two-thousand years of egalitarian ideology, as a negative thing’ ([de Benoist, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_32): 2). This ‘right to difference’ was a foundational axiom of the ‘newness’ of the French new right. It was their embrace of (and essentialist vision on) diversity that allowed them to claim a ‘differentialist anti-racism’ that ‘holds that the irreducible plurality of the human species constitutes a veritable treasure’. Differentialist anti-racism makes every effort to restore an affirmative meaning to ‘the universal’, not in opposition to ‘difference’, but by starting from the recognition of ‘difference’ ([de Benoist & Champetier, 2000](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_31)).

It was this differentialist position and their plea for ethno-pluralism that allowed them to dissociate themselves from fascism, Nazism, white supremacy and racism in general. At the same time, it also allowed them to introduce a new racist paradigm. This differentialist racism, as Taguieff called it, shows us how theoretically innovative de Benoist and his comrades were in reworking the ideas of the German conservative revolutionary intellectuals from the 1930s and adopting them for re-emergence in a new package. This new racism reflected the timespace in which it was created: a world which was changing faster and faster as a result of decolonization, globalization, rise in 3mobility, new technologies and neoliberalism. As Balibar ([1991](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_5)) has shown, this neo-racism had in the early nineties of the 20th century already escaped the theoretical works of *La Nouvelle Droite* to become a very powerful social phenomenon. Balibar argued that this neo-racism was a meta-racism that cleverly appropriated the post-World War II anti-racist claim that the essence of humankind is to be found in its diversity. In this synthesis, a new racism was created that substituted race for immigration and thus used culture as its main diacritic ([Balibar, 1991](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_5): 20). This new diacritic reorganized racism to be able to deal with the reversal of population movements, the rise in migration and mobility, the negative connotation racism had acquired and what would in retrospect be called superdiversity ([Arnaut e.a., 2016](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_2)). Just like Balibar, Titley and Lentin ([2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_92)) argue that this new racism is still very much a racist ideology that creates ‘Others’ that are excluded from society. This new cultural racism caused what Appadurai ([1996](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_1): 12) called the ‘substantialization’ of culture which brings it ‘back into the discursive space of race, the very idea it was originally designed to combat.’ The main difference is that as a result of its metapolitical strategy of embracing the notion of anti-racism, differentialism allows it to distance itself from the ‘racist’ label and all its negative connotations. Lentin has called this ‘not-racism’ ([Lentin, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_53)). Lentin ([2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_53): 402) defines not-racism as a rhetorical device born of the primacy placed on distancing oneself from the accusation of racism and a way of controlling the definition of racism. ‘Not-racism’, says Lentin, ‘takes the right to define racism away from those affected by it and, in this way, is a form of racist violence’ ([Lentin, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_53): 406).

This not-racism, as a dominant form of racism in the West, has its roots in the differentialist logic of *La Nouvelle Droite*. Differentialism, or the new right celebration of diversity, is in effect, a celebration of an ‘ethno-pluralist’ world constituted of homogeneous communities. It is thus not a coincidence that Lentin’s ‘not-racism’ is suggested to be on par with minority groups’ interests in preserving their cultures and traditions, whereas the real function is to shield autochthones in power from ‘cultural, social and economic incursion’ ([Lentin, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_53): 408). *La Nouvelle Droite*’s ethno-pluralism has always been an explicit attack on liberal accounts of multiculturalism and on diversity within one territory in general. It attacks the foundation of all humanisms. Not surprisingly, it generated a new anti-migrant and culturally grounded racism (see Wallerstein & [Balibar, 1991](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_5); [Blommaert & Verschueren, 1992](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_11), [1998](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_12); [Schinkel, 2008](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_84)). This new racism in the form of anti-Muslim racism or culturalism in general is still very much present today and it serves a nationalistic agenda ([Titley & Lentin, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_92): 300). In other words, the differentialist anti-racism of the French new right preconfigured one of the goals of the school of thought: a new world order grounded in homogeneous organic communities. It also took on board the need to ‘protect’ our people and the fight for its culture and identity and naturalized racism within a diverse 4society. Racism (and violence) was now framed as a natural response to the unnatural diversification within one society. This idea, propagated through a complex network of different voices through time, has become part of the mainstream, and it results in the construction and exclusion of the Other and the renewal of what Zeev Sternhell calls the anti-Enlightenment tradition in the form of nationalisms, regionalisms and the embrace of the homogenous cultural communities in general.

Throughout the seventies and the early eighties, *La Nouvelle Droite* had a serious impact on far-right, conservative and liberal parties and eventually also saw the birth of many sister movements throughout Europe ([Bar-On, 2012b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_9): 25; [Camus, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_23): 75). Not only has its discourse been taken up by right-wing politicians and intellectuals in the whole of Europe since the eighties and nineties of the last century ([Bar-On, 2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_10): 25), this ideology of homogeneity has had a huge impact on the political mainstream ([Blommaert & Verschueren, 1998](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_12)) in the context of integration and migration debates ([Maly, 2009](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_56), [2018b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_60)), and especially in the context of anti-Islam discourse ([Maly et al., 2007](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_55); [Lentin, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_53); [Titley & Lentin, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_92)). More than 40 years after the birth of this school of thought, we see that some of those new right assumptions and key ideas like ethno-pluralism or differential racism are omnipresent among far-right activists of the identitarian movements, far-right politicians ([Maly, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_71)), the alt-right and even full blow terrorists like Brenton Tarrant. Even worse, we see that they are sometimes in a more ‘light’ version adopted by mainstream politicians and journalists. They have become hegemonic.

## New right metapolitics

To understand the success of ethno-pluralism and the contemporary rise in far-right activists, politicians and even terrorists, we need to understand the concept of metapolitics. Metapolitics is inseparably connected to the project of *La Nouvelle Droite* in France. In the seventies, Alain de Benoist called upon the importance of metapolitics, and Gramsci in particular, for the re-emergence of a ‘true right’. He argued that the right should focus on the long term and thus understand that cultural power ‘acts upon the implicit values around which the consensus indispensable to the duration of political power crystallizes’ ([de Benoist, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_32): 7). According to de Benoist and *La Nouvelle Droite*, this cultural battle was crucial for any political success of the right. Their metapolitical project started from the analysis that the left had acquired cultural hegemony and that the only way to counter that power was to start a far-right cultural battle by intellectual means. This (selective and partial) appropriation of Gramsci fused left-wing analysis with right-wing goals and focused first on acquiring cultural hegemony before trying to acquire political power. It is from this insight that *La Nouvelle Droite* was 5commonly coined the ‘Gramscians of the right’ ([Seidel, 1986](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_85); [Spektorowski, 2003](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_86); [Griffin, 2008](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_43); [Bar-On, 2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_10); Maly, 2018). This cultural and intellectual battle was and still is focused on attacking liberal democracy, egalitarianism, socialism, liberal multi-culturalism, cosmopolitanism, human rights, consumerism and materialism in general.

Metapolitics is not a new concept, nor was it exclusively used by far-right activists or intellectuals (see [Zienkowski, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_107) for a discussion). Metapolitics, in the context of this book, will be understood from an emic perspective, from how it is used and understood first and foremost by the intellectuals of *La Nouvelle Droite* themselves and how it has been taken up by other far-right actors in the last decades. The adoption of metapolitics by *La Nouvelle Droite’s* intellectuals has to be framed in relation to the post-World War II context. In this context, all extremisms and forms of ultra-nationalism were associated with ‘war, destruction, genocide, and calculated inhumanity on a horrendous scale’ ([Griffin, 2000](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_42): 165). The old right, and in particular fascism, national socialism and ideologies that resembled those like the conservative revolution or reactionary modernism, were not able to mobilize the masses anymore. The ideologies and political manifestations were deeply unpopular and were pushed to the margins. Metapolitics was the answer of de Benoist and his colleagues to prepare the resurgence of a militant right-wing that rejected liberalism, socialism, capitalism and egalitarianism.

Metapolitics can be seen as the result of a ‘double critique’, as de Benoist called it: ‘an ideological critique of the left and a methodological critique of the right’ ([de Benoist, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_32): 18). This double critique was aimed at a synthesis of left and right: a meta-project. A true synthesis, said de Benoist, ‘is a surpassing. It is not a little of this and a little of that, in succession, but this and that, with the same intensity, at the same time’ ([de Benoist, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_32): 15). From a methodological point of view, *La Nouvelle Droite* embarked on a different path than the national socialists and fascists. Metapolitics meant disregarding key components of modern far-right and fascist politics. They advocated against setting up an electoral party, a paramilitary army or a mass social movement. They purely focused on the production and circulation of their ideas without a connection to a political party or even a movement ([Sylvian, 2005](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_87): 9). The French new right also had no problem with explicitly denouncing fascism and Nazism (de Benoist in [Versluis, 2014](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_104): 81; [de Benoist, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_32)). On the contrary, de Benoist saw denouncing ‘the totalitarian temptation’ as a precondition to reinvigorate key right-wing values (de Benoist, 1977: 4). Important to stress is that this synthesis was still a synthesis ‘from the right’, as de Benoist called it. Among scholars of the new right, there is a general consensus that this school of thought is reviving ideas that are common among the so-called conservative revolutionary, reactionary modernist and fascist intellectuals ([Griffin, 2000](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_42), [2008](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_43); Spektorowksi, 2003, 2013; [Bar-On, 2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_10); Maly, 2018). Alain de Benoist and Guillaume Faye not only regularly 6quote or use ideas from all these intellectual traditions, they are also openly engaging with them. Alain de Benoist for instance not only wrote the preface of Mohler’s book ([2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_79)) on the conservative revolution, he is also open about his shared assumptions with conservative revolutionary intellectuals. He clearly takes a revolutionary stance when arguing that there is no contradiction between conservation and revolution ([de Benoist, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_33)). And a similar point can be made about the number two of the French new right, Guillaume Faye. Even though in his Archeofuturism he explicitly argues that the conservative revolution is not enough, we see that throughout the book he constantly engages with key intellectuals of this intellectual tradition.

The result of this ideological and methodological synthesis should thus be understood in terms of renewal and continuities. Spektorowski ([2003](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_86): 111–112) described this ‘neither right, neither left’-synthesis as a ‘neo-fascist third way’ that ‘pits a right-wing theory of multiculturalism’ – the ethno-pluralism described above – against ‘a liberal multiculturalism’. *La Nouvelle Droite* not only propagated this neo-racism, its ‘differentialism’ was inherently connected to a larger worldview that is not only trying to create ethno-homogenous spaces, but also comes with an ideological attack on liberal democracy, Universal Human Rights, liberalism and socialism. This ethno-pluralist world order not only normalizes neo-racism, it also provides a full alternative for an Enlightened democracy. Interestingly, this anti-democratic project is, for metapolitical reasons, presented as in favour of democracy. But just as their differentialist anti-racism is in reality filled with a new meta-racism, we see that their embrace of democracy infuses democracy with an anti-democratic discourse ([Maly, 2018b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_60)). Whereas democracy within the Enlightenment tradition is understood as a representative democracy grounded in the rule of law, the separation of powers, a constitution and Universal Human Rights (Israel, 2008, 2010), *La Nouvelle Droite* proposes an ethnocratic definition of democracy ‘linking ethnic ties to qualitative democratic participation’ ([Spektorowski, 2003](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_86): 112). *La Nouvelle Droite*, its metapolitics and its differentialism are not only at the heart of an intellectual project that reshaped the post-World War II far-right, they are also inseparable.

## Metapolitics and violence

Griffin compellingly argued that GRECE’s metapolitics succeeded in changing the face of post-war fascism. The metapoliticization of fascism led numerous far-right formations to abandon the party politics and even the arena of activist struggle. They all started to focus on the intellectual battle for ‘ideas’ ([Griffin, 2008](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_43): 195) that should, in the long run, contribute to the creation of a new world order. It is also this metapolitization that gave birth to contemporary far-right movements like the identitarians in Europe and the alt-right in the United States ([Johnson, 2012](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_49); [Hawley, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_45); [Nagle, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_81); 7[Maly, 2022b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_73)). Even Stormfront has taken over the differentialism that is so emblematic for the metapolitics of *La Nouvelle Droite* (Miller-Idriss, 2017: 136). And it eventually also gave rise to far-right terrorists like Brenton Tarrant. The paradox is clear. *La Nouvelle Droite* embarked on its metapolitical project to distance itself from the methods of the old right. Its violence and genocidal tendencies were explicitly rejected, and the school of thought also explicitly constructed an alternative for far-right activist movements. It also didn’t see a need in supporting political parties: metapolitics was first and foremost a collective intellectual exercise in the long term.

Today, 50 years after the erection of GRECE, it seems that this project went full circle and ended up in the rise of the extreme-right and radical right politicians and parties, movements and even in violence again. Auger ([2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_4)) even speaks of a fifth global wave of right-wing terror. Between 2014 and 2018, a 320% increase in right-wing-extremist attacks (Institute for Economics & Peace, 2019) occurred. Far-right terrorist attacks in 2020 increased by 250% on a global level, and 89 persons died in a far-right terrorist attack in 2019 ([Brzozowski, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_20)). As always, global doesn’t mean that the rise of far-right violence is the same everywhere. It is clear that some continents, countries and regions have seen a more spectacular rise than others. In Western Europe, we tend to have less violent attacks than in the United States. In the last 30 years, violent far-right attacks with casualties have been declining in Europe. And within Europe, most far-right terrorist attacks and violence occur in Germany, the UK, Greece and Italy ([Ravndal, Thorstensen, Jupskås & Macklin, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_82)). On average, in Western Europe, we see that ‘while 2020 is among the five least deadly years in terms of fatal attacks, it is, with 11 fatalities, among the ten most deadly years in terms of fatalities’ ([Ravndal, Thorstensen, Jupskås & Macklin, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_82)). The latter is the result of the mass-casualty attack of the Hanau shootings, which is in turn a good example of the fifth global wave of right-wing terror, as Auger calls it. Just like Brenton Tarrant in New Zealand and the shooter in Halle, the Hanau shooter prepared messages for uptake. Not only did he set up his own website, with several links to online information and a manifesto, he also prepared several videos posted on his YouTube channel. The manifesto was addressing all Germans, while at least one video was addressing all Americans. In all these messages, he wanted to ‘inform’ his readers and viewers about the secret services surveilling people, but also about the threat of migrants, and especially Islam. The format of the attack, including the attention to the uptake of the message, in combination with racism, anti-feminism and conspiracy theories, is emblematic of this new far-right format of violence.

Even though the Hanau shooter is not legitimizing his mass murder with a discourse that echoes the theoretical renewal initiated by *La Nouvelle Droite*, it is clear that at least several do, especially the New Zealand and Buffalo shooters, who speak with an identitarian voice. This fact is important, as it 8forces us to at least question the strict distinction scholars in far-right terrorism and activism make between violence and metapolitics as methods for far-right activists ([Ravndal, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_82)). The Great Replacement theory connects the most mediatized far-right killing sprees in 2019 ([Crawford & Keen, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_29)). The Christchurch terrorist and the attacks in Halle, Pittsburgh, Poway and El Paso were all grounded in the belief that ‘white people’ were being replaced or occupied. Usually, this conspiracy theory is attributed to Renaud Camus ([2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_24)), but the origins of it go back a long way. Guillaume Faye made this argument already at the end of the 20th century in a series of books. A lot of research on the surge of far-right terrorists has started looking into the role of digital media and the distribution of conspiracy theories ([Davey & Ebner, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_30); [Auger, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_4); [Crawford & Keen, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_29); [Ebner, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_35); [Weimann & Masri, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_106)), but they tend to overlook the longer cultural battle from which contemporary far-right digital cultures have grown.

A second problem with the clear distinction between ‘metapolitics’ and far-right violence as strategies of right-wing revolutionary resistance is the assumption that violence is only physical violence, and terrorism in particular. In this study, violence will be interpreted in a broader manner. Next to terrorism and physical violence, we should focus on what Bourdieu and Passeron called symbolic violence. Bourdieu and Passeron ([1990](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_19): XV) famously argued that symbolic violence is the effect of a power that ‘succeeds in imposing meanings and in imposing them as legitimate in disguising the relations of power which are at the root of this force, add its own force, that is a specifically symbolic force to those relations of power’. Symbolic violence is thus closely connected to the domination of one social group by another through the normalization or naturalization of those unequal power relations. As Wacquant argues, symbolic domination is the result of symbolic power, or

> the capacity to impose and inculcate means of understanding and structuring the world, or symbolic systems, that contribute to the reproduction of the social order by representing economic and political power in disguised forms that endow them with legitimacy and/or taken-for-grantedness – the best warrant for longevity any social order might hope for.
> 
> ([Wacquant, 1987](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_105): 66)

Bourdieu’s notion of symbolic violence resonates with Gramsci’s conceptualization of hegemony. As is commonly known, hegemony, in Gramsci’s work, stood for the ‘cultural domination’ of one class – the bourgeoisie – over the others: the proletariat. This cultural domination, or symbolic domination in Bourdieu’s conceptualization, cannot be dissociated from the hard power of the dominant social group. As Blommaert ([2005](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_13): 167) stresses, there is no clear distinction to be made between hegemony as a dominant factor of power and force as a determinant factor: the reproduction of dominant 9culture is sustained by a coercive and disciplining system of education. Importantly, in the context of this book, metapolitics is all about the construction of narratives that normalize the exclusion of ‘the other’.

## Metapolitics and digitalization

This metapolitical strategy has been very successful, especially in the digital age. Far-right and extreme-right parties and activist groups are on the rise, not only in Europe and the United States, but globally. Organic and even blood and soil nationalism, radical new right regionalism, anti-feminism, homophobia, racism, and anti-migration rhetoric are moving from the margins to the mainstream ([Maly, 2018a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_59); Tufekci, 2018; [Fielitz & Thurston, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_37); Russell, 2019). The alt-right in the United States and the identitarians in Europe probably have the most visible activist groups, but they are certainly not the only ones. It is in the margins of that ‘new normal’ that we see further radicalizations in mainstream discourse, a vibrant field of far-right activists and a peak in far-right terrorism. Several scholars connect the rise of the far-right at least partially to the affordances of digital media. And while some scholars refer to the algorithms in those radicalization processes, most stress the importance of the socio-technical assemblage in the new digital (meta-) political battle ([Nagle, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_81); [Lewis, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_54); [Maly, 2018a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_59), [2019a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_63), [2020a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_66)). Mainstream digital media like YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram are used by radical right and far-right actors in connection to niched websites, boards, crowdfunding platforms, click farms, bot-networks, and alt-tech to engage in a contemporary metapolitical battle. The democratization of recording and the banalization of transmission ([Thompson, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_91)), in combination with datafication, gamification and programmed sociality, have allowed far-right actors and movements to upscale their reach and work. Even more, as a result of digitalization, we see an enormous diversification of far-right actors: activist movements, meme-pages on Instagram, YouTubers, influencers, trolls, and far-right online encyclopaedias like Metapedia (Arnstad, 2016) create a networked niche within the digital ecosystem in which ideas circulate and are reinforced. These new right actors take up a specific place within and outside the platform ecosystem. This ecosystem is ‘a corporate space that in the Western hemisphere is dominated most notably by the Big Five tech companies known by the acronym GAFAM (Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon, Microsoft)’ ([van Dijck, de Winkel, Schäfer, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_100): 4). Most actors, be it politicians, movements, influencers, activists or platforms, at least started within this socio-technical infrastructure, and they relied on those platforms for their first political and metapolitical successes, with some even finding their funding there. Over the last five years, more and more new right actors have struggled to keep themselves integrated into this ecosystem, but the impact of those platforms has been foundational.

10The appropriation of digital culture and digital technologies has changed the metapolitics of the far-right. Not only the intellectual but also the activist, the politician and the prosumer are now imagined as part of the new right metapolitical battle ([Maly, 2020c](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_68)). Much has been written about the far-right’s adoption of meme culture ([Nagle, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_81); Bogaerts & [Fielitz, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_37); [Maly, 2019a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_63)), LARPing (the ironic and metapolitical use Live Action role Playing in order to do or say things that are too outrageous for normies) ([Tuters, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_95)), harassment ([Conversi, 2012](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_26)), trolling ([Hodge & Hallgrimsdottir, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_46)), metapolitical intimacy and far-right vloggers’ use of the practices of influencer culture for metapolitical goals ([Lewis, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_54); [Leidig, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_51); Maly, 2020, [2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_71); [Tebaldi, 2022](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_88)a, [2022](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_89)b). These new practices are not just new ways of distributing the same ideas; they change the essence of metapolitics. Metapolitics in the digital age is not only about the circulation of ideas but also about digital literacy and digital culture. It is not only an intellectual affair; it has been ‘democratized’ or networked.

It is exactly this connection between *La Nouvelle Droite*’s metapolitics and its quest for cultural domination, the rise in far-right movements, digital culture, and symbolic and terrorist violence that I want to explore in this book. I will argue that we indeed cannot fully explain this rise and influence of far-right discourses without (1) having detailed attention for the history of new right metapolitics, (2) adopting a perspective on culture in the digital era and (3) considering how the digitalization of the media-landscape has fundamentally altered the reach, scope, uptake and practices of new right ‘metapolitics’. It is by adopting this cultural perspective that we can explain why we not only see a fifth global wave of terrorism as Auger ([2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_4)) argues, but also see a rise of far-right symbolic violence in the form of racist, antifeminist, anti-left and anti-intellectual discourses and the normalization of these discourses. New right discourses are more and more entering the mainstream, and thus structuring and, more importantly, normalizing power relationships between groups in society. It is not a coincidence that migrants, LGBTQ+, women and leftists are the object of those discourses and attacks. They are the same groups who are the object of those discourses and government policies ([Titley & Lentin, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_92)).

## Metapolitics 2.0

Metapolitics 2.0, as I coin these contemporary forms of metapolitics, is not necessarily about the production of ‘original’ highbrow intellectual theory, and nor is it about designing a new theoretical synthesis. Metapolitics 2.0 is the synchronization of metapolitics and web 2.0 ideology – or digital utopianism, as Turner coined it – embedded in the mainstream digital media platforms. Web 2.0 echoes a techno-utopian belief grounded in keywords like participation, creativity, openness, connecting, the strength of networks, transparency 11and information sharing. Marwick ([2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_74)) argues that web 2.0 ideology ‘is the child of both Silicon Valley entrepreneurial capitalism and activist subcultures like independent publishing, anti-globalization activism, Burning Man, cyberdelic rave culture and free and open-source software’ ([Marwick, 2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_74): 24). Turner ([2006](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_94)) carefully analysed how this ideology grew in a strange coming together of hippie culture, libertarianism and American new right ideologies. Throughout several decades, and with Stewart Brand and the Whole Earth’s cybernetic tradition as an important facilitator, this technology-centric ideology gave birth to digital technologies that were steeped into deregulationist politics to digital technologies ([Turner, 2006](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_94): 222). This media ideology shaped digital media and how we use and think about them. Web 2.0 ideology argues Marwick stresses digital exceptionalism – ‘the idea that the internet is different from other forms of communication and therefore not bound by the same legal and market forces’ ([Marwick, 2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_74): 25) – and a do-it-yourself spirit that ranges between alternative media activist and entrepreneurial realization. The result of this web 2.0 media ideology was:

1.  the construction of new, mostly unregulated media platforms (from blogs to social and user-generated media),
2.  promising to empower individuals by giving them the possibility to participate, to have a voice and to be able to connect,
3.  attracting financial investment with the promise of rapid returns, and
4.  wrapped in a progressive discourse (including the style) that promised to have transformative characteristics.

This Californian ideology, as Barbrook and Cameron ([1996](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_7)) labelled the digital utopianism of web 2.0, gave birth to new constellations of technologies and created a ‘climate in which participating in the culture of techno-business, sharing personal information online, and commanding and maintaining a large audience have become modern status symbols’ ([Marwick, 2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_74): 76). Web 2.0 was launched as horizontal, democratizing peer-to-peer platforms devoid from hierarchy: it was celebrated by users, platform managers and academics as a new public sphere. But as van Dijck ([2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_98)) has carefully described, web 2.0 was from 2005 onwards slowly but surely turned into large for-profit businesses. Digital cultures that were nurtured in this new environment are shaped by the interactions of citizens and communities with these new technological institutions and their values.

These new digital cultures and technologies have given way to a new generation of metapoliticians who produce and (re)produce (snippets of) ideas and propagate them using specific digital practices to new audiences through a network of mainstream or non-mainstream digital media. As these digital media are steeped in this web 2.0 ideology, communication through those media is not entirely free: using those media successfully means integrating in 12a ‘culture of connectivity’. Van Dijck ([2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_98): 20–21) lists three main characteristics of this culture: (1) sociality is not simply rendered technological: coded structures are alternating the nature of our connections, creations and interactions; (2) it is a culture where the organization of social exchange is staked on neoliberal economic principles: all users are pressured to expand through competition and gain power through alliances; and (3) the culture is part of a longer historical transformation resetting the boundaries between private, corporate and public domains. In practice, this means that metapolitical communication in such a digital environment is not only focused on the transmission of ideas. It is at least as focused on the construction of a brand that has to be positioned in the attention market. Metapolitical influencers like The Golden One or Brittany Pettibone-Sellner, for instance, focus at least as much on the construction of their online identity, or in the case of The Golden One, on nutrition and exercise advice (see [Chapter 3](#C_010_c3.xhtml)), than on metapolitical ideas. Their private life becomes part of this brand, and thus of contemporary metapolitics: they mobilize, like all online influencers, strategic intimacy and strategic authenticity ([Marwick & boyd, 2011](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_76); [Marwick, 2015](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_75); [Hou, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_47)) to bond with their audience. This metapolitical intimacy, or metapolitical seduction, as Tebaldi ([2022b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_89)) calls it, is very productive: it helps to establish para-social bonds between the influencer and their followers.

Just like contemporary politicians, contemporary metapolitical movements, activists, intellectuals and influencers create ‘message’ ([Lempert & Silverstein, 2012](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_52)). Message is used here as an analytical term, and refers not only to the ‘literal message’, but also to the style and identity of the speaker. This identity is constructed as a collage in motion of communicative events – posts, vlogs and blogs – in which the influencer narrates him or herself to their audiences ([Lempert & Silverstein, 2012](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_52): 16). In the digital realm, this identity in itself becomes a metapolitical asset.

In order to have metapolitical influence in the digital world, it is not enough to produce message. One also needs digital literacy in order to remain integrated into the viral economy and to succeed in generating uptake. Metapolitical activists need to develop specific strategies and make full use of the affordances and algorithms of different media, as well as the specific media logic, to build an audience and/or community, and to make sure that their voice circulates. Furthermore, understanding and adjusting to the culture of specific platforms is equally important in generating metapolitical impact. We thus have to analyse contemporary metapolitical projects not only in relation to online persona but also in relation to context—that is, in the social, political, historical, cultural and digital, algorithmic environment in which they produce their voice. Mainstream digital media not only have a crucial role in the circulation of metapolitical messages, but they also help shape the messages. Metapolitical actors need to make sure that they are and stay integrated into each platform culture by adjusting to the community 13rules. This adjusting in itself, I will argue, contributes to the metapolitization of far-right messaging.

The management of visibility, as well as avoiding non-visibility, is a constant worry for all actors in this media system ([Bucher, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_22)). It is by now a truism that digitalization has fundamentally reshaped and reorganized the fields of media and of (meta)-politics, but it is important to grasp the exact way in which those fields have changed. In his seminal work on the hybrid media system, Chadwick ([2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_25)) argues that we now see a ‘chaotic transition period’ in which ‘old media’ and ‘newer media logics’ interact with and are interdependent among each other. The result of the interaction and interdependence of those media logics in the reflexively connected social fields of media and politics is what he labels as the ‘hybrid media system’ ([Chadwick, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_25)). The hybrid media system is a system, not just of ‘old’ and ‘new’ media, but the result of the interaction and interdependence of different actors. Politicians, influencers, journalists, activists or alternative media try to ‘create, tap, or steer information flows in ways that suit their goals and in ways that modify, enable, or disable the agency of others, across and between a range of older and newer media settings’ ([Chadwick, 2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_25): Xi). It is in this battle, and thus the use of different technologies and platforms, that the hybrid media system takes shape.

In this highly competitive hybrid media system, legacy media, social media and user-generated content media, just like politicians, activists and prosumers, are trying to get attention for their message. And even more, they will try to redirect the attention others are getting to their own medium. The democratization of content production has not only disrupted the media field, or changed the relations between actors or democratized publishing, it has made attention a scarce good. Attention, and not information, is subsequently one of the main drivers of the hybrid media system and the digital economy ([van Dijck, Poell & De Wael, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_99); [Venturini, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_103): 128). Attention, data and user valuation have become popular means of monetization for platforms ([van Dijck, Poell & De Waal, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_99): 10). This monetization is important for many contemporary metapolitical organizations.

## Metapolitics 2.0, audience labour and uptake

In the commercialized, attention-based digital economy, users have a central role: they have attention to give and function as producers of raw data. The front region of the digital infrastructure is organized around keeping those users hooked ([Eyal, 2014](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_36)) so that data can be extracted. Enabling users to become producers is not only a case of democratization, it is first and foremost a key ingredient of the digital economy.

Audience labour ([Fisher, 2015](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_38)) is a crucial ingredient of the attention-based economy and metapolitics 2.0. Clicks, shares, comments, views, posts, 14status updates and reach are all data that are measured and organize visibility in the hybrid media system. Only when people interact with the post of an activist it will become visible to others and thus potentially grab their attention and get the message out. Audience labour triggers the algorithms of the platforms that read user engagement as a proxy for popularity and subsequently make the content visible in more places. All media in this hybrid media system are increasingly grounded in an algorithmic logic ([Gillespie, 2014](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_41)). Algorithms – as socio-cultural assemblages – produce normativities, and these normativities co-create new communicative economies. The reason why uptake matters is because it is programmed in the algorithms. The like, the comment, the view, the click and the share function as proxies of attention ([van Dijck, 2013](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_98)). Digital media are not just intermediaries but have algorithmic agency ([Tufekci, 2015](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_93)), which affects the uptake and input of messages. Algorithms affect uptake as they ‘select and prioritize content by algorithmically translating user activity into ‘most relevant’ or ‘trending’ topics’ (Poell & van Dijck, 2014). Digital media (re)shape and re-organize the communicative structure of the ‘input’-discourse ([Georgakopoulou, Iversen, & Stage, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_39)). A tweet has only a limited amount of characters that can be used. A YouTube video should use SEO to be found and so on. The message is not just distributed but also shaped and altered by digital media, or in other words, the digital ecology co-constructs digital cultures. Self-branding, posting pictures of a homely situation or one’s food on Instagram are all connected to the specific affordances of specific platforms. And we will see that metapolitical actors adopt such more mainstream digital cultures for metapolitical goals: from meme culture to body culture or DIY culture: it can all become infused with a metapolitical project. Metapolitical messaging in the digital age is not a linear process between sender and receiver, but involves a multitude of human and non-human actors that are all potential senders and receivers, and all have a potential impact on the production and circulation of messages.

As a metapolitical actor in such a hybrid media system, it is thus not enough to produce ‘content’ to gain visibility; metapoliticians need to build a network that actively interacts with their message. Influence, as Gruzd and Wellman ([2014](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_44)) argue, is now *networked influence*, and this in two ways: ‘by occurring in social networks and by propagating through online communication networks’. Having ‘influence’ in digital media landscapes thus starts with building an audience, a network that interacts with your message. But that is also not enough. Digital media not only affords discourse production, it also directs behaviour: certain digital affordances request, encourage and push users towards ‘particular communicative and interactive practices by means of quantified processes’ ([Georgakopoulou, Iversen & Stage, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_39): 24). Contemporary media savvy politicians, activists and metapoliticians in general don’t passively wait for uptake, but facilitate it, ‘gamify’ it, pay for it, 15actively organize it or even make use of influencers, click farms and non-human activity like bots and bot-networks to trigger the algorithms ([Bucher, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_22); [Maly, 2018a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_59), [2018b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_60); [Jacobson, Gruzd, Kumar & Mai, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_48)). This uptake is also discursively important as reach, likes and followers are used to stress that those actors actually articulate the voice of the people or their generation ([Maly, 2018a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_59), [2018b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_60), [2018c](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_61), [2019a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_63)). Attention-based metapolitics thus means investing in content, in building algorithmic knowledge (Maly, 2018; [Varis & Hou, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_101)), and in developing an algorithmic imagination ([Bucher, 2015](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_21)).

In the digital ecology, *uptake* of ideas is of crucial importance for any metapolitical project. With uptake, I refer to (1) the fact that within the digital ecology, users are not only consumers but also (re)producers of discourse, the so-called ‘prosumers’ ([Miller, 2011](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_77)), and (2) that algorithms and the interfaces of digital media play an important role in the dissemination and reproduction of ideas (Maly, 2018, 2020, [Blommaert, 2020a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_16)). Uptake through human and non-human actors (from bots over the algorithms organizing the communication on a platform) has become a crucial part of any political and metapolitical battle. Note here that seemingly simple ‘reproduction’ actions like retweeting, reposting, liking and sharing are not just ‘copies’ of the same discourse, but ‘re-entextualizations’ ([Varis & Blommaert, 2014](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_102)): a share (and sometimes even a like, depending on the algorithms of the platform) is the start of a *new communication* process where the initial message is now part of a new communicative act performed by a new producer who communicates to new addressees in a new type of interaction. Concretely, the metapolitical work of Alain de Benoist or Guillaume Faye is not only found in their books, it is mediatized (and mediated) through different actors and systems of communication. That work is not just copied but acquires a new meaning to new people. All those re-entextualizations not only change the initial meaning of the message but also the uptake. What should be remembered for now is that this new communicative economy creates a polycentric world of communication. Such a world is far more complex than a world dominated by the so-called ‘mass media’. The many-to-many communicative logic of mediated online interaction ([Thompson, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_91)) creates pluriform, transnational and polycentric media networks with many different niches within which audiences subscribe to certain snippets of ideologies. The general changes in the media field have profound effects on the (meta)political field. Metapoliticians do not just need to present themselves in the mainstream media, they (and their team) need to manage their visibility on a broad range of media to draw attention to their message ([Lempert & Silverstein, 2012](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_52)), gain support and engage in a discursive battle to normalize their ideology ([Maly, 2016](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_58)). Especially for outsider parties, politicians and activists that are considered ‘extreme’ or ‘populist’, digital media bring new opportunities to have their voice circulating in niched public spheres.

16 

## About this book

In the second decade of the 21st century, the new right cultural battle is not only embedded in conferences, essays, journals and books anymore. In the digital age, millions of citizens, activists and even algorithms (re)produce new right metapolitics ([Maly, 2018a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_59), [2019a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_63)). The transnational uptake of *La Nouvelle Droite’s* legacy by alt-right and identitarian movements, activists and new right influencers happens in a post-digital context ([Fielitz & Thurston, 2019](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_37)). Cramer ([2014](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_28)) introduced the concept of post-digital to highlight that the digital revolution has occurred and is now a ‘normal’ part of societies around the world. This new normality has profoundly affected the flow of ideas, which in turn has fundamental effects on the construction and circulation of (meta)political messages and meanings, and of course also on the study of these meanings ([Blommaert, 2020a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_16)). This new digital reality is a key ingredient of the metapolitical battle of the new right in the 21st century. When Alain de Benoist and Champetier ([2000](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_31)) stress the importance of metapolitics, they not only stress the importance of culture and ideas in fuelling revolutions, but they also adopt a specific view on the role of intellectuals and the ‘masses’. Whereas intellectuals are implicitly understood as authoritative producers of ideas, the masses are imagined as sheep-like individuals taking up the ideas of intellectuals. Not only have intellectuals lost part of their authoritative role in the production of ideas, but also in the attention economy of the post-digital era, the ideas of intellectuals have to compete with many other actors: individuals are not just passive consumers of metapolitical ideas anymore, they (re)produce them as well.

The basic assumption of this book is that we cannot and should not analyse contemporary metapolitics and find reasons for the rise of far-right activism and even violence *in the texts* these new right actors produce. At all costs, we should avoid the fallacy of internalism as Thompson ([1990](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_90)) called it. With this concept, Thompson criticized the widespread idea that the meaning of a text is only to be found in the text itself (and thus not in the attribution of meaning through the uptake and reproduction of texts). He stressed that ‘the analysis of ideology in modern societies must give a central role to the nature and impact of mass communication’, and argued that cultural experience is profoundly shaped by the diffusion of symbolic forms distributed through mass media ([Thompson, 1990](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_90): 264). As a result, the study of ideology should – if one wants to avoid the fallacy of internalism – be focused on all three aspects of mass communication: ‘the production/transmission, construction, and reception/appropriation of media messages’ ([Thompson, 1990](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_90): 24). If we follow Thompson’s argument, we should at least direct some attention to the algorithmic nature of the distribution of discourse and ideology in contemporary societies ([Maly, 2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_71)).

17On the other side, we should also try to avoid taking easy refuge to *a priori* contextual explanations for this rise (See Blommaert’s critique on the use of globalization or power as décor for analysis in [Blommaert, 2005](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_13)). I’m thinking about classic tropes that are common places in media reporting on the rise of the right because ‘they capture the voice of the losers of globalization’, ‘they articulate the feelings of the people’ or ‘they align with the spirit of time’. Or the even more classic explanation is that their rise is a result of the migration crisis in 2015. All these explanations de-historicize and decontextualize the rise of the far-right. I therefore adopt a more complex, historical, ethnographic discourse analytical perspective that doesn’t disregard the agency of far-right actors today and throughout a longer history. Concretely, I will study new right activists and their metapolitical strategies as socio-technological assemblages

1.  In which concrete actors use the affordances of digital media, acquire and apply algorithmic knowledge and produce metapolitical messages that are made for uptake in particular socio-cultural, historical and technological timespace or chronotope. Chronotopes invoke a sociolinguistic and ethnographic understanding of the context that takes on board the idea that ‘concrete and socioculturally recognizable timespace configurations involve nonrandom modes of social action and lead to specific social effects’ ([Blommaert, 2020b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_17)).
2.  In which uptake, in the sense of likes, shares and comments, is important not only for the distribution and circulation of messages but also because they constitute re-entextualizations that give birth to new groups and new forms of metapolitics.
3.  In which digital media and their algorithms are analysed as having agency and power. Algorithmic systems help metapolitical actors bring certain ideas and realities into being ([Bucher, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_22): 3), and they also direct certain (multimodal) behaviour ([Georgakopoulou, Iversen & Stage, 2020](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_39)).
4.  In which contemporary successes cannot be dissociated from their historical trajectory and the discursive battles of the past.

In order to be able to zoom in on the details, the history of contemporary metapolitics, in relation to the context of uptake, I will make use of a case method. The analyses of the cases presented in this book contribute to a theory on how far-right actors are using the affordances of digital media to radicalize their audiences. It also builds a theory of the global new right as a complex system. The analyses and many case studies are part of a long-term digital ethnographic discourse analytical research project dedicated to the study of contemporary new right movements and politicians and their use of digital media (see [Maly, 2012](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_57), [2016](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_58), [2018a](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_59), [2018b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_60), [2018c](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_61), 2019, 2020, [2021](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_71), 2022). This project started as an ethnographic and discourse analytical 18project (see [Maly, 2012](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_57), 2015), but increasingly morphed into a more digital direction. Along the way, it became obvious that this research project begged for an interdisciplinary approach blending history, critical algorithm studies, web sciences, fascism and radicalization studies with an ethnographic or multimodal discourse analytical approach.

After explaining my methodology in [Chapter 1](#C_008_c1.xhtml), I start the second chapter by going back to the roots of new right metapolitics. I introduce metapolitics in the works of Alain de Benoist and *La Nouvelle Droite* and contrast those conceptualizations of metapolitics with the critique of Guillaume Faye, the former number two of *La Nouvelle Droite*. Faye criticizes the ‘intellectual conception’ of de Benoist’s metapolitics in two influential books ‘Why we fight’ and ‘Archeofuturism’. I argue that it is Guillaume Faye’s conceptualization of metapolitics that has found uptake in many contemporary far-right movements. The argumentation is grounded in a detailed analysis of the uptake of Faye’s ideas by alt-right intellectuals like Greg Johnson (Counter-Currents), Richard Spencer (National Policy Institute) and by Martin Sellner of the identitarian movement Generation Identity. I analyse a series of YouTube videos that Martin Sellner dedicated to Guillaume Faye’s book ‘Why We Fight’.

In the third chapter, I build further on the idea that contemporary metapolitics is grounded in a digital ecology. I show how this digital ecology not only reshaped metapolitical strategies and practices but also gave birth to a global new right culture. This new right cultural niche is a typical product of globalization processes facilitated by digital media and rising mobility. Contrary to what popular parlance and new right theories on globalization want us to believe, globalization doesn’t produce a homogenization of culture, a global mono-culture. In order to analyse and grasp the full meaning of new right metapolitics, we need to adopt a global perspective and overcome ‘methodological nationalism’.

By taking on board a sociolinguistic theory of globalization (see [Blommaert, 2010](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_14)), I analyse the Flemish identitarian movement Schild & Vrienden. In this case study, I adopt a perspective that focusses on the mobility of resources and the layeredness of local activism. I show the productiveness and necessity of an ethnographic approach that takes digitalization and globalization as context by analysing the remediatization of a storming of an old castle in Ghent, Belgium, by Schild & Vrienden. In this action, its formatting and the discourse they deployed, we see the synchronization of different discourses and practices from different parts of the world. Even more, I show how activists from all corners of the worldied to push the uploaded video to virality on Facebook. On the basis of this case, I argue that the rising importance of global networks, cellular systems and global cultural and political flows is emblematic of this latest phase of globalization and is largely undertheorized when it comes to new right activism.

19In the fourth chapter, I focus on the emergence of a global new right culture and the role of influencers in that emergent culture. New right activists have set up a whole ecology of digital media platforms for metapolitical goals ([Lewis, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_54)). In doing so, they adapt to the technical requirements of those platforms, they integrate into their cultures and their content is made to fit the content and form requirements of these platforms. As LaViolette ([2017](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_50): 6) argues, platforms can be seen and analysed as Goffmanian frames that circumscribe ‘discourse and becomes crucial for its interpretation’. Contemporary new right culture, style and discourse are created as a socio-technological assemblage. In this chapter, I show that the performance of the new right identity is in itself a metapolitical deed. It is through this careful stylization of hair, body, clothes and language that new right actors address different audiences and introduce far-right ideas. After discussing the emergence of that culture in detail, I zoom in on two metapolitical influencers: the Swedish bodybuilding YouTuber The Golden One and #pizzagate promotor and wife of Martin Sellner, Brittany Pettibone-Sellner. Both represent two sides of a crucial new right metapolitical battlefield, which could be labelled the ‘gender war’ or the antifeminist battle. This battle aims at restoring the ‘natural order’ of things by promoting the heteronormative nuclear family and traditional gender roles for men and women as part of a larger metapolitical battle to centre around the construction of homogenous, white and organic communities. Both cases illustrate the importance of brand and integration in the digital mainstream for contemporary metapolitics.

In the fifth chapter, I present three cases that all focus on the use of data voids for metapolitical goals. Data voids are search queries that don’t result in much qualitative data. Those voids can easily be used for metapolitical goals. The web can be seen as one giant learning environment ([Couldry & Hepp, 2016](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_27); [DeCook, 2018](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_34); [Blommaert, 2019b](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_15)), and the search engine is emblematic of this. Google is a crucial infrastructure in this learning environment. Since 2015, YouTube has had over 1 billion daily users ([Moore, 2016](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_80): 9). In 2019, 91.8% of the searches worldwide were done through Google, and on mobile phones this increases to 96% of all searches ([Moore, 2016](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_80): 13). This dominance of Google is the result of an almost hegemonic media ideology ([Gershon, 2010](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_40)): the idea that Google is the best search engine and that it will help us find what we are looking for ([Vaidhyanathan, 2011](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_96); [Moore, 2016](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_80): 15). Gershon ([2010](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_40): 3) defined the term media ideology as ‘a set of beliefs about communicative technologies with which users and designers explain perceived media structure and meaning’. Media ideologies thus shape how we look at media and their functions and at least partially determine how we use those media. We could expand this media ideology associated with Google to search engines on other platforms as well. Most people do not realize it anymore, but to ‘surf’ the web in many cases starts by entering something in a search box. The search has become a normal way of navigating the web. This normality 20is as always a site of power, or more concretely, it has powerful effects. As a result of this normality associated with search engines, and the existing media ideologies around search, algorithms of search engines have potentially powerful metapolitical effects. Far-right actors haven’t missed this, and they produce data in relation to the search engine algorithms for metapolitical goals. In order to understand how the far-right tries to metapolitically exploit these data voids, I analyse three cases. In the first case, I analyse the so-called Groyper War that was waged during the 2020 Trump election campaign. In the second case, I will show how YouTube conspiracy theory vlogger Paul Watson exploits the coronavirus breaking news data void for his metapolitical agenda. In the third case, I zoom in on the Feniks, a Flemish new right movement that used Covid-19 for metapolitical goals

The sixth chapter zooms in on the link between violence and the discourses of *La Nouvelle Droite*, the *identitarian movements* and the American white nationalist media. I do that by analysing the manifestos of Dylann Roof and Brenton Tarrant from an intertextuality and cultural perspective. ‘Intertextuality refers to connections between texts over time as well as synchronically’ ([Blommaert, 2005](#C_007_c101.xhtml#r101_13): 253). Studying the intertextual connections between texts, and especially between manifestos and the wider new right texts, allows us to analyse the manifestos as social products. Adopting a cultural perspective makes visible that even though Roof and Tarrant have been socialized in quite different far-right niches operating on different scales within the global new right, they both started from a shared hegemonic notion within that niche: the idea that there is an undeclared war going on. That is why they saw their violence as necessary, not only to defend the ‘white race’, but also to create consciousness about that ongoing war. Both terrorist acts are emblematic of what I call metapolitical terrorism. Their killing sprees were not only executed to install fear, they were instruments in a cultural war to make ‘white people’ conscience about ‘the great replacement’ and to spur them to action.

In the last chapter, I look at the impact of states and platforms on the normalization and abnormalization of far-right actors. Or more concretely, I look at the impact of external actors on the visibility and invisibility of the contemporary new right. The role of deplatforming, banning and deplatformization is described from a meta-perspective. I focus on how external actors shape and reshape the global new right. The global new right, I argue, is best understood as a complex system that is perpetually in motion as a result of internal and external forces.

# 1 Ideology and activism in the digital age Theoretical and methodological reflections

DOI: [10.4324/9781003283379-2](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003283379-2)

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

Digitalization has affected all fields of society, and thus also the field of (meta)politics. Digital media have become a normal, and to a large extent invisible, part of our world. They are just there, ready to be used. Digital platforms, their algorithms, and the ideologies that are embedded in them are part of the invisible and self-evident systemic core organizing daily life ([Maly, 2022a](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_70)). Just because of this central status in the information environment of contemporary societies, digital media are crucial in any contemporary metapolitical project. It is therefore necessary to examine and study the impact of this digital revolution on metapolitics. Digitalization not only gives birth to new ways of circulating messages, new discourses and new practices, but it also allows activists to easily cross borders, cooperate on a transnational scale, organize manifestations and events and find money to pay for all of that metapolitical and activist action. Digitalization makes clear that globalization is the context in which far-right activists shape modern metapolitical action. It enables what Dugin calls a ‘conservative internationalism’ ([Southern, 2018a](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_92): 17, 45). In this chapter, I want to (1) zoom in on the relation between ideology, metapolitics and algorithms, (2) explain what I mean with digitalization and globalization as context, (3) explain my methodological approach and methods and (4) sketch the ethnographic situation of the data analysed in this book.

## The algorithmic logic of post-digital societies

Digitalization and algorithmic culture have rapidly reshuffled the media system and the information flows and interactions within that system ([Gillespie, 2014](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_37); [van Dijck, Poell, & De Waal, 2018](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_101)). Politicians, activists, journalists, 28intellectuals and common citizens politically engage in a very different context than in the 1990s, let alone the 1950s. We now live with an algorithmically powered attention-based hybrid media system ([Chadwick, 2017](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_25)). The different types of media – newspapers, television, radio and social media platforms – do not merely coexist, but form a media system that is constantly changing. That perpetual change is the result of the reciprocal actions and interactions between those different media and their media logics. In that new media system, the distinction between ‘old’ and ‘new’ media or digital and non-digital media has almost become non-existent. Tweets become news and the newspaper tweets. Moreover, the newspaper is also more and more algorithmically produced ([Bucher, 2018](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_22)).

All media in this hybrid media system are increasingly grounded in algorithmic logic ([Gillespie, 2014](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_37)): our interactions with algorithms determine which information becomes visible, to whom and on which scale. Algorithms, datafication and the affordances of digital media that allowed for the democratization of transmission, and the banalization of recording ([Thompson, 2020](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_98)), disrupt the status quo. We cannot understand the rise of Trump and Trumpism, or the rise of Generation Identity, Schild & Vrienden or The Golden One without taking this new media environment into account. While we should carefully avoid the trap of technological determinism, we cannot disregard the importance of including this new socio-technological context in our analysis of far-right metapolitics in contemporary societies (see Maly, 2019, 2020 for illustrations). Post-digital societies create new possibilities and constraints for the production and circulation of discourse. New producers and new relationships have been established between the different actors in this media system and they have had fundamental effects on the construction and circulation of (meta)political messages and meanings.

In the last two decades, the digital infrastructure has become an inherent part of the social fabric of society. It is one of the deep, generic drivers of concrete human behaviour in hypermediated societies ([Couldry & Hepp, 2016](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_26); [DeCook, 2018](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_28); [Blommaert, 2020a](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_10)). Digital media, and the hybrid media system at large, has a central role in shaping contemporary cultural experiences. They facilitate and encourage the massive production and diffusion of symbolic forms distributed in that hybrid media system. This social structure has such a profound effect through the affordances it provides for humans to act and interact and its agency in the form of algorithms. Following J.B. Thompson’s warning to avoid the fallacy of internalism I discussed in the previous chapter, taking the relation between digital media and ideology seriously means that we should not only study the metapolitical texts of new right intellectuals, activists and politicians, but also zoom in on the interdependence of the production, transmission, construction, reception, appropriation and the human and algorithmic interaction facilitating the diffusion and uptake of metapolitical messages. Considering the role of digital media and the algorithmic logic in the hybrid media system, we should at 29least direct some attention to the algorithmic nature of the distribution of discourse and ideology in contemporary societies.

## Algorithmic culture and the attention-based media system

It is important to note here that algorithms are much more than mere technological instruments. They are socio-technical assemblages. Algorithms only work if they are fed with data. In other words, algorithms should be understood from a relational perspective. Not only do programmers (their values and their companies’ goals) matter, but also the interfaces, the data structures, and what people do with algorithms deserve our attention. The idea – so prevalent in public debate – that algorithms just do things and that users do not have an impact is false. It is not YouTube’s algorithms that radicalize people, but people using YouTube and its algorithms, in order to radicalize people. The recommended videos on YouTube are the result of the interactions between the recommendation algorithms of YouTube, viewers, and how producers prepare their content for uptake. Not only algorithms matter, it is algorithmic culture that truly matters. People will try to optimize their content, link to each other, have a network of fans which they ask to share content, or even have bots push certain content.

Algorithms and people have agency. It is in the interaction between humans and algorithms that the contemporary production and circulation of ideology – and thus metapolitics – should be understood. When we take the assumption on board that algorithms have agency, then it is important to understand the socio-technical and the economic context in which they are created ([Maly, 2022a](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_70)). The objectives of the platforms are clear. Beneath all the fine talk of big tech boasting about ‘connecting the world’ and ‘doing no evil’ lies the quest for profit. Social platforms make profit by commodifying our digitally networked social relationships: our emotions, photos, posts, shares and likes are repackaged into ‘tradable commodities’ ([Zuboff, 2019](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_108)). Or more concretely, data is used to predict the likelihood that certain audiences will be receptive or give attention to certain messages from companies or politicians. The more data those companies have about their users, the more accurately they think that sellers can target them, and the more profit big tech can extract from that behavioural data. The result is an unbridled surveillance and datafication. Even if users don’t post or like and don’t leave comments, they still produce data that can be processed and traded.

In order to gather more data on their users, digital media platforms nurture a specific culture in which audience labour takes a central place ([Venturini, 2019](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_105): 130). We have all become prosumers: we do not only consume information, we also produce it ([Miller, 2011](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_75)). This has crucial consequences: information – including good quality information – is now abundant. It is no longer a scarce commodity. We have ended up in the opposite of an 30information economy: an attention economy. In order to convert that attention into profit, attention is codified and categorized. The like, the comment, the view, the click and the share function as proxies of attention ([van Dijck, 2013](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_100)). The digital infrastructures of the attention economy are not only organized to keep the users hooked, but they also facilitate audience labour and thus data production ([Eyal, 2014](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_31)).

This commercial algorithmically programmed attention economy creates a very specific environment in which we develop our social relationships. ‘Popularity’ has become a crucial factor ([van Dijck, 2013](#C_008_c1.xhtml#r1_100)).
