> We don’t fight for the ‘cause of peoples’, because the identity of every people is its own concern, not ours (…) we fight only for the cause of our own people’s destiny. Our political activities (…) are guided by the imperative of all Grand Politics: that is, by the struggle for the heritage of our ancestors and the future of our children.
> 
> ([Faye, 2011](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_29): 41)

Reconquest is only possible according to Faye in the sense of a renewel of archaic values and the re-establishment of homogenous groups. The pan-European manifestation of the identitarian movement is a pre-configuration of Faye’s dream of a European revolution. The first step is metapolitical: people should see migration in terms of colonization. After the action at the Grand Mosque of Poitiers, Generation Identitaire tried to legitimize their actions by arguing:

> a nation can recover from an economic crisis or a war, but not from the replacement of its population: without the French, France will no longer exist. It is a question of survival: this is why each nation has an absolute right to choose whether it wants to accept foreigners and in what proportion.
> 
> (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 19)

The goal of Generation Identitaire is

> Not a matter of gaining an electoral majority, but of remaking a people! We are a UFO in a political landscape that is fossilised as that of France – a vanguard to awakened the people, not a bunch of little politicians hiding behind their neckties. (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 40). They are defenders of ‘direct democracy’, federalism and localism.
> 
> (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 32)

Generation Identity, just like Faye and de Benoist & Champetier, understands democracy as based on the identity of a homogenous people. Direct democracy works if it is grounded in localism. Their battle, again like Faye’s, is 90understood in biological and cultural terms, as embedded in ‘our blood, our soil and our identity’ (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 10). Whereas the alt-right especially highlights the racial component of democracy in Faye’s work, we see that identitarians leave this more implicit, but they all stress the necessity of homogeneity for democracy. Identitarian activist Markus Willinger ([2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_102): 41), for instance, again just like Faye refers to Athens when he speaks about the identitarian embrace of direct democracy and its battle against representative democracy. And he also understands democracy as based on identity and a people. And just like Faye, and *La Nouvelle Droite* in general, identitarians envision this identity in European – not nationalist terms: ‘Europe, is a community of civilisation and culture. (…) Europeans must recognize this bond which has united us for 30,000 years now’ (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 37). This vitalistic constructionism of an archeofuturistic Europe, the stress on race and ethno-pluralism, the hatred towards Islam and Muslims and advocating an organic democracy expressing the will of the European people ([Willinger, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_102)) makes several scholars see the identitarian movement ‘as the direct-action arm of the (French) new right intended to make new right topics such as identity politics, homeland politics and anti-immigration agitation particularly attractive for youth by adapting modern communication methods to this end’ ([Salzborn, 2016](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_77): 50). What is missed in this type of assessment is that GI explicitly takes Faye’s lessons on board and less those of Alain de Benoist. Generation Identitaire does not support the right of all individuals and communities, immigrant and non-immigrant alike in one nation, like de Benoist. They fight against Islam and for the homogenous Europe of European people.

Faye’s influence on Generation Identity is not only visible in the fact that he is regularly quoted in the manifesto ‘We are Generation Identity’ or in the consistent use of the concept of ‘Reconquest’ (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 12, 28) as their goal, it is especially visible in their strategy. Generation Identity sees itself as a fighting community, as the ‘awakeners of the people’ and ‘role models’ whose sensational activism and its re-mediatization on social media is made for uptake by mainstream media. They target the sensationalist commercial mainstream media logic ([Chadwick, 2017](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_12)) in

> Order to sow the seeds of the Reconquest to come. We are a signal light toward which many young people will turn once the ethnic and political polarisation of French society leads to the return of social and political movement.
> 
> (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 34)

From the start, Generation Identity wanted to overcome the ‘Gramscian metapolitics in which cultural victory is a condition for political victory: it’s 91super-politics’ (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 34). It is a fighting community, not for an abstract ‘rights of peoples’, but for regional identities and the European identity. Faye’s understanding of the metapolitical as necessarily complementary to other forms of action is at the heart of the movement and their sensationalist activism. In the beginning, Generation Identity was set up as

> one of three pillars of the identitarian movement founded in 2002. This movement joins together the Bloc Identitaire, a political party and networking tool, the association Les Identitaires, which organises an identitarian summer camp each year – a place for political and militant training (…) – and Generation Identity, a fighting community.
> 
> (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 40)

Generation Identity is not only an offline activist movement, it is (or at least was) also very much present online. The launch of *Generation Identitaire* didn’t go unnoticed in 2012. The spectacular ‘occupation’ of the roof of a mosque under construction in Poitiers created a buzz, not only in France but also throughout the hybrid media system in Europe. The movement was only one month old at the time, but its ‘Declaration of War’ video was seen over 93,000 times on YouTube. The reupload of that video in 2018, after the original one was deleted for copyright infringement, managed to be seen by 68,000 viewers. The original video was already ready in summer, and it was shown to the activists during their 2012 camp (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 15). After its launch in October 2012, many identitarian activists throughout Europe used the affordances of YouTube to add subtitles. ‘Prosumers’ translated the declaration of the movement into different languages and the English version very quickly had more views that the original French one. The same thing happened with the introduction video of *Génération Identitaire*, which was translated ‘in German, Spanish, English, Greek, Italian (…) In each case the translations were personal initiatives on the part of Europeans we do not know’ (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 16). The message of Génération Identitaire was re-entextualized and targeted new audiences in new languages.

This stress on the ‘organic uptake’ is a central argument in the discursive positioning of the moment. As co-founder of *Génération Identitaire* Alban Ferrari mentions in a 2012 interview, the Austrian chapter started independently as a Facebook page (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 16), and the Facebook pages *Generation Identity: Germany* and *Generation Identity Italy* appeared after the sensational action of *Génération Identitaire* at the Mosque in Poitiers. In their communication, they like to stress the ‘spontaneous’ nature of the uptake and support. When asked if they translated the video, Ferrari highlights that ‘We had intended to, but we were beaten to the punch by spontaneous, independent initiatives’ (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38):16). In this 92discourse, the translations and birth of different national identitarian chapters across Europe are framed in a populist logic as touching a nerve among a generation: ‘the video’s success proves we are on the right track and that our way of thinking is shared by most of the young people here’ (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 15). If we look at this populism as a chronotopic mediatized communicative relation ([Maly, 2018e](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_59)), we see the importance not only of the populist claim to speak in name of a generation, but also of some understanding of what ticks among some people who are willing to engage with your message. That uptake of the message can then be discursively used to claim the legitimacy of that claim. The actions of the ‘prosumers’, the likes, shares and the followers are being presented as evidence that they truly speak in the name of this generation, not only in France but also in Europe and even in the United States. ‘Since Poiters, our call to action has been heard’, said a press release of the movement. Génération Identitaire also claimed to have received 500 messages in two days, and the Bloc Identitaire, nearly 3,000 messages. When researchers, encyclopaedia (see the Wikipedia page on the Generation Identitaire) and legacy media ([FranceInfo, 2021](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_31)) take over this label of populism, the discursive framing is successful: an extreme-right discourse has then been rebranded in ‘articulating the voice of the people’ ([Maly, 2018e](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_59)).

The occupation in Poitiers functions as a format that can be applied by the different chapters in the different countries. The action at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, where 15 activists from the *Identitäre Bewegung* put up banners reading *Sichere Grenzen, sichere Zukunft* (Secure Borders, secure future) and *Grenzen schützen! Leben Retten*! (Closed Borders! Save Lives), follow the exact format as the original action at Poitiers, including the remediatization and the attention of mass media all over the world. And also in 2020, the French chapter proves the usefulness of the format to grab media attention when they dropped a banner saying ‘Justice pour les victim du racisme anti-blanc’ from a building in Paris during a Black Lives Matter protest in June 2020 in the French capital. Whereas the French slogan is made for local uptake, the hashtag #whitelivesmatter below the slogan not only directs viewers to Twitter in search, it also indexes an intended international audience and an international association, especially with the alt-right.

### Defend Europe: metapolitics and digital media

The different ‘media guerrilla actions’ on a local, national and European scale have constantly enabled the movement to enlarge its audience and its reach. This media tactic clearly worked. In May 2017, when they launched their Defend Europe Mission, the National French chapter of the pan-European movement alone had over 124.000 likes on Facebook. This mission was supported by all the European chapters, but of course also by the regional branches of the movement. The French chapter alone had branches in Nice, 93Paris, Nantes, Bretagne, Dauphiné and Lille. Those branches had offline gathering locations in the form of bars and boxing clubs and had their own Facebook pages to give information, recruit members and organize events. These Facebook pages were useful in the dissemination of information from the local to the national and the European scale, and back: they created a pan-European network of influence. A network that could share and like the remediatized actions of the movement and spread it through Europe and the hybrid media system. Just like Generation Identitaire started in 2012 with their ‘Declaration of War’ video’, the Defend Europe Mission started with a video and the launch of a brand new pan-European website.

> Every week, every day, every hour – ships packed with illegal Immigrants are flooding into European waters. An invasion is taking place. This massive immigration is changing the face of our continent. We are losing our safety and our way of life and there is a danger we Europeans will become a minority in our own European homelands. Our future is under attack.
> 
> (Defend [Europe, 2017a](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_18))

This quote started the Mission Defend Europe video that was posted on the Facebook page of Generation Identitaire on 14 May 2017. The uptake of this video was again huge. By December 2017, the video was watched over 319,000 times on Facebook, shared 2,000 times and over 13,000 profiles reacted with a thumbs up or another emoticon. In the video, we see four young identitarian militants talking about migration as a threat to Europe. Their discourse echoes Faye’s conceptualization of migration as an invasion and a danger for Europe and its way of life. At the same time, it also echoes the discourse that many radical right and far-right politicians were articulating in the mainstream media. Politicians like Theo Francken ([Maly, 2018a](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_55)) from the New Flemish Alliance, Salvini in Italy and Le Pen in France were advocating the necessity of ‘pushback’ and praising the ‘Australian Model’ (Generation [Identitaire, 2017](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_37)) of pushing ships back. This political discourse circulated freely in mainstream media, and it had the effect of normalizing or de-radicalizing the actions of Generation Identity.

The Defend Europe Mission was supported by different websites and social media of the national and regional branches of the identitarian movement, but they also launched a European website and specific social media channels for this specific action. On the website, which was designed according to the corporate identity of the movement, one could not only read up on the mission, or find news, one could also click on the support button. At first, this button brought visitors to a PayPal account, but after June 2017 this was not possible anymore. PayPal blocked the identitarian account.

This backlash was also an opportunity to convince the followers of the movement to donate money and frame this act of PayPal as an attack from 94the globalists. The Thumbnail clearly framed the action of PayPal as an anti-patriotic action. Considering the discourse of this movement, this act of PayPal can be seen as a reinforcement of the idea that ‘the globalists are against them’. In the video, Martin Sellner argued that through this mission ‘We want to show PayPal, Twitter and all these globalists and the mainstream media, that they can censure us, that they can block us, but that they can’t stop us’ (Defend [Europe, 2017b](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_19)). The videos that were recorded and posted in German (10,000 views) and English (6,900 views) generated quite some uptake. Many people commented that they had or will be transferring money or even doubling their donation. Sellner also makes sure to stress that their followers shouldn’t believe ‘the shitstorm’ started by the mass media and thus should donate. Mass media and globalists want you to believe that ‘we want people to drown. That we want the rescuing missions to end. No’, Sellner says, ‘we want the human trafficking to end. We want to rescue people before the Libyan coast, but we want to bring them back from where they came’ (Defend [Europe, 2017b](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_19)). Note how Sellner stresses that they are on a rescue mission. Rescuing refers to pushing migrants back and even more importantly: ‘we want to start a rescuing mission to save the future of Europe’ (Defend [Europe, 2017b](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_19)). The dominant discourse is thus one that fits into the narrative of Faye and Camus: they are on a mission to stop the replacement. And that mission is urgent. As Sellner stresses in another video, a couple of days before the ship would be on its way to the Libyan coast:

> We live in a time of decision. This time, in our day and age, it will be decided if Europe and the whole West will have a future. At the moment this future is looking dark (…) that’s why we don’t plan our vacations, we plan to defend Europe this summer.
> 
> (Defend [Europe, 2017c](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_20))

By the first of August 2017, the ship was on its way with the identitarian crew to the Libyan coast. In a short vlog, Sellner stressed that this boat sailing out was the nightmare of ‘Soros’ and all the globalists (Defend [Europe, 2017d](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_21)). Underneath that video, one could read a short status update in French, Italian, English and German. It also contained a link to their WeSearchr account. WeSearcher was set up by Charles Carlisle Johnson, an American far-right activist and troll, as an alternative to Crowdfunding sites that banned far-right projects. Even though this platform was short-lived, Generation Identity managed to collect over 300,000 dollars to fund their Defend Europe Mission (234,000 to charter the ship, and another 83,000 dollars for the crew and other expenses).

The mission was a success in terms of hybrid salience. Maniou and Bantimaroudis ([2018](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_73)) introduced the notion of ‘hybrid salience’. ‘Hybrid forms of salience’, they say, ‘should be approached as indices of mediated significance 95derived from interdependent and asymmetrical distributions of media power, divided between mainstream media outlets as well as grassroots digital platforms including various in-between hybrid media formations’. Hybrid salience highlights the fact that salience has now been fragmented over different media, actors and niches. In the case of Defend Europe, this salience was not only the effect of their own communication, but it was also the result of the Canadian far-right YouTuber Laura Southern praising the plans of Generation Identity during a live stream on Periscope in May 2017 that was posted on Twitter. Southern was later joined by the American far-right YouTuber Brittany Pettibone. Both Southern and Pettibone would regularly tweet and post vlogs on YouTube to update their followers. These postings were also amplified on Buzzfeed ([Broderick, 2017](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_9)). Considering their status in the alt-right, and globally in the case of Southern at the time, it is no coincidence that lots of key figures in the United States would support the Defend Europe Mission. The ‘ironic’ neo-Nazi site The Daily Stormer advocated the action and the former grand wizard of the KKK asked his Twitter followers to support the mission. From a metapolitical perspective, the action was a great success. It was also a success in the sense of networking. After the Mission, Sellner joined Brittany Pettibone in the United States. This trip with Pettibone was mediatized on YouTube as a work trip to allow the US movement to learn about the European identitarian movements and vice versa. It was also the start of their relationship.

Social media were thus very much part of the infrastructure of this movement. This was the case locally, but also on a national and transnational level. Most of its impact, and especially the upscaling from a French to a pan-European movement, is a result of its embeddedness in social media. The pan-European movement Generation Identity is clearly a post-digital phenomenon ([Fielitz & Thurston, 2019](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_30)): not only is their digital presence at least as important as their offline activism, but it is also based on digitally enabled reproduction of their message. This movement from the start benefited from the network effects of digital media: they use the affordances of digital media to connect, organize and structure different chapters on a pan-European scale and remediatize their activism for upscaling the metapolitical effect. It is also clear that they do not see the political field as separate but as an essential part of their metapolitical battle. Already in 2012, they are explicit about their connections with existing movements and youth movements of political parties like the Flemish Interest (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_38): 16). In 2019, we see that the different national chapters of the official and unofficial identitarian movements in Europe have very close relations to the so-called radical right ‘populist’ parties like Rassemblement National in France, Flemish Interest in Belgium, FPÖ in Austria, Forum For Democracy in The Netherlands, the AFD in Germany and UKIP in the United Kingdom ([Maly, 2018e](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_59); [Murdoch & Mulhall, 2019](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_76)). Generation Identity was built on sensational mediatized 96actions. It was a brand that gave a very clear collective identity to its militants. The movement was grounded in a digital and offline infrastructure enabling militants to build strong ties. Throughout the last decade, they succeeded in building a clear repertoire of collective action, readymade for uptake in the hybrid media system. It was those actions and their structure that allowed them to upscale the movement to a European and even a trans-European scale. But in the end, the real fundament of Generation is found in its metapolitics. And their version of metapolitics is the legacy of Faye.

### Martin Sellner, fashwave and Faye's metapolitics

Martin Sellner, the de-facto face of Generation Identity on a European scale was de-platformed in August 2018 by YouTube in the wake of his e-mail contact with the Christchurch shooter and the juridical actions against him. Since his channel was re-instated, he has been reluctant to use his English YouTube channel. Even more, he deleted several older videos and put others on private. Among those private videos is a series of five videos he posted in 2017 that were dedicated to the work of Faye, especially focusing on his work ‘Why We Fight’. In the first video of this series, Sellner says that he read ‘Why We Fight’ in 2010 – thus before the birth of the Austrian Chapter of Generation Identity – in its German translation as part of a reading group in Vienna and claims that this book, even though he doesn’t agree with Faye on all points, has changed him ([Sellner, 2017a](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_79)). ‘Why We Fight’, says Sellner is one of the important inspiration sources of the identitarians ([Sellner, 2017b](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_80)).

Before we zoom in on the actual content of the videos, it is useful to have a look at the graphics. The opening sequence echoes a vaporwave aesthetics then quite popular online. In the first shot, we see a nineties white Lamborgini Diablo driving on vaporwave techno beats and neon rasters. The Diablo was produced between 1990 and 2001. It is an object of nostalgia, referring back to the ‘near past’. The Diablo, as the successor of the Countach, is a typical poster child and thus comes with strong emotions, especially for young petrolheads. This nostalgic feeling about a past where everything is better is enhanced by the vaporwave graphic. This adoption of vaporwave aesthetics by far-right movements was common practice around 2017 and was called fashwave. This trend combines far-right discourse with the then popular hype of synthwave. The result of this assemblage is the use of nostalgic ‘futurist’ imagery reminiscent of nineties video game culture, neon colours with a preference for purple and pink and synth beats from the eighties and nineties to promote a far-right message. The style has roots among neo-Nazis and was popularized by Andrew Anglinm from The Daily Stormer in August 2016, who called synthwave ‘the Whitest music ever’ and soon after began the ‘Fashwave Friday series posting retro sci-fi images and sounds’ (Hermansson, Lawrence, Mulhall & Murdoch, 2020:110). The style was also very popular 97among Germanica Reconquista who used the fashwave style to make historical references in their memes come across as less old-fashioned and more appealing to a younger audience (Bogerts & Fielitz:146–147). The Lambo first seems to cruise along without a real goal, but in the end, accelerates towards the lambda sun. From the moment the Lambo reaches the sun, the title of the show appears: Identity quest.

![Figure 2.1 Fashwave intro of Martin Sellner’s series on Guillaume Faye’s Why We Fight. ¶ Source: Martin Sellner’s English YouTube Channel.](images/Figure0097-01.jpg)

Figure 2.1 Fashwave intro of Martin Sellner’s series on Guillaume Faye’s Why We Fight. ¶ *Source:* Martin Sellner’s English YouTube Channel.

This opening sequence could be read through Faye’s Archeofuturism as a blend of nostalgia and futurism. With it, Sellner taps into a dominant nostalgia among the youth. Nostalgia, as is richly documented, is a key part of capitalist consumer societies. Interestingly, since the nineties of the last century, that nostalgia is not only very much present in advertisements, but the object of nostalgia changed fundamentally. Appadurai argued that ads increasingly:

> Create what might be called “imagined nostalgia,” nostalgia for things that never were. This imagined nostalgia thus inverts the temporal logic of fantasy (which tutors the subject to imagine what could or might happen) and creates much deeper wants than simple envy, imitation, or greed could by themselves invite.
> 
> (1996: 77)

Sellner is indeed tapping into such an imagined nostalgia designed for uptake among 20 to 30-year-olds who see the eighties and nineties as ‘the past’ and 98as an epitome of coolness. It is not a coincidence that a lot of clothing and also nineties TV shows are coming back just now. Also, implicitly, it harks back to a time were most television shows – think of Friends or even Miami Vice – are mostly dominated by a heteronormative and white cast. Ergo, this vaporwave aesthetic frames his series on metapolitics through the opening sequence as something relevant for the youth, and relevant to find one’s true identity. What that identity is, and how to find it or fight for it becomes clear in the videos. In the introduction video of the series, Sellner makes it explicit why the idea of metapolitics, as Faye introduces it, is important. He argues that he sees two trends among new activists that he considers very negative. The first one is:

> A radicalisation spiral, of people who think the most edgiest thing, the thing that is provoking the most, that is creating the most reactions in the internet in a comment or in a post, is the most courageous, the most true, the smartest thing to do.
> 
> ([Sellner, 2017a](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_79))

Sellner disagrees: ‘I don’t think that is true’. ‘The other spiral’, he identifies, ‘is an opportunistic spiral, people who just want to pander to the mainstream’ ([Sellner, 2017a](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_79)). Both spirals, according to Sellner, show a lack ‘of strategic understanding, of metapolitics’. That’s why he dedicates this series of vlogs to Faye’s book. If we want to help establish an ‘archeofuturistic future’, says Sellner, we need ‘to school ourselves and that is why I will present this book’ ([Sellner, 2017a](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_79)).

Identity is the first concept that Sellner picks out of Faye’s metapolitical dictionary as the stuff that can inform new identitarian activists. The first video is dedicated to the ‘Identity’-lemma. Sellner calls the lemma on Identity in Faye’s metapolitical dictionary ‘prophetic’ and subscribes to the idea that culture is ‘ethnic’, that it ‘can’t be detached from the people that created it’ ([Sellner, 2017b](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_80)). Culture and identity are imagined to be grounded in ‘biology’, and thus in race. Humanity is ‘not universal, one united forum and then there are some superficial differences. No, the differences are very deep and very essential. (…) humanity is pluralistic’ ([Sellner, 2017b](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_80)). Pluralism, identity, humanity and metapolitics are thus understood in a biological and racial frame and echo Herder’s pluralism. In his copy of ‘Why We Fight’, shown in the vlog, Sellner has written an exclamation mark next to two paragraphs. In those paragraphs, Faye argues that the ‘European Identity is (…) neutralised, emptied of substance’ in contrast to ‘African, West Indian, and Arab-Muslim identities’ that are being ‘encouraged’ ([Faye, 2011](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_29): 172). Sellner reads those passages in full in his vlog, and of course immediately links this with Generation Identity’s battle for maintaining the European identity and against the replacement. ‘We, as identitarianists, we cherish this (identity), 99while globalists (…) want to deny this, to overcome this’ ([Faye, 2011](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_29): 172). Not only does Sellner subscribe to Faye’s definition of identity, but he also defines the actual goal of Generation Identity and their strategy in line with Faye’s focus and even explicitly reproduces his actual words and writings, but he does that in a whole new context and to a whole new audience: young English speaking identitarians.

The second vlog is entirely focused on the idea of metapolitics. ‘Metapolitics’, says Sellner, ‘is a very important concept for us, as we define ourselves as a metapolitical movement’ ([Sellner, 2017b](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_80)). Sellner’s introduction of Faye’s lemma on ‘metapolitics’ is immediately connected to the fundamental goal of the identitarian movement: the fight for European identity. In the vlog, Sellner not only shares Faye’s understanding of metapolitics and his critique on the ‘too metapolitical strategy of GRECE’, he explicitly takes up his copy of *Archeofuturism* to read Faye’s ([2011](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_29): 29) claim that GRECE overlooked the fact that Gramsci’s cultural battle was linked to the political and economic battle of the communist party. Just like Johnson and more in general the American alt-right, Sellner not only subscribes to Faye’s critique *of La Nouvelle Droite*, he stresses that his own movement – Generation Identity – has learned from those failures. In Austria, Sellner says, the intellectual right was purely metapolitical and distinct from the activist right. ‘Brain and fist’ were separated from each other. Generation Identity, he says, is the first movement to follow Faye’s advice to ‘unite brain and fist’ ([Sellner, 2017c](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_81)).

New identitarian activists are thus advised to move beyond ‘pure intellectual metapolitics’, to unite brain and fist to fight for identity and against ‘globalism’ ([Sellner, 2017d](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_82)) and ‘individualism, the poison of the West’([Sellner, 2017e](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_83)). Metapolitics is – according to Sellner, key here: activism, politics and cultural activity should all be seen as ‘part of that Ancient battle for ideas’([Sellner, 2017e](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_83)). A battle that Sellner, just like Faye, *La Nouvelle Droite* and the anti-Enlightenment tradition, in general, directs against the idea of ‘the primacy of the individual’ and society as ‘based on a social contract’ ([Sellner, 2017e](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_83)). ‘The essence of society’, Sellner counterargues with references to Schmitt and Spengler, ‘is the community, not the individual. It is the primacy of the community’ ([Sellner, 2017e](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_83)). As always, the emancipation of the individual and his rights, the primacy of this individual and materialism are understood as part of that attack on the good society. ‘Modernism and individualism are replacing organic communities and replacing them with abstract systems and an atomized version of humanity’ ([Sellner, 2017e](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_83)).

The ideas of the French new right, especially in Faye’s version, are re-emerging in the second decennium of the 21st century in new digital practices, new forms of activism deeply embedded in the (mainstream) digital economy ([Maly, 2019a](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_63)) and in complex forms of activism addressing new audiences. ‘Archeofuturism’ and ‘Why We Fight’ are not only products of their time,

## Guillaume Faye and the birth of metapolitics 2.0

Guillaume Faye’s role in the popularization of metapolitics, and especially the broadening of metapolitics from a purely intellectual practice to a broad ideological battle carried by a wide range of different actors, has played a key role in the genealogy of metapolitics 2.0. The rise of new right activists, intellectuals, movements and parties in the 21st century is not only connected to the digital economy and the digital literacy of the metapolitical activists but also to Faye’s conceptualization of metapolitics and the archeofuturistic future. His celebrity intellectual status within the global new right and the global praise after his death underline this legacy (Maly, 2022). Faye is not only an agent provocateur or a radical messenger of de Benoist ideas but also an educator. His identitarianism is a new blend of anti-Enlightenment ([Sternhell, 2010](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_93)), reactionary modernist, conservative revolutionary and *Nouvelle Droite* ideas repackaged in a new discourse, advocating new strategies, imaginaries and providing a new generation with a new geopolitical horizon and practical advice.

Generation Identity, but also key figures of the alt-right like Richard Spencer, Greg Johnson and Jared Taylor, are his living legacy: they have appropriated or re-entextualized his ideas in new practices, new battles and new contexts directing them to new audiences. Spencer even explicitly labelled himself an archeofuturist (Hawely, 2017: 65). It is in this uptake that we see why analysing ideology should not be limited to classic texts of intellectuals but should take Thompson’s lessons on board and also analyse uptake, distribution and reproduction of these ideologies within a new digital ecology. This focus on the uptake and the morphing of ideological reproduction allows us to avoid the fallacy of internalism and direct attention to an empirical understanding of the impact and meaning in society. It also forces us to take the infrastructure itself into account ([Maly, 2022a](#C_009_c2.xhtml#r2_71)).

When we do that, we not only realize that metapolitics has been taken up as a key ingredient of new right groups around the world, but we can see that many of those movements and activists mobilize similar topics and discourses in order to fight that cultural battle. The idea of white genocide or the Great Replacement, the attack on our identity, culture and values, the idea that boomers have destroyed Western society or the fight against political correctness, the left, LGBTQ+ acceptance and migration, they all have become standard discourse ingredients of the far-right around the 101world. Metapolitics 2.0 is fundamentally different than *La Nouvelle Droite*’s conception of metapolitics. Metapolitics 2.0 is co-constructed by the affordances and interfaces of digital media: it is an effect of the uptake of a broader conception of metapolitics as advocated by Guillaume Faye and the integration in digital cultures facilitated by the digital utopianism ideologies underpinning major digital media platform. As a result, metapolitics has been ‘democratized’: not only intellectuals engage in metapolitics, but also activists, influencers, movements and politicians. The metapolitical strategies of new right actors are not only visible in the classic metapolitical structures influenced by *La Nouvelle Droite*, but are embedded and enabled by digital cultures. Metapolitics can now also be found in blogs and vlogs, memes, podcasts and influencer culture and in offline practices influenced by digital culture. In the next chapters, we will further unpack metapolitics 2.0 by zooming in on metapolitical activism ([Chapter 3](#C_010_c3.xhtml)), metapolitical influencers ([Chapter 4](#C_011_c4.xhtml)) and conspiracy theories ([Chapter 5](#C_012_c5.xhtml)). In [Chapter 6](#C_013_c6.xhtml) we focus on the offline impact of this new metapolitical digital culture.
