# 3 The global new right and the algorithmic activism of Schild & Vrienden

DOI: [10.4324/9781003283379-4](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003283379-4)

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

In the previous chapter, I showed how *La Nouvelle Droite’s* metapolitics as an ideological project has been taken up by activists in Europe and the United States. I first showed the historical context of metapolitics and subsequently stressed the processes of re-entextualization in which metapolitics slowly but surely was expanded to include new strategies and new actors. Metapolitics 2.0, as I call it, was profoundly mediated by Guillaume Faye. In this chapter, I will argue that contemporary new right metapolitics not only binds together different generations of actors but also different actors around the world ([Johnson, 2012](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_39); [Hawley, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_33); [Nagle, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_67); [Maly, 2018d](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_51)). Several scholars have highlighted the translocal and global dimensions of contemporary far-right groups, activists and even far-right terrorism ([Miller-Idriss, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_64); [Maly, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_48), [2018b](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_49); [Auger, 2020](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_4); [Caniglia, Winkler & Métais, 2020](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_13)). This seems paradoxical, as the new and far-right is usually associated with an anti-globalist position. I will therefore start by analysing new right discourse on globalization and arguing why we should abandon methodological nationalism, and start analysing the contemporary new right from a global context. The digital media ecology, I argue, not only allowed for the globalization of metapolitical commitment, strategies and practices, but it also reshaped them, and maybe more importantly, it gave birth to a global new right culture. Metapolitics 2.0 is one of the global ingredients of the contemporary new right.

## Globalization, globalism and the global new right

Already in the nineties, new right intellectuals and far-right politicians used the rupture caused by cultural or neoliberal globalization to mobilize 108people for national, regional, anti-liberal, racist and especially anti-left stances ([Blommaert & Verschueren, 1998](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_12); [Kriesi et al., 2008](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_43); [Wodak et al., 2014](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_98)). In a widely read and translated paper, Alain de Benoist tapped into the anti-globalist left of the nineties and the first decade of the 21st century and argued ([de Benoist, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_19): 125) that globalization, ‘through a flood of universal images and sounds, (…) contributes to the standardization of lifestyles, to the reduction of differences and particularities, the conformity of attitudes and behaviours, the eradication of collective identities and traditional cultures’. Globalization is here understood as a process of homogenization – and not in left-wing terms as imperialistic, causing exploitation and inequality – driven by ‘egalitarianism, the reducer of the world’s diversity’. The anti-globalization discourse is in essence directed towards a specific form of globalization. It does this by adapting popular theories on globalization as a McDonaldization (see for instance the bestselling book from [Barber \[1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_5)\] on Jihad vs McWorld) and thus linking to mainstream popular knowledge about globalization. This so-called anti-globalism discourse is a dominant narrative among contemporary new right activists. It is paradoxically globalized and has become one of the global characteristics of the global new right. The success of this anti-globalism discourse is not only due to the preparatory work of *La Nouvelle Droite* but also the result of contemporary new right actors like Lana Lokteff, Brittany Pettibone, The Golden One, Lauren Southern, Millennial Woes and many others who have global reach and are globally connected that spread it around in different niches. Of course, Donald Trump ([Blommaert, 2019b](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_9)) and many other figures with access to the mainstream have certainly contributed to the further popularity and mainstreaming of this discourse.

Contrary to most popular and new right literature on globalization in the nineties of the 20th century, many fine-grained ethnographic studies contradict the growth of a so-called homogenizing global monoculture, or in more popular terms, the McDonaldization of the world (see for instance [Pennycook, 2012](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_70)). Mature theories on cultural globalization see it as a plurality of imagined worlds ([Appadurai, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_1): 5), and the imagination of the collective through every day (mediated) practices is more and more diversified, transnational or even post-national. Even more, it is not necessarily ethnic or national anymore ([Maly, Blommaert, & Ben Yakoub, 2014](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_63)). Culture in post-digital and globalized times is best understood as ‘a more “niched” complex of processes, developing at different scale-levels, some of them truly global, but most of them regional, national or even sub-national’. ([Blommaert, 2010](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_7): 77). The truly global world of the elites, the business people and the top politicians and diplomats do impact ordinary life and usually falls beyond the reach of the common man. This scale level is highly exclusive and powerful, but globalization is more than that. Globalization also works on lower scales – the vernacular globalization that Appadurai spoke about – 109and takes the form of translocal networks of locally embedded groups that are jointly producing culture in networks ([Castells, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_14)). The global new right is, as we have seen, paradoxically an example of this. Digitalization has a central role in this globalization of the new right. The new generation of new right intellectuals and activists use digital media not only to engage in a metapolitical battle, or to organize offline protest, but digital media form a crucial infrastructure that allows activists to educate themselves, to network, to build culture and to shape their activism. Digital media allowed far-right activists to learn from each other, and as a result, a global new right network and culture was born.

### Understanding the globalization of the new right

Global culture shouldn’t be understood as a synonym for a homogeneous culture on a global scale. Contrary to what popular parlance and new right theories on globalization want us to believe, globalization or globalism doesn’t produce a homogenization of culture, a global monoculture (See Blommaert, 2011 for a detailed discussion), but a world of countless cultural niches operating on different scales. The global new right culture is one of those cultural niches. And within that niche, we see a complex web of different centres of normativity operating on different scales. The result is a layered, transnational and polycentric culture that preconfigures the new right world order. Material and symbolic ties within that cultural niche are very real, but they are only real in unpredictable and complex ways that beg for detailed analysis. The contemporary new right is thus not a swarm of individuals, reacting autonomously but synchronized, they are structured networked publics around sites, think tanks, intellectuals, influencers, movements and activists who lead them, sometimes as reluctant leaders ([Gerbaudo, 2014](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_30)), sometimes taking up the role of leader. This new right global cultural niche is not unique, but a typical product of globalization processes facilitated by digital media and rising mobility.

In order to analyse and grasp the full meaning of contemporary new right metapolitics, I employ a global perspective that focusses on the mobility of resources and the layeredness of activism. In short, I argue that if we truly want to understand new right metapolitical activism in the 21st century, we need to overcome ‘methodological nationalism’. Research on politics, and in particular on nationalism and the far-right, to a large extent, still displays ‘methodological nationalism (…) the assumption that the nation/state/society is the natural social and political form of the modern world’ **(**[Wimmer & Glick Schiller, 2002](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_96)). Even though there are reasons to do that in far-right research (the regional and national claims for instance), we should realize that methodological nationalism blurs the fact that the world has always been transnational and turns a blind eye to the impact of cellular systems 110([Appadurai, 2006](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_2): 27) in the construction of the contemporary (political) world. More importantly, it blurs the fact that globalization is actually used for nationalist and regionalist goals. Miller-Idriss ([2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_64): 132), for instance, argues that ‘many of these nationalist movements have distinctly and strikingly global aspects’ as a result of the ‘rapid transformation in communication and knowledge sharing across national boundaries’.

Methodological nationalism ignores globalization as context in meaning-making processes and thus in culture production. Contextualizing national and regional new right practices and discourses is crucial to understand the contemporary new right. Miller-Idriss describes the effect of globalization in terms of ‘deterritorialization’: far-right activists can now ‘align, cooperate, communicate, and support each other across national contexts’ ([Miller-Idriss, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_64): 134). Miller-Idriss rightfully focuses on the global and mobility of meanings, but at the same time, she seems to overstate the ‘de- territorialisation’ and the ‘de-contextualization’ that globalization and digital media cause. Even though I fully support Miller-Idriss’ plea to move beyond a national or an international comparative approach and thus focus on the global and effects of mobility on meaning-making, I do think that a sociolinguistic approach to culture and globalization can deepen our understanding of far-right cultures and practices in the 21st century, and provide a more empirical and detailed account of the effects of globalization on far-right culture. The starting point in such an approach is that mobility of signs and discourses is not ‘a mobility across empty spaces, but mobility across space filled with codes, customs, rules, expectations and so forth’ ([Blommaert, 2005](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_6): 73). This in practice means that signs are never fully de-contextualized or de-territorialized: they are used in those contexts and thus filled and shaped according to the norms, codes, rules and expectations of their users.

The rise of digitalization and mobility since the nineties of the 20th century has created a juncture visible in the scale, intensity and scope of globalization processes ([Appadurai, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_1); Arnaut et al., 2016). Migration and digital media have not only reshaped our imagination of the world ([Appadurai, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_1): 3), they also enabled the democratization of global (cultural) flows. Whereas in non-digital times, the transnational dimension of politics was to a large extent embedded in the networks of national political elites and vertebrate ‘inter-national’ organizations, this has changed in the last decades ([Appadurai, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_1): 32; [Maly, Blommaert & Ben Yakoub, 2014](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_63)). Today, digital media function as infrastructures that enable and structure global networked activist movements **(**[Klein 2002](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_42), 4; [Wolfson, 2014](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_99); [Tufekci, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_88)). The rising importance of global networks, cellular systems and global cultural and political flows are emblematic of this latest phase of globalization and are largely undertheorized when it comes to new right activism. By taking on board a sociolinguistic theory of globalization (see Blommaert, 2011), I will 111analyse the Flemish identitarian movement Schild & Vrienden from a global perspective, but first I want to shed some light on digital media and the global flows in contemporary far-right culture.

## Metapolitics 2.0 and the global new right

Whereas the far-right has always used digital media to propagate their ideologies ([Winter 2019](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_97); [Weimann & Masri, 2020](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_94)), we have seen that the adoption of the metapolitical strategy has changed the form and the strategies that are being used today. Even the actors themselves have changed: metapolitics has been democratized. From highbrow far-right intellectual work, it has now morphed into a broad rhizomatic network of actors (re)producing far-right ideas in many different forms using many different channels and addressing many different (niched) audiences. These changes have had fundamental effects, not only on the metapolitical battle itself but also on the structure and scale on which far-right actors operate. The affordances of digital media have shaped and facilitated the globalization of new right actors. Some of those actors work on a local scale, others on a national or European scale, and some of them operate on a truly global scale. Martin Sellner for instance is not only a prominent member of the Austrian chapter of Generation Identity, but he also plays a crucial role on a European and even a global scale. A similar argument can be made about a key figure like The Golden One (see [Chapter 3](#C_010_c3.xhtml#c3)). This far-right bodybuilder and influencer may be located in Sweden, but his uptake is global and is explicitly designed for global uptake. Alexander Dugin is another example. The Russian new right philosopher merged GRECE and the Traditionalism of Julius Evola for the Russian market, but at the same time, he has become one of the most influential new right intellectuals on a global scale. He is invited to congresses around the world, interviewed by mass media and translated and distributed by Arktos. In the 21st century, the new right is a polycentric, layered and transnational new right network ([Maly, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_48)). This network was in the last years the object of increasing academic attention and has been labelled as the international alt-right ([Hermansson, Lawrence, Mulhall & Murdoch, 2020](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_35)), new right 2.0 ([Watson & Barnes, 2022](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_93)) or the European-American radical right ([François, 2019](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_27)). All those labels describe the transnationalization of the contemporary far-right and the legacy of *La Nouvelle Droite* on that transnational scale. I choose to use the label global new right for four reasons:

1.  In my analysis, the alt-right is tied to activism that is first and foremost connected to the advancement of new right metapolitics in the United States. This movement in itself is indeed an international network (see [Figure 3.1](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_1)), but the focus of that network – even though it has received global uptake – is first and foremost the United States.
    
    ![Figure 3.1 Network analysis Alt-right 2017 – Copyright: Ico Maly. Return to text.⏎](images/Figure0118-01.jpg)
    
    Figure 3.1 Network analysis Alt-right 2017 – Copyright: Ico Maly. [Return to text.⏎](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_1b)
    
2.  112The alt-right itself is more effectively and correctly described as a deglobalization of the European new right. The alt-right is (was) an important centre within the global new right, but it was certainly not the only centre, nor the only important one, nor the first one.
3.  The theories of the intellectuals of *La Nouvelle Droite* are – as I argued in the previous chapter – the ideological roots of contemporary movements that are described by those labels. In all actions of contemporary new right movements and actors around the world, we see the metapolitical injection of *La Nouvelle Droite*. This injection does not limit itself to Europe or the United States. Dugin for instance has appropriated it in Russia, dreaming of a Eurasian empire.
4.  The metapolitical strategy of *La Nouvelle Droite* is one of the elements that creates unity in this global movement. Metapolitics has been globalized, meaning that the new right battle for culture has taken roots in many different countries of the world. It was a global injection that was subsequently deglobalized by local actors like the alt-right in the United States, Generation Identitaire in France or Schild & Vrienden in Belgium.
5.  The different activists, sites, intellectuals and influencers form a truly global network. They read, share and support work from each other and use it to legitimize local and translocal goals. The Golden One reads *La Nouvelle Droite*, promotes Arktos books, is invited to congresses in the Ukraine and is viewed from all corners of the world.
6.  The ideas and the battle of the contemporary new right are explicitly global in nature. They do not just imagine a national world, they fight for a new world order. They call it a pluriversum, an ethno-plural world or and multipolar world. The crux is that they do not limit themselves to nationalism, but they think in terms of civilizations and empires. They think, but as we will see, also act, on a global scale.

The global new right is in this sense a far more precise term. The global new right refers to all those sites, publishers, conferences, activists, politicians, intellectuals, influencers and media sites operating as centres of normativity. What binds them is their resistance against the ‘modern world’, the egalitarianism that supports contemporary cultural globalization. They fight democracy, universal human rights, liberalism and socialism, and fight for a second modernity based on the rights of people, organicism and tradition. Not globalization is the main enemy, but globalism: the neoliberal form of contemporary globalization.

### Arktos and the globalization of anti-globalism

Far-right publishing house Arktos is an excellent case to understand this alternative form of globalization. Arktos was founded in 2009 and launched in 1132010, and is now the ‘largest retailer of radical right literature in the world’ ([Teitelbaum, 2019](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_84): 270). Arktos is the inheritor of Integral Tradition Publishing, a Danish publishing company which started in 2005, and Nordiska Föglaget, the far-right publishing house of Nordiska Fördbundete. Integral Tradition Publishing started as an online bookstore and publishing company specializing in occult books and texts on mysticism that promoted traditionalist and esoteric worldviews ([Valencia-Garcia, 2020](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_89)). The Nordiska Fördbundet publishing house was Daniel Friberg’s first attempt to set up a metapolitical publishing house and media empire ([Teitelbaum, 2019](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_84): 265). It is thus not a coincidence that Arktos, as a fusion of those publishers, claims not to propagate

> any specific ideology, a system of beliefs or viewpoint, nor do we seek consistency. Rather, we want to provide a voice for individuals and viewpoints who are often overlooked by the mainstream, but who offer original and challenging alternatives to our prevailing culture that cannot be found elsewhere.
> 
> (Website Arktos accessed in 2022)

Former editor-in-chief John Morgan also claimed that Arktos is not pushing a specific ideology, but that they do provide ‘alternatives for modernity’ (THA [Talks, 2016](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_85)). The claim not to ‘push an ideology’, is thus not to be mistaken for being neutral, or Arktos being open to each ideology. ‘Ideology’ is here used in the narrow sense, as clear-cut ideologies like liberalism, fascism, or Nazism. Ideologies with clear boundaries. Arktos is an ideological publisher in the sense that it advocates all books that support, feed and shape the anti-Enlightenment tradition. Morgan, for instance, clearly argues that a pro-multiculturalist viewpoint or liberal one would not be considered for publication (THA [Talks, 2016](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_85)). In other words, Arktos is open to several ideologies, as long as they question the current modernity. ‘Our mission is very simple’ says Friberg: ‘to spread the ideas of the most important thinkers of our times as broad as possible’ ([React, 2016](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_73)). The ‘luminary thinkers’ that shape the contemporary anti-Enlightenment tradition promoted by Arktos are amongst others: Alain de Benoist, Guillaume Faye, Pierre Krebs, Alexander Dugin, Julius Evola, Generation Identity, Arthur Moeller van Den Bruck, Charles Maurras, Dominique Venner, H.P. Lovecraft, Markus Willinger, Oswald Spengler, James Kirkpatrick, Daniel Friberg, Jared Taylor, John Bruce Leonard and Koenraad Van Elst. Arktos publishes key thinkers of *La Nouvelle Droite*, contemporary far-right activists like (Markus Willinger, Generation Identity, Jared Taylor), Traditionalists (Julius Evola, Alexander Dugin) and Conservative Revolutionaries (Oswald Spengler, Charles Maurras). The most important thinkers are explicitly anti-liberal or more in general, anti-materialistic. This explains why Arktos can on the one hand claim to be not 114ideological, and to be proud that it ‘has established itself as the principal publisher in English of the writings of the European “new right” school of political thought’ (Arktos website, last accessed May 2022).

Arktos *de facto* functions as a foundational new right centre of normativity operating on the highest scale of globalization. It is a metapolitical infrastructure providing ideological education to far-right activists and intellectuals around the world. It is also a truly global infrastructure. Arktos itself has set up shops in Sweden, Great Britain, Hungary and India. Its authors come from France, Italy, Belgium, the United States, the UK, Russia, Iran and many other countries. Arktos also publishes in 16 different languages. Most of these languages are European in origin: English, Dutch, Hungarian, Polish, German, Spanish, Czech, Croatian, French, Greek, Italian, Latvian, Portuguese, Serbian, Slovak & Swedish. Next to Red Ice, Arktos is one of the sponsors of the Identitarian Ideas conference and it was a founding partner of the now-defunct website Altright.com. All these initiatives attracted intellectuals, activists and visitors on a global scale. Arktos also doesn’t hide the fact that its operation is global in nature. On the contrary. Not only does Friberg eagerly explain that this international form of Arktos was deliberate ([Teitelbaum, 2019](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_84): 270), ‘making anti-globalism global’ is the official motto of the publisher on their Facebook page. Even more, they also proudly retweeted a cartoon from Ben Garrison with the same slogan shown together with cartoon versions of Alain de Benoist, Guillaume Faye, Daniel Friberg and Alexander Dugin.

Many scholars see this motto as a paradox, a *contradictio in terminis* ([Valencia-Garcia, 2020](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_89): 311). What is missed is that Arktos explicitly rejects ‘globalism’, and not necessarily globalization as such. Globalism is presented as the real enemy. Globalism here refers to a specific form of globalization, one that is associated with Enlightenment, democracy and egalitarianism, with multiculturalism and feminism, and of course with institutions like the EU, the UN and NATO. Interestingly enough, it also refers to the notion of cultural Marxism ([Blommaert, 2019b](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_9)). In other words, globalism indexes the egalitarianism so detested and fought against by *La Nouvelle Droite*, the identitarians and the alt-right. The fight of Arktos aligns with them, not in rejecting globalism in the form of technology, travelling or global connections, but in rejecting the specific form of globalization that is associated with open borders, the great replacement, the attack on tradition and local cultures. Globalism is the name of the ideology – egalitarianism in traditional *Nouvelle Droite* discourse – that shapes contemporary globalization. Arktos is promoting different ideologies that give an alternative to this particular modernism, a different globalization and modernity. The bio on their Facebook page is clear on this:

> Increasingly, people sense that something seems terribly wrong with the modern world. Arktos has been founded to offer such individuals - however 115varied their philosophic and aesthetic inclinations - the resources necessary to discover for themselves a true alternative to the onslaught of modernity.

The alternatives promoted by their authors can range from the radical traditionalism of Julius Evola to Guillaume Faye’s archeofuturism. What connects these authors is a metaphilosophy ([Lievens, 2013](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_45)) that rejects Enlightenment in its contemporary form: the anti-Enlightenment tradition.

Just like the reactionary modernists ([Herf, 1984](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_34)) combined traditional values with the embrace of technology, Arktos, and the contemporary new right in general, embrace technologies for metapolitical goals. In that sense, they are modernists: they do not want to go back to an old pre-technological traditional society; they embrace technologies if it helps to revive traditional values, cultures and languages. It is a common misconception that the far-right’s reactionary politics would entail that they want to go back to a pre-technological era: they, on the contrary, want to fuse tradition and technology. The embrace of technology is realized by undoing the ‘spirit grounding those technologies’ ([Lievens, 2013](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_45)), the spirit of neoliberal globalization and fusing it in an archeofuturistic way, to use Faye’s discourse. All mainstream media are regularly criticized by the new right authors for being liberal, left-wing or cultural Marxist, but at the same time, they try to use them as much as possible. Arktos is a classic example of this fusion. The publisher uses print on-demand to make its business sustainable, it advertises and is present on all major mainstream social media and streaming services like Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and Spotify (with the exception of Twitter where it got banned). It also is present on more alternative niched platforms like Odysee, GAB, VK and Telegram. While all these social media and user-generated platforms are important for the metapolitical quest and the marketing of Arktos books, the most crucial is Arktos’ integration with Amazon. Several Arktos books are distributed by different book sites like Book Depository, Barnes & Noble, Free Speech library and Logik.se, but only Amazon sells them all. Even if you buy books on the website of Arktos, you are forwarded to Amazon. Customers cannot only buy the published books by Arktos there, several Arktos titles are freely available if you have Kindle Unlimited subscription and available as audiobooks on Amazon’s Audible platform. Amazon thus functions, not only as a platform that provides revenue for Arktos, it *de facto* functions as a metapolitical infrastructure.

It should be clear that Arktos knows its way around the globe. It is an example of globalization. Even though Arktos publishes in 16 different languages, English is the lingua franca of the publisher. That is no coincidence as it indexes the intended audience of the publisher and thus its goal to cater to an international far-right market. The translations of the English books index the world order they try to help construct: a multipolar world, but also a world characterized by a shared anti-Enlightenment tradition. This 116specific example of globalization may use the infrastructures of neoliberal globalization, but it does so to build a different form of globalization.

Arktos is an emblematic example of how globalization reshapes the far-right. The result of that interconnected and mediated cultural production is rarely a global monoculture, but is better understood as ‘locality transported in locality’ ([Blommaert, 2010](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_7): 79) through processes of englobalization of local cultures and symbolic forms and deglobalization or re-indigenizing them in other places. This vernacular globalization as Appadurai ([1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_1)) calls it, or translocalisation, connects local groups with the cultural practices of other local groups. The globalization of far-right, new right and anti-liberal margins is such a vernacular globalization that has been enabled by digital media and is operating at one particular scale level, lower than the fully global one: ‘it is the connectedness of small pockets of people located (and “local”) in many different parts of the world’ (Blommaert, 2011: 77). Important here is that these globalized margins are:

1.  Fighting metapolitically to become global on the highest scale, to globalize their ideology in such a way that it organizes/structures the world.
2.  These groups are not necessarily as marginal on a national or regional scale. It is probably not a coincidence that in 2014, Arktos set up its headquarters in Hungary. The same country where the identitarian movement set up its bank account.
3.  The power of these groups is not necessarily stable but can fluctuate as a result of sudden or long-term changes. The alt-right is a case book example. The alt-right, as a result of the electoral victory of Donald Trump, suddenly became an important centre in that global new right network. It not only became highly visible in the global hybrid media system, but it also played – for a relatively short period – a central role in the culture production within this global niche.

### The global new right: transporting locality in locality

As a result of digital media, digital culture and global actors like Arktos, we should seriously question the notion of national new right or Identitarian movements. In [Chapter 2](#C_009_c2.xhtml), we already stressed that globalization is the context in which cultural forms are produced and circulated. Taking globalization seriously as context means that we also have to question the idea of local movements. The idea of ‘local movements’, using local practices and local discourses to fight for local causes, seems more and more a fiction. This was clearly visible on a European scale when we analysed Generation Identity as a pan-European and even trans-Atlantic phenomenon in the previous chapter. This reality seems emblematic of many contemporary new right movements. Even though all new right actors claim to resist globalization, 117universalism and cosmopolitanism, they are touched by the cultural globalization processes. Central to this transnationalization and the construction of this network is the theoretical and methodological renewal of *La Nouvelle Droite* that broke down the integral nationalism of the old right and of course the impact of digitalization. It is through digital media that these new metapolitical actors contribute to the metapolitical project. Digital media not only allow them to connect on a global scale but also allow some intellectuals like Alexander Dugin to operate globally. Dugin, just like Arktos, embraces this and explicitly calls for a ‘conservative internationalism’ that comes together in a fight against ‘modernity’ (Southern, 2018a): he embraces ‘multipolarity’ and therefore pleas for an ‘international of nations vs. the international of the elites’ ([Dugin, 2021](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_25): 32). It is in these global networks that they share cultural products and are involved in processes of joint cultural production.

The global new right illustrates, contrary to their own narrative on globalization, the point Appadurai already stressed in the nineties: ‘globalization is not the story of cultural homogenization’ ([Appadurai, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_1): 11); it transports locality into locality. The deglobalization and indignation of the Pepe meme already made this point clear. This can be further demonstrated by zooming in on the alt-right as a movement, and more generally on the cultural impact of the alt-right within the global new right. The alt-right, as a local American centre within the global new right, was responsible for producing very specific discursive materials (memes, podcasts, vlogs) and practices (trolling, algorithmic activism) to further a new right agenda. Even though the uptake of these practices was global ([Maly, 2018e](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_52)), the practices and discourses were, as we have seen, not instances of a global monoculture within the far-right niche. Memes and trolling practices were not just shared or copied, they were deglobalized by local actors who re-entextualize them and use them in different forms and with different meanings in a local metapolitical battle. And the alt-right itself was also not ‘a local’ network. Let’s unpack these two arguments.

The alt-right movement itself gradually came into existence as a polycentric network. This network was embedded in all kinds of far-right media (Counter-Currents, Vdare, Taki Magazine, The Daily Stormer, TakiMagazine, Occidental Observer), think tanks (American Renaissance, National Policy Institute), publishers (Arktos, Radix), congresses (New York Forum, Amren conference), and fora (see [Figure 3.1](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_1)), and of course mainstream digital media like YouTube and Facebook. All these online and offline infrastructures were used as ‘metapolitical instruments’ and resemble the type of organizations new right movements have set up all over Europe in the 20th and 21st centuries ([Griffin, 2000](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_32); cfe. [Salzborn, 2016](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_75)). At the same time, we see that new actors emerge in the metapolitical battle of the alt-right: trolls, influencers and Twitter activists using mainstream digital media to further the metapolitical battle. What has been labelled as ‘the alt-right’ was in reality different cells, 118media, boards, groups and individual actors of the alt-right into a networked movement: ‘it is a many-headed hydra made up of a collection of figures and groups, none of which fully control the loose movement’s direction’ (Hermansson, Lawrence, Mulhall & Murdoch, 2019). This movement was united in some actions under hashtags such as #altright and #cuckservative in their discursive battle to get Trump elected ([Hawley, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_33); [Maly, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_53)). Even though these cells frame themselves as promoting an extreme-right alternative to the neoliberal and neoconservative Republican party and globalization (or globalism in their lingo; [Hawley, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_33); [Nagle, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_67); [Maly, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_53)), it is important to realize that this networked movement has global dimensions.

1.  First of all, different actors and cells in that networked movement are not based in the United States (Arktos is operating from London and Hungary, Weev from The Daily Stormer lives in Europe and Red Ice is partly based in Sweden).
2.  Second, in setting up these infrastructures and defining their metapolitical goal, several alt-right key figures like Richard Spencer, Greg Johnson or Daniel Friberg explicitly claimed to find inspiration in *La Nouvelle Droite.*
3.  The digital infrastructure they use in their battle is clearly global in nature. This is, as we have seen after Charlottesville, not a detail. On the contrary, the success and impact of the alt-right were clearly connected to their integration into the mainstream. It is also the digital media that allowed for the global impact of the alt-right.

119From this global perspective, alt-right figures like Greg Johnson and Richard Spencer, the radical right publishing house Arktos and identitarian activists are best understood as contemporary *indiginizations*, or re-territorializations, of the metapolitical and ideological agenda of *La Nouvelle Droite*. The alt-right for instance exists, according to John Morgan (editor of the radical right publishing house Arktos), first and fore most as ‘a culture primarily of blogs, memes, podcasts, and videos’, which he claims is the ‘natural outgrowth of the anti-intellectualism inherent in Anglo-American political and cultural discourse (…)’ ([Morgan, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_65)). In other words, the elitist intellectual battle of *La Nouvelle Droite* transformed into a digital culture battle carried by memes, soundbites, tweets and hashtags. This local alt-right culture was in turn taken up by other movements in other corners of the planet where the de-contextualization process starts again.

One of the most successful metapolitical instruments of the alt-right was the appropriation of the meme and the embeddedness of the metapolitical battle in the ongoing culture war between 4channers and the normies after Gamergate ([Nagle, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_67): 24). This memification of the metapolitical battle for the ideals of the conservative revolution caused a global uptake and subsequent renewal of the metapolitical battle, first in the United States, but very soon on a global scale. This very specific repertoire of collective action – deeply embedded in the contemporary algorithmically determined public space – was very quickly adopted by new right and Identitarian cells around the world.

In 2016 and 2017, Pepe the Frog memes were, as we have seen, a successful export product. In [Figure 3.2](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_2), you can see how the profile pic of the Flemish meme page ‘De Fiere Vlaamse Meme’ (The proud Flemish meme) uses Pepe in a local Flemish context (see [Figure 3.2](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_2)). Pepe the Frog is here positioned on a shield. On top we see Pepe wearing what resembles a war helmet from the Middle Ages and what appears to be a ‘Goedendag’, a weapon originally used by the militias of Medieval Flanders. Below Pepe, we see the Flemish region with the Flemish flag. On the border of the shield we read ‘1302 E Meme Divisie – Schild en Vriend’. The date 1302 refers to the old Flemish nationalist myth about the so-called ‘Brugse metten’ in 1302. In this myth, the social conflict dimension of this historical battle is downplayed to frame it as the first legendary Flemish nationalist battle against the French. ‘Schild & Vriend’ was used as a shibboleth to be able to identify the French enemies ([Tollebeek, 1999](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_87)). By choosing the baseline *Schild & Vriend*, the page positions itself in a very long tradition of Flemish nationalist politics. The E Meme Divisie probably refers to Electronic Meme Division and is clearly inspired by alt-right meming and trolling practices. Pepe is mobilized for the Flemish nationalist cause, without of course fully erasing his ‘edgy history’ in the United States. The sign itself has different layers of meaning that need to be peeled away. Whereas Pepe indexes contemporary internet 120culture and alt-right metapolitics, the words ‘Schild en Vriend’, the Flemish flag and 1302 refer to a very different spatio-temporal frame. We thus see the synchronization of different digital practices and different chronotopes in one movement.

![Figure 3.2 Profile picture of far-right Facebook meme group De Fiere Vlaamse Meme 2017 (The Proud Flemish Meme). Return to text.⏎ ¶ Source: https://www.facebook.com/defierevlaamse.](images/Figure0120-01.jpg)

Figure 3.2 Profile picture of far-right Facebook meme group De Fiere Vlaamse Meme 2017 (The Proud Flemish Meme). [Return to text.⏎](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_2b) ¶ *Source:* [https://www.facebook.com/defierevlaamse](https://www.facebook.com/defierevlaamse).

These semiotic resources are not only de-territorialized as Miller-Idress argues, but they are also constantly re-territorialized and re-contextualized. In many local American and non-American activist discourses, we will see materials and strategies reflected from other activists in other places. Not as generic or de-territorialized resources but as re-entextualizations and re-territorialized materials. These resources are all indexes of the systematic global nature of this type of metapolitics, and thus also of the specific world order they try to build. Note also how this layeredness of metapolitical memes has phatic effects (Varis & Blommaert & [Varis, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_91)). The identarian activist group Schild & Vrienden was born out of the Flemish nationalist and new right meme page (Ceder, 2017) and connections with radical right student fraternities. It is their adoption of these far-right memes, and their 121schooling by Generation Identitaire, that allowed them to construct not only a new type of activist movement on a local scale but also connect different (individual) actors, movements and cells from different corners of the world, and thus contribute to a feeling of belonging and a shared group identity that transverses national boundaries. New right memes contribute to an imagination of a networked global new right community.

This meme page, along with many other actors operating on different scales in different countries make up the global new right. The global new right is thus not only a layered, polycentric and transnational niche in which practices and discourses are produced and distributed. It is also a very productive cultural learning environment where groups or individual activists are not only rapidly exchanging cultural products and discourses enabling learning from each other, but also helping each other in metapolitical battles. The result is that even seemingly local activism is deeply influenced by this global layered and polycentric cultural niche. I will illustrate this in more detail by analysing the above-mentioned Flemish Identitarian movement Schild & Vrienden.

## The global new right and Schild & Vrienden's metapolitics

On March 3, 2018, ‘Schild & Vrienden’ organized an activist intervention to derail ludic protests by civil society organizations at the Gravensteen Castle in Ghent, Belgium. This Flemish far-right Identitarian movement was born out of the meme page – De Fiere Vlaamse Meme – where youngsters from different Flemish nationalist student unions (National Student Union \[NSV\] and Catholic Flemish High Student Union \[KVHV\]) and youth divisions of political parties (the extreme-right Flemish Interest \[VB\] and the radical right New Flemish Alliance \[N-VA\]) found each other. They stormed the castle because civil society organizations were protesting the ‘inhuman European migration policies’ ([GentInsight, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_29)). Schild & Vrienden showed up with 20–30 activists. They pulled down the giant European flag hanging on the wall of the castle and filmed their intervention. This video material was later edited into a 3-min clip and uploaded on the Schild & Vrienden Facebook page. The video immediately went viral. Before that uptake, the offline intervention already generated visibility in mass media ([EDG, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_26); [VTM Nieuws, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_92)) and right-wing partisan media ([Decker, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_22); [‘Schild & Vrienden Activists Took Action’, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_77)), which helped their video post go viral.

Attention even multiplied after Schild & Vrienden’s Facebook video was deleted and different right-wing media framed it as an effect of politically correct censorship ([Decker, 2018b](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_23)). After Facebook banned the movie (in reality because of copyright infringement), Schild & Vrienden reuploaded it with a 122different soundtrack on March 8, 2018, at which point it went viral again. One year later (7 March 2019), this second uploaded video managed to attract 185,000 views, 2,900 interactions, 1,200 shares, and 1,006 comments. These numbers, seen from a Flemish or Belgian perspective, are impressive. At face value, they suggest a huge fan-base. No wonder the post triggered massive mainstream media attention in Flanders (23 articles in the Flemish press in May 2018) and put them on the radar of (far-) right-wing outlets around the world like the Gateway Pundit and Red Ice TV. All this media coverage in turn boosted the fan and follower base of Schild & Vrienden’s Facebook page from around 4,000 to over 10,000 in a couple of days (May 2018). In 2021, they acquired more than 39,000 friends on Facebook, but were also blocked on Twitter and Instagram.

In the rest of this chapter, I will analyse how Schild & Vrienden use digital media for its metapolitical battle. I will argue that the movement successfully exploits the logic of ‘new’ media and old mass media to draw the attention of a broad audience to its message. Reach on social media is used as proof that they articulate ‘the voice of a new Flemish generation conscience about their heritage’. That massive reach is used as part of the populist communicative relation ([Maly, 2018e](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_52)). I will first address the historical situatedness of their activism and their metapolitical strategy. After that, I will show how that metapolitical strategy is adopted in relation to the digital environments by analysing the mediatization of their intervention at the Gravensteen castle in Ghent, Belgium. Concretely, I will use the concept of algorithmic activism ([Maly, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_48), [2018e](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_52)) to stress how Schild & Vrienden not only fights a discursive battle but also uses knowledge of the digital environment to make their message go viral. I will show how the online and offline activism of Schild & Vrienden uses the media logic and affordances of digital media to stretch the so-called Overton window in mainstream media. In summary, I will make the case that their activism should be understood as a metapolitics 2.0. And connected to this, we cannot understand Schild & Vrienden as a local movement.

### Schild & Vrienden and the deglobalization of the global new right

The Facebook page of Schild & Vrienden was established in March 2017. The group, from the start, was hierarchically structured with Dries Van Langenhove, a student at Ghent University, as its leader. Around him circled a core group of 30–40 activists and many less active activists/supporters. Van Langenhove was, after he became famous as the leader of Schild & Vrienden, elected as an independent on the election lists of the extreme-right party Flemish Interest.

On the one hand, Schild & Vrienden was stylized as a Flemish chapter of the pan-European movement Generation Identity ([Maly, 2018d](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_51)). Several 123members of Schild & Vrienden, including Dries Van Langenhove, were trained at the summer university of Generation Identitaire in France in 2015. The movement still has close ties to identitarian movements in Europe and beyond ([Maly, 2019a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_54)). Van Langenhove, especially after Schild & Vrienden was exposed on television as racist, anti-Semitic and extreme-right, was very open about their support for Generation Identity. The activism-format that Schild & Vrienden uses is clearly modelled on the successfully mediatized activist interventions of Identitarian movements in France, Germany, and Austria. Short, controversial, and small-scale offline interventions are mediatized on social media to generate attention, build an audience, and intervene in the public debate.

On the other hand, Schild & Vrienden drew inspiration (see [Maly, 2018d](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_51)) from the meme-culture of the alt-right movement. Not only did they post memes on their Facebook page, but Schild & Vrienden was also embedded in a whole network of Facebook pages (e.g., Make Vlaenderen Great Again, De Fiere Vlaamse Memes, or Departement Der Vlaemsche Memes) dedicated to spreading ‘new right’ Flemish nationalist memes in general, and supporting Schild & Vrienden and Dries Van Langenhove in particular ([Maly, 2018d](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_51)).

At the heart of this type of activism is the idea of metapolitics. Van Langenhove describes his movement as follows: ‘Schild & Vrienden defends the interests of the Flemish youth. We are doing this independently from political parties. We are a metapolitical movement, online as well as offline’ ([Patyn, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_69)). Just like in other movements, metapolitics is used by Schild & Vrienden to refer to not only a cultural battle, but also an anti-Enlightenment battle. These ideological ingredients are fully visible in Schild & Vrienden. As we shall see, key topics that are addressed on the Facebook page are the Flemish nation and ‘the replacement of white autochthone Flemings’. Anti-left, anti-migration, anti-Islam, and anti-political correctness – discourses tackling the ‘fake news of mainstream media’, digital media ‘censorship’, ‘identity politics’, and LGBTQ+ issues are abundantly found. In this sense, Schild & Vrienden resembles the Identitarian new right movements in Europe, the United States, and the rest of the world. The stickers that they sell in their web shop are a good indication of their ideological positioning. They sell stickers with alt-right slogans (‘White Lives Matter’, It’s Okay to be White), classic Flemish nationalist (*Linkse ratten, rol uw matten* \[leftists rats, get out\], Leuven Vlaams \[*Leuven Flemish*\]), translations of French identitarian slogans (Zekere Grenzen, zekere toekomst), and an adaptation of Trump’s election slogan: ‘Make Vlaenderen Great Again’. The Identitarian and alt-right slogans are accompanied by stickers framing legacy media as fake news and other anti-left and anti-Islam discourse.

What is remarkable in the light of metapolitics is that Schild & Vrienden in the first instance tried to position the movement as ‘positive’ by avoiding 124‘far-right’ connotations. In all mass media interviews, Van Langenhove stressed that Schild & Vrienden ‘wants to tell a positive story’ (Ceder, 2017 (my translation)). Central in that ‘positive story’ is the stress on the Flemish identity and its culture: ‘We want to create a resilient Flemish youth’, said Van Langenhove,

> And give them a perspective on a future. In our country, there are too much sissies walking around who are afraid of their own shadow. Be proud to be a Fleming, realize that we are only one generation in a long and rich tradition.
> 
> (Ceder, 2017 \[my translation\])

As always, we see that this battle for the future is grounded in nostalgia and a narrative of decline: ‘In the last decennia, Flanders lost track’, stresses Van Langenhove. The reasons why can be expected: ‘Individualism and mass immigration have alienated us from each other. In a land without religion, and a remarkable loss of norms and traditions, it is easy for the youth to lose the meaning of life’ (Ceder, 2017 \[my translation\]). This narrative of decline and nostalgia for a past that never was positions Schild & Vrienden as the rescuer of the Flemish identity and thus its future: ‘With Schild & Vrienden, we want to provide the youth with meaning again. Which greater good is there, than to take care for your family, and your people’ (Ceder, 2017 \[my translation\]).

The discourse strategy of Van Langenhove resembles the political discourse of the National-Flemish Alliance (N-VA) (see [Maly, 2012](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_46), 2016, for a detailed analysis of this discourse) more than the discourse of the extreme-right Flemish nationalist party Flemish Interest (see [Maly, 2020d](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_60)). Just like N-VA, he articulates a ‘soft’ anti-Enlightenment ethno-cultural nationalism ([Sternhell, 2010](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_83); [Maly, 2018b](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_49)) and avoids (a too) explicit blood-and-soil discourse. The fact that the Pano reportage of the public broadcasting company was understood as ‘unmasking Schild & Vrienden’ as extreme-right, racist, and sexist is an index of the success of that message ([Cools, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_17); [Lesaffer, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_44); [SN, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_82)). At the same time, we see that as a consequence of the strategic ambivalence that is so central in the political use of ‘ironic’ memes, whiteness was put central (see for instance the sticker ‘it’s okay to be white’ in the webshop, a reference to the alt-right meme campaign).

This played moderateness shouldn’t surprise us. Metapolitics was always more than just a long-term political-ideological strategy. Metapolitics gave *La Nouvelle Droite* an aura of intellectualism and moderation, despite the very radical anti-Enlightenment nature of their project ([Maly, 2018d](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_51)). Metapolitics was used to position this ‘school of thought’ as ‘new’, and thus 125seemingly different from the ‘old right’.¹ The construction of normality was inherent to the metapolitical strategy that advocated using accepted and even scientific language as vehicles for new right ideas. Hegemonic concepts like democracy, feminism, and antiracism as we have seen were infused with very specific new right meanings (see [de Benoist & Champetier, 2000](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_20)). *Nouvelle Droite* intellectuals like Alain de Benoist, but also contemporary Flemish new right politicians like Bart De Wever (president of N-VA), openly quoted leftist sources and positioned themselves as *ni droite, ni gauche* ([Maly, 2016](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_47)). This metapolitical strategy was from the start also deployed by Schild & Vrienden, who wrapped their anti-Enlightenment discourse in ‘positive’ rhetoric.

The activism of Schild & Vrienden is an excellent case study to show how the global new right functions as a transnational learning environment. Schild & Vrienden is emblematic in this respect and allows me to highlight how contemporary new right movements use the affordances of digital media for their ‘metapolitical battle 2.0’. Their activism can best be seen as a fusion of all three forms of contemporary metapolitics. Digital media are central to this type of activism: they use these digital media to have a voice ([Hymes, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_37)) in a hybrid media system. Growing an audience was thus important. By the end of 2017, the group amassed 3,700 likes and more than 4,000 followers. The fact that by 2019, Schild & Vrienden had 33,000 followers on Facebook, 14,000 on Instagram and 5,687 on Twitter (1 March 2019), shows that they at least succeed in reaching an audience and mobilizing it for metapolitical goals, and thus can be understood as knowledgeable concerning the logics and affordances of new and old media.

An important dimension of this type of activism is the digital literacy of these activists. To engage in metapolitics 2.0, one has to have a very broad range of digital skills and insights. As a collective, they should not only be able to film, edit and design their content, make memes or post statuses, but they also need to have insights into the nature of the digital ecology. Discursive and mobilization power in this hybrid media system is about controlling the information flows in the whole media system ([Chadwick, 2017](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_16): 285). Setting up successful socio-technical activism means that one should understand the contemporary media ecologies. Within these ecologies, popularity is a coded and quantified concept, and as such, it is manipulable ([van Dijck, 2013](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_90): 13). It is this digital notion of popularity that opens a whole new domain of digital activism. I ([Maly, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_48)) called this algorithmic activism: ‘algorithmic activists use (theoretical or practical) knowledge about the relative weight certain signals have within the proceduralized choices the algorithms of the media platforms make as proxies of human judgement, in relation to the goals of the medium itself’ ([Maly, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_48)). This type of activism presupposes that activists not only subscribe 126to the message they interact with but also understand the affordances and the algorithmic construction of the medium. That they understand how interaction – according to the popularity principle – generates visibility. As we shall see, the new right activists of Schild & Vrienden use this knowledge about platforms and algorithms in service of its metapolitical strategy. Metapolitics 2.0 inevitably has an important ‘algorithmic activist’ dimension.

### The metapragmatics of the Gravensteen activism

Let’s return to the central case of this chapter and zoom in on how Schild & Vrienden prepared their content for uptake. First, I shall revisit the video and analyse it at the level of ‘metapragmatics’ ([Jacobs, 1997](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_38)). This metapragmatic approach focuses on the indicators of the producer’s reflexive awareness of its audience and the communicative context. In other words, we can look at the producer’s intended (algorithmic) audiences, the preferred uptake of this clip (Blommaert & [Maly, 2016](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_47)) and their knowledge of the communicative context. In [Figure 3.3](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_3), we see the different members of Schild & Vrienden march in the streets of Ghent. Dries Van Langenhove, the leader of the movement, is walking upfront with a megaphone in his hand. The framing shows us a leader and his militant followers on their way to boycott the manifestation at the Gravensteen Castle.

![Figure 3.3 Screenshot of Schild & Vrienden Facebook video after 15 min. Return to text.⏎ ¶ Source: https://www.facebook.com/schildenvrienden/videos/1537012479753819/.](images/Figure0126-01.jpg)

The first important finding is the use of English. Not only is the title of the video (‘Protecting our heritage’) written in English, the whole video is subtitled in English (see [Figure 3.3](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_3)). This is especially relevant considering the importance of the Dutch language within the Flemish nationalist tradition. It informs us that the message itself was from the start produced with an international audience in mind and was thus not only targeted at the Flemish population. We will come back to this point later. The second element that deserves our attention is the accompanying Dutch Facebook status: ‘The Flemish Youth fights for its heritage and its future. P.S.: The leftist tears are more visible in HD!’ (my translation from Dutch). The deployed linguistic resources in this status refer to different spatio-temporal frames.

The first sentence clearly positions Schild & Vrienden as a Flemish movement fighting for a Flemish future and trying to protect its Flemish heritage. This aligns well with the use of Dutch and is designed for Flemish uptake. But there is more. They use a populist, or more concretely, a generational 128populist format: they speak in the name of the ‘Flemish Youth’. That is also the dominant communicative frame in the Facebook video: Schild & Vrienden is positioned by its leader Dries Van Langenhove as the representatives of *the* Flemish youth, and that Flemish youth seemingly hates ‘the leftists’ and fights to preserve the Flemish traditions and heritage.

This discursive frame indexes the influence of *Generation Identitaire*. From the start, the identitarians clearly positioned themselves as generational movements, fighting against the ‘babyboomer’ generation or the ‘soixante huitards’ who are accused of advocating multiculturalism and open borders (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_28); [Willinger, 2013](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_95)). New right activists around the world have adopted this discursive frame. They all claim that they are just like the students in the sixties. And all of them, from the kekistani in the United States ([Maly, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_48)), De Lavendelkinderen in the Netherlands, to the Identitarian activists of Generation Identity operating in the different European countries, frame themselves as the avant-garde of this youth counter-culture (cf. [Dols de Jong, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_24); [Rusman, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_74)). And Dries Van Langenhove reproduces it too, not only in this video but also in numerous posts and interviews with mainstream media. In an interview with the Flemish mainstream newspaper *De Morgen*, he for instance says, ‘The left-wing elite of May 68 has had its say for way too long. (…) it is time for a new counter-culture. Schild & Vrienden wants to be the avant-garde of this’ ([De Ceulaer, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_21)) (my translation).

In the video, following this classic new right frame, the Flemish youth are constructed as distinct from the ‘the leftists’, even though the images in the video show many young ‘leftists’. Van Langenhove claims in the video that at the Gravensteen Castle, the ‘leftists were all 40, 50 or 60 years old. People who still believe in a dream that we should become a multicultural society with completely open borders’ (Schild & [Vrienden, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_76)). Van Langenhove triggers this public by mobilizing all these classic discursive new right tropes and explicitly accusing ‘left wing’ babyboomers of ‘wanting to attract hundreds of millions of new illegal migrants that have no future here. This way, the leftists are endangering our future, and the future of the whole of Europe’ (Schild & [Vrienden, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_76)). Implicitly, we see how Schild & Vrienden reproduces the white genocide/great replacement trope.

This frame is a truly global dimension of contemporary local nationalist activism and taps into already discursively constructed ‘public formations’ or affective publics ([Papacharissi, 2015](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_68): 4) by extreme-right and radical right nationalist parties, Identitarian activists, and mass media in the last decades: the so-called ‘angry white man’ ([Kimmel, 2013](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_41)). The status and the communicative frame of the video are designed as a politics of recognition. It connects to affective traces that bind a new right translocal networked public together in their fear and anger. As a consequence, this format will be recognized by and resonate with identitarians throughout Europe. Not surprising, thus, that it generates instant applause and interactional support that helps this type of activism (see table) go viral.

If we now zoom in on the second part of the status update, we see a reference to a very different spatio-temporal frame. The concept of ‘leftist tears’ in the status update is an index of the influence of the alt-right movement in the United States. In the United States, alt-right activists and 4channers predominantly use the concept ‘liberal tears’ to make fun of the ‘liberals’ and the ‘lefties’ who are portrayed as ‘snowflakes’ ([Seargeant & Monaghan, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_79)).

Countless memes are produced and distributed reproducing this idea (see [Figure 3.4](#C_010_c3.xhtml#f3_4)). Through digital media, memes travel across borders and become global phatic instruments generating feelings of the community ([Varis & Blommaert, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_91); [Papacharissi, 2015](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_68); [Procházka, 2016](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_71)). New right activists around the world encounter these memes and adapt them for local purposes: They get deglobalized or *indigenized* without fully erasing their global recognizability. Liberal tears, in a Flemish context, would not really work, as ‘liberals’ in Flanders are commonly understood as a (centre-) right party. This adaptation not only shows how digital media enable the mobility of resources, but it is also an index of the global dimension of local action. It shows how local activism is creatively produced in interaction with resources circulating through digital infrastructures. We will come back to this point in the following sections.

Figure 3.5 Facebook video Schild & Vrienden: shares per country – Copyright Ico Maly 2019.

If we now first switch our attention to the form, we get an insight into the digital literacy and the media ideology of these activists. The fact that the video fared quite well on Facebook, and that this is not a lucky shot, shows us that the activists are knowledgeable about the digital environment of Facebook and which content the medium will push under which conditions. 130When we zoom in on their digital literacy, their theoretical or practical knowledge of the algorithmic environment, and what is needed to ensure uptake, we, first of all, see that the activists use a content type that at the time was favoured by Facebook: the uploaded video. Facebook videos were a relatively new feature on Facebook, a feature Facebook launched to compete with YouTube. As a consequence, the digital platform pushes (short) videos on its platform.

The video of Schild & Vrienden is relatively short (2 min 50 s) and uses subtitles. As many people scroll through their newsfeed on their smartphone or computer in places where the sound of the video would be inappropriate, subtitles are a crucial feature to have ‘reach’ and ‘engagement’. Failing to adhere to these format guidelines means that the video will not ‘take off’ and thus fail in its metapolitical goals. Timing is also crucial. In this case, the video was published 10 min before 10 o’clock in the morning, when most people are already behind their computers ready to interact. Immediate interaction with the post in terms of likes and comments, but especially in terms of ‘shares’ (Maly & Beekmans, 2018), is crucial for uptake on Facebook. Interestingly, members of Schild & Vrienden are among the first to like, share and comment on the post. That is no coincidence and I will return to this below.

If we analyse the interaction with the video, we see that the activists of Schild & Vrienden clearly know the game. In the first 15 min (see Image 14), 131the video generated 330 views, 157 interactions, 17 comments, and 24 shares. After half an hour, it generated 880 views, 221 interactions, 27 comments, and 41 shares. The uptake of the clip was spectacular, and as a result, the Facebook algorithms further pushed the video. The uptake shows that the producers managed to tick all the boxes: not only did the clip go viral two times, it gathered a solid number of views (92,000) and likes (2,200) (May 2018). If we zoom in on these likes, we see that around 1,500 profiles ‘like’ the video, 536 ‘love’ it, and around 100 profiles are ‘sad’, ‘angry’, or ‘surprised’. This result is remarkable, especially if you realize that the video was posted on a Facebook page with only 3,000 followers. This wasn’t a lucky shot either, as Schild & Vrienden manages to acquire impressive reach on Facebook.

### Virality and populism as a communicative relation

Virality, likes, shares, comments, and overall ‘Facebook reach’ are important ingredients of the populist discourse of Schild & Vrienden. In a tweet, Dries Van Langenhove, the president of Schild & Vrienden, claimed that their Facebook community has a monthly reach of 250,000, up to 500,000 people. He ends his tweet with the suggestion of non-Schild & Vrienden fans ‘that there is a world outside their bubble’. The reach of Schild & Vrienden on social media is thus used as proof that ‘the other’ – the left – is living in a bubble. It is this quantitative dimension of ‘reach,’ followers, and views that are regularly used to support the claim that Schild & Vrienden speaks ‘in name of the Flemish youth’. In his discourse, Van Langenhove frames his movement and its social media success as a generational effect, as proof that they articulate the voice of the young generation:

> Especially Generation Z, let us say, everyone who today is between 15 and 25. That generation is more conservative than Generation Y, the millennials, and even that generation was already more right-wing and more conservative than the previous one. Schild & Vrienden resembles the spirit of time.
> 
> ([Segers, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_80) \[my translation\])

Uptake online is an inherent part of the communicative relation that is necessary to make the populist claim stick ([Maly, 2018e](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_52)). It is here that you see how Schild & Vrienden acquires political capital by using the popularity logic of digital media to assure mass media attention and construct their message of articulating the voice of a generation. As KhosraviNik ([2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_40)) states, the essence of social media logic is constructing creditability ‘gained by visibility/popularity in a context where popularity results commercial gains regardless of their consequences’ (p. 438). Success on social media leads to visibility in mass media. And not surprisingly, one of the main motives in questions of mass media journalists when interviewing Van Langenhove and reporting on Schild & Vrienden is their ‘social media success’ (see, e.g., [Segers, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_80)). 132In mainstream media, a rise in likes and followers on the social media of Schild & Vrienden is frequently understood as a rise in popularity and support for the movement (see, e.g., [Raeymakers, 2018](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_72)). In such cases, virality is interpreted within the generational populist frame that Schild & Vrienden produces and is read as support from the Flemish youth, and thus contributes to the construction of the meaning of their activism. The populist discourse is legitimized through a discourse that focusses on vanity metrics: likes, shares and (positive) comments are framed by Van Langenhove as proof of them articulating the needs of their generation.

The facts do not support this populist reading of uptake. If we look in more detail at the profiles sharing the Facebook video from Schild & Vrienden (see Image 18), the activity that generates the largest reach on Facebook (Maly & Beekmans, 2018) – we not only get to see how ‘niched’ and ‘targeted’ but also how global their audience is. This spread was not a coincidence either, as the clip, from the very start, was not only formatted in order to generate algorithmic uptake, but it was also designed for global uptake.

On the first day, March 8, 2018, the video was shared 127 times (by 123 different profiles) (of which only one profile shared it to criticize them). This considerable number of shares could easily be mistaken for popularity among the Flemings, the Flemish youth or even among ‘concerned citizens’ approving the message and the offline intervention by Schild & Vrienden. 133The thing is that from the 123 profiles that shared the post on that first day, only 55 indicate that they are from Belgium (four profiles do not give a country of origin). Seventeen people claim to be from the United States; 13 people indicate that they live in the United Kingdom. Profiles from 24 different countries shared this post on the first day it was online.

![Figure 3.6 Last 70 shares Facebook video Schild & Vrienden. Copyright Ico Maly 2019.](images/Figure0133-01.jpg)

Figure 3.6 Last 70 shares Facebook video Schild & Vrienden. Copyright Ico Maly 2019.

If we look at the last 70 shares of the video (see Image 19), we see that the Belgian profiles only account for 10% of the shares. South Africa (nine shares), the United Kingdom (seven shares), and 16 sharing profiles don’t give a ‘home-base’. Especially, these last 16 profiles are truly ‘global’ new right activist profiles: They only seem to exist in order to share (new right) content from all over the world.

The claim of Schild & Vrienden and the superficial reading of some mass media journalists, in which the shares in themselves are read through a populist framework, only contribute to the metapolitical goal of these shares. It is part of the populist communicative relation ([Maly, 2018a](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_48)) and legitimates the populist claim of Schild & Vrienden that they speak in the name of the Flemish youth.

The data, as illustrated, clearly point in a very different direction. These shares are best understood as metapolitical activism of an affective new right public embedded within a global new right mediascape ([Appadurai, 1996](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_1)). The virality of the remediatization of their offline activism is to a large extent the result of this translocal network. This affective public and its 134infrastructural dimension became very visible when I revisited all the profiles sharing the Schild & Vrienden video on May 30, 2018. At that time, Tommy Robinson, the former head of the English Defence League and Pegida UK, who is well networked with Martin Sellner of the Austrian chapter of Generation Identity, was sentenced to 13 months of imprisonment for contempt for the court. Robinson was arrested on Friday, May 22, 2018, and pleaded guilty. Within five hours he was arrested, sentenced, and jailed. New right activists around the world set up petitions and posted their outrage on social media. His arrest was framed as proof of the power of the liberal elite and the fact that the truth had to be silenced. If we look at the profiles initially sharing the Schild & Vrienden post, we see that 51 of the 123 profiles also shared at least one post on Tommy Robinson between 28 and 30 May. And again, this was an example of the global dimension of this new right activist network. Activists from 12 different countries posted memes, petitions, and outrage in favour of Tommy Robinson.

### Generational populism, new right metapolitics 2.0 and algorithmic activism

The shares and the superficial reading of shares as an instance of ‘networked individualism’ ([Castells, 2015](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_15)) are analytically insufficient. From the moment one starts to give attention to the ‘details’ and starts investigating the profiles that share the video, we see the ‘organized’ nature of this ‘popularity’. This is not a spontaneous movement that starts from a spark of outrage. These are not just ordinary citizens showing their support for this message by sharing. It is also not an act of ‘slacktivism’ or a feel-good activity as Morozov ([2011](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_66)) and Gladwell ([2010](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_31)) would call it: virality is an essential ingredient of metapolitics 2.0 in which new right activists wrap their radical ideas in normalcy by claiming to articulate the voice of the people by organizing virality.

Considering the importance or ‘reach’ and virality of the populist claim, it is important to understand how this virality is achieved. Key ingredients of virality are simple packaging, humour, augmented participation tools, prestige, positioning, and the provocation of strong emotions ([Shifman, 2014](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_81): 94–96). This understanding of virality, implicitly, assumes that virality is an organic phenomenon. That virality is the result of producing a good message, a message that is ready for uptake and resonates with the people. This understanding of virality contributes to the populist claims of new right movements. Trying to explain virality by only looking at the content of the video would be committing the fallacy of internalism ([Thompson, 1995](#C_010_c3.xhtml#r3_86)). New right activists would like you to think that this uptake happens ‘organically’ and locally. It is this assumption that legitimates their populist discourse.

As I have shown, most of the classic elements of virality are in place, but there is more. The video was not only formatted and metapragmatically prepared for algorithmic and global uptake; the uptake itself was actively 135organized. The first people who were liking, sharing, and commenting on the video were largely members and dedicated followers of Schild & Vrienden. In many cases, they would react by tagging fellow activists to notify them that the video was back online, and ask them to share or tag their ‘men’ (see Image 20). The tagging led to the activation of more structured interaction with the posts from militants and local pages of the extreme-right Flemish party Flemish Interest. Very quick, one would see a rise in people sharing the video, or reacting underneath it, all in similar ways: tagging, liking, and sharing.
