### Modest fashion as metapolitics

The feminine equivalent for the male costume is ‘modest fashion’. Modest fashion developed three decades ago and is, according to Lewis ([2013](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_32)), now a predominantly youthful phenomenon of women who want to express their religious and collective identity – instead of an individualized identity – through their style. Far-right influencers Brittany Pettibone, Lauren Southern and Lauren Chen use Instagram to mediate modesty, femininity, moderateness and fashionability. Their modest fashion style, just like the Brooks Brothers costumes of Richard Spencer, combines a vintage feel, reminiscent of a Mad-Men-like sixties style. This type of fashion, even though it is clearly a mass-produced commercial product, challenges the very idea of fashion. It suggests timelessness or traditionalism in the sense of Dugin. In the screenshot below, we see how Brittany Pettibone stresses her feminity by wearing classic dresses with a vintage feel, Garbo-style makeup and understated timelessness. Only once can she be seen wearing jeans and that is when she went hiking. This nostalgic feminine clothing is emblematic of all metapolitical influencers and tradwives (see for instance also Matheis’ analysis of Lana Lokteff, 2018), and it distinguishes them from the stereotype and meme they construct of the shouting, ugly, fat and hysterical leftist feminist.

This nostalgic fifties style, reminiscent of a mid-century Sears catalogue, as Tebaldi ([2022a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_71)) stresses, is only one form of visualizing this traditionalism. It 156can also be communicated as sporting clothing from further back in history. What all these tradwives’ styles share is that ‘all of these women insist on their role defending the timeless, natural traditional femininity from feminism and social decline’ ([Tebaldi, 2022a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_71): 1). The clothing, and the discourses of these women, are filled with an ‘imagined nostalgia’ ([Appadurai, 1996](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_1): 77) for an age where gender roles were supposed to be simple and beautiful. It is an imagined nostalgia because it is directed to a time that was never there. A time when men were men and women were women and both were successful and happy. More than just a nostalgia for the fifties and sixties when white males dominated culture and norms in Western societies, it is a performative act indexing a new future era they strive for based on traditional norms. The Instagram posts are archeofuturist preconfigurations. The evocation of the past in those far-right media practices is always future-oriented. As Griffin argues, the evocation of the past is always done ‘to enlist slumbering nationalist forces in the battle for a new civilization’ ([Griffin, 2008](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_23): 37).

The post on the Instagram page ‘Worth Fighting For’ (cannot be displayed in this book due to the policies of Taylor and Francis) is emblematic of this entangled-ness between norms of ‘masculinity’ and ‘feminity’ and a larger battle against modernism and for an ethno-plural world. ‘Worth Fighting For’ is a very successful Instagram page with 77.6K followers dedicated to ‘Traditional aesthetics’ under the motto ‘tradition is not the worship of ashes but the preservation of fire’. The page is connected to an online shop and has a second handle – Western Aesthetics – in case one is deleted. Considering its followers, and the accounts liking posts from the page, we can without exaggeration state that it is an influential hub in the global new right. Dries Van Langenhove from Schild & Vrienden follows it. Brittany Pettibone/Sellner liked several posts. It can thus be said to resonate with key figures in that global new right and contribute to the construction of the far-right style. The post is typical of content ‘Worth Fighting For’ posts. It is a slideshow of eight images. The first picture has the text ‘Make Marriage and family the dreams of children’ written on top of a romantic picture of two kids – not coincidentally a blond white girl and a light brown-haired white boy – in a vintage car, dressed for a wedding. The frame communicates the importance of marriage, family and children. The second picture in the series adds a more combative stance to the first one. It shows a man sitting on the mountains with the slogan ‘revolt against the modern world’ echoing the works of Julius Evola typed on top. Marriage, having a family, is portrayed – next to believing in Jesus (picture 3) – as traditional, and thus as a revolt against modernity. The different gender roles in that marriage are clearly defined in pictures 4 and 5. Men are excepted to be alpha men, men who work out, have discipline and go to work. Through the fifties, nostalgic pictures of women are painted as caring housewives and mothers. This traditional style is not only linked to gender roles but it is also linked to the revolt against modernity. This identity emblem in turn can be bought in the form of a t-shirt.

157Style is clearly not meaningless. On the contrary, it is in their style that we see the nano-politics of identity and new right culture in general in detail. To become an identitarian individual, one needs to perform lots of identity work. Identity work is here understood as discursive orientations towards sets of features that are seen (or can be seen) as emblematic of particular identities ([Blommaert & Varis, 2015](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_8)). These features are manifold (hip youth culture, vintage style modest fashion, or the more explicit traditional T-shirts from ‘Worth Fighting For’) and include a variety of semiotic means (hairstyles, brands, fabrics, styles, modes of language) depending on the different orders of indexicality. Identities thus appear as constellations – specific arrangements or configurations of such emblematic features. The features are not organized at random. To become an identitarian, one needs to combine several identity emblems (hip or traditional clothing, looking part of the mainstream, but being edgy at the same time) with a very specific far-right metapolitical discourse. This allows for recognition by one’s peers and to stay integrated in the group and the mainstream. The traditional style thus indexes a specific (meta)political position.

### Digital media, digital culture and metapolitical influencers

In order to understand the ideological and stylistic normativities – the orders of indexicality – in the contemporary new right culture, it is important to understand the individual and collective creativity and the richness of the semiotic processes and outcomes, as well as the more structural elements, the infrastructures and linguistic ecologies/economies. Arnaut et al. ([2017](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_2): 13) echoing Calhoun et al. ([2013](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_10)) conceptualized this nexus between agency or creativity and structure as the ‘poiesis-infrastructures nexus’. Poiesis here is used to capture human activity as the result of creative social interaction. This interaction is of course embedded in infrastructures, and thus not totally free. These infrastructures both enable and constrain creativity and meaning-making ([Calhoun et al., 2013](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_10): 197). Digital media not only affords discourse production, but it also directs behaviour: certain digital affordances request, encourage and push users towards ‘particular communicative and interactive practices by means of quantified processes’ ([Georgakopoulou, Iversen & Stage, 2020](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_21): 24). Social media function, as LaViolette ([2017](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_29)) argued in relation to Reddit, as a ‘Goffmanian frame’ that ‘circumscribes’ discourse and becomes crucial to its interpretation ([Goffman, 1974](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_22)). The notion of the poiesis-infrastructures nexus thus ‘envisages the double process of emergent normativities and sedimentations, on the one hand, and the creative and material production processes unsettling these on the other hand’ ([Arnaut et al., 2017](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_2): 15). Analysing new right influencers as orders of indexicality forces us to analyse how they interact, not only with their audiences but also with the platforms themselves. Digital media are a key infrastructure of 158contemporary metapolitics. The new right metapolitical strategy is first and foremost focused on a deep integration in the (digital) mainstream ([Maly, 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_39)). New right activists try to use the digital mainstream as leverage to reach new audiences. Even though many new right activists openly criticize the ‘left-wing’ bias of Zuckerberg and Dorsey, in practice we see that they try to conform to the (literal reading) of the community standards of these social media.

As a result of this interaction between activists and platforms, we see new (metapolitical) practices ([Maly, 2018a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_34), [2019a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_40), [2019b](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_41), 2022), and new norms and cultures ([Hou, 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_25): 16–18) emerging. The described new right style is linked to the cultural practices embedded in this digital environment. One of these cultural practices is what is known as ‘influencer’, ‘micro-celebrity’ or ‘social media celebrity’ culture. Marvick, together with boyd and Senft, argue that micro-celebrity should be understood as ‘a self-presentation technique in which people view themselves as a public persona to be consumed by others, use strategic intimacy to appeal to followers, and regard their audience as fans’ ([Marwick and boyd, 2011](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_52); [Senft, 2013](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_67); [Marwick, 2015](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_51)). This ‘edited self’, as García-Rapp and Roca-Cuberes ([2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_20)) call it, is at the same time a product of the internal norms of each community shaping discourses, styles, looks and ideologies, the technical affordances and media-ideology of the platform (visible in its community standards and norms), and the intrinsic features of online content. Influencer culture is a socio-technical assemblage: the voice and performance of the social media influencer are not entirely ‘free’, but a product of socio-technological interaction between the vlogger, the platform(s) and his or her followers. This micro-celebrity culture is an integral part of the so-called attention economy, or what Venturini calls the ‘economy of virality’ ([Venturini, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_81): 133). ‘Success on YouTube is rooted on sustained attention, thanks to an ever growing, loyal and engaged audience’ ([García-Rapp & Roca-Cuberes, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_20)).

Micro-celebrity culture finds its material base in the technological programming of digital infrastructures. The practice of influencers helps attract the attention of their followers, and as such contributes to the profit of large internet companies. It explains why somebody such as conspiracy theorist Paul Watson stays integrated: he not only tries to comply with the community standards, but he himself also contributes to the goals of the platform. He captures many eyeballs. In order to sell the user’s attention, social media platforms set up a technological system that allows them to measure, quantify and standardize ‘attention’ in the form of ‘reach’, ‘views’, ‘interactions’, ‘likes’ and ‘shares’. Metapolitical influencers are not just ‘using’ these digital media to have an impact and reach; their integration in the ecology of mainstream digital media contributes to the monetization of that audience labour and thus to the goals of the platforms. Social media influencers are crucial building blocks of the digital economy.

159In order to be fully integrated into this economy of virality and generate uptake, metapolitical influencers need to be media literate. They need to develop specific strategies to make use of the affordances and algorithms of the different media (and their specific media logics) to build an audience and/or community ([Varis & Hou, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_80): 231). The adoption of strategies of personal branding by influencers is done in relation to this economy of virality and the affordances of digital media. As the functioning of the algorithms of the different platforms is not known by anybody outside of the company that builds them, the acquiring of media literacy is based on an algorithmic imaginary ([Bucher, 2015](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_9)). This imaginary is constructed on the basis of practical experience and the careful monitoring of metrics, the number of likes, shares, followers and comments. These ‘vanity metrics’, as Rogers ([2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_66)) calls them, not only give birth to the culture of influencers and social media celebrities, they also bring into life networks of influence. The more people that follow an influencer, the more chances that their content will be liked, shared and distributed in the network. These networks of influence ([Jacobson et al., 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_26)) – within an attention economy – not only have economic value (in terms of data production and usefulness for marketing campaigns), but they also have metapolitical value: they contribute to the spread of metapolitical ideas, fashions and styles. The adoption of social media celebrity practices can thus help to construct a metapolitical network of influence and let their metapolitical ideas circulate and contribute to a shared style. Interestingly, in the case of metapolitical influencers, that style seems highly gendered. Female metapolitical influencers mobilize a highly ‘feminine style’ that stresses softness, nostalgic or modest fashion and combine it with a discourse about the family, gender roles and of course the re-emergence of the community. This metapolitical seduction, as Tebaldi calls it ([2022](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_72)b: 23), ‘blends sexual intimacy with gendered regimes of value, in order to produce a desirable subject position of men.’ Male influencers create a mirror image and mobilize alpha male masculinity.

### Brittany Pettibone, The Golden One and antifeminism

In what follows, I will zoom in on two metapolitical influencers: the Swedish bodybuilder, online fitness guru, entrepreneur and far-right YouTuber, The Golden One (aka Marcus Follin), and #pizzagate promotor and wife of Martin Sellner, Brittany Pettibone, known since their marriage as Brittany Sellner. Both represent two sides of a crucial new right metapolitical battlefield, which could be labelled as the antifeminist battle or the battle to recreate the nuclear family as the foundation of a healthy community. This metapolitical gender war aims to restore the ‘natural order’ of things by promoting the heteronormative nuclear family and traditional gender roles for men and women. This battle has a long new right history. In their new right manifesto, 160de Benoist and Champetier ([2000](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_11): 35) make it very clear that, to them, ‘the distinction of the sexes is the first and most fundamental of natural differences (…) humanity is not one, but rather two’. This existence of biological feminine and masculine nature is considered as evident and as the basis of gender. And even though they admit that ‘due to genetic factors or socio-cultural choices’ people can deviate from these categories, they stress that ‘in general, a large number of values and attitudes fall into feminine and masculine categories’ ([de Benoist & Champetier, 2000](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_11): 36). ‘Feminine values’ (cooperation, mediation, seduction, empathy, synthetic intuition) are then contrasted with ‘masculine values’ (competition, repression, domination, detachment, aggression, abstract, analytical intellection). It is from this position that they advocate a ‘differentialist feminism’ which recognizes men as well as women by acknowledging the equal value of their distinct and unique natures.

‘Recognizing’ gender in the new right discourse has a very specific meaning. Differentialist feminism metapolitically constructs gender roles that align with the ‘biological nature of the two genders’. This differentialist position is, as always, pitted against ‘universal feminism’ and thus against egalitarianism. This focus on the rebirth of traditional, biological gender roles and the family is embedded into a discourse focused on the ‘demographic crisis’, the ‘anti-natalism’ or ‘ethno-masochism’ ([Faye, 2010](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_16): 60) promoted by the left. Traditional gender roles and the stress on the power of family units ([Faye, 2010](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_16): 81) are in this new right discourse instrumentalized as building blocks of homogenous organic communities. To arrive at an organic community, it is necessary, according to Faye ([2010](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_16): 70), to develop a family policy in the light of the rebirth of traditional values and a Europe of people. In order to counter ‘anti-natalism’, one has to try, according to Faye, to reinstate traditional values and stop the ‘emasculation process’. Men should again be men and women should be women again: or in plain wording, housewives should take care of many white children. The fashion and styles that we have just discussed contribute to the metapolitical goal that The Golden One and Brittany Pettibone personify. As metapolitical influencers, they function as role models for the ‘alpha male’ and the ‘trad wife’.

## The Golden One and the metapolitical warrior

The Golden One started his YouTube channel in 2012 and has now amassed (March 2021) over 110K subscribers and over 12 million views. He has become one of those far-right influencers operating on a global scale. He has been invited to give lectures in the Netherlands for the far-right group Erkenbrand (The Golden [One, 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_76)), in the Ukraine for Reconquista ([2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_64)), The Scandza Forum in Sweden (The Golden [One, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_77)) and did collabs with many key figures and online shows in the far-right alternative influence network ([Lewis, 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_33)) like Millennial Woes ([2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_55)) or Red Ice TV ([2015](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_65)). 161‘The Golden One’ was also one of the many key figures of the global new right that praised Guillaume Faye after his death. His condolence tweet was not the first time this blonde Swedish YouTuber praised Faye. Already in 2015, he made a (now blocked) YouTube video praising Faye’s book ‘Why We Fight: Manifesto for a European Renaissance’ as ‘one of the best books I have read’. The Golden One is one of those influencers that regularly promotes new books from Arktos and can thus be seen as a key figure within the global new right operating on the highest scale of vernacular globalization.

The Golden One recommends Faye’s *Why We Fight*, especially if you ‘are a beginner in the political or philosophical world or need ammunition to fight off or debate the leftists’ (The Golden [One, 2015a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_73)). Note here how The Golden One adopts metaphors of war in relation to the idea of political debate or philosophy. That is not a coincidence, and the words ‘the debate’, ‘philosophy’ or ‘metapolitics’ are not only used as synonyms by him, but his whole message also argues that metapolitics is crucial in the fight for the future of Europe and the European people. These fighting metaphors also reflect, as we have seen, the central motif in Faye’s book: the motive of decline and the need for a rebirth or renaissance. Faye starts *Why We Fight* with the idea that ‘Europe today faces the greatest danger in her history, a danger threatening the very existence of her civilization. For she is at war and doesn’t know it’ ([Faye, 2011](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_17): 29). This danger is brought upon us because our elites do not fight for their people and let us be colonized by migrants and Muslims in particular. The idea of the ‘great replacement’ was already very much present in those books from Faye. Even more, to not be replaced is why we should fight, according to Faye. We should fight ‘for the cause of our own people’s destiny’ ([Faye, 2011](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_17): 39). Faye describes the world in Schmittian terms as a struggle between ethnic peoples and civilizations for survival and domination. ‘The base of everything is biocultural identity and demographic renewal’, says Faye ([2011](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_17): 37).

The Golden One completely agrees with Faye. ‘Culture stems out of blood’, he says in his video praising Faye. This fight for the survival of the biocultural identity of Europe, or in less metapolitical discourse, the white European race, is according to Faye, not only metapolitical: it is very much about the will to power, the will to become culturally, morally, economically and politically superior as people. Faye’s stress on this struggle for dominance and superiority between Europeans and the Islamic colonizers is exactly the message that The Golden One puts forward on his channel. This idea, The Golden One says, ‘resonates very well with the kind of aesthetics that I’m trying to portray with this channel, about strength and such virtues’ (The Golden [One, 2015a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_73)). This aesthetics refers to the stereotype of the virile, strong and muscular alpha male. The Golden One’s bodybuilding aesthetics personifies the old motif of the warriors and strong men willing to fight and sacrifice themselves for the group. Just like Faye, The Golden One stresses 162the importance of the *Warrior virtues* and stopping of ‘deviralization’ as Faye calls it. The Golden One sees himself as helping to construct a new legion of metapolitical warriors: troops of real alpha men who combine physical strength with metapolitical strength. In a lecture for the Ukrainian-based far-right Azov Movement and the ND-National Militia, The Golden One stressed the importance of combining real fighting and violence with the philosophical or metapolitical. In essence, he pleads for a fusion of metapolitics and the willingness to use violence in the idea of the ‘metapolitical soldier’ or ‘metapolitical crusader’ (The Golden [One, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_77)). In this lecture for the ND-National militia, he stresses that soldiers need to have a solid ideological world view and activists or politicians also need to be able to physically fight. This notion of the metapolitical crusader is central in the social media communication of The Golden One. All his online activity has been dedicated to the creation and education of that legion of far-right metapolitical crusaders.

### The alpha male and the metapolitical crusader

A central tactic to his attempt to create this metapolitical legion of warriors is addressing young men who are struggling with their identity and with their future. He not only addresses that audience directly, but he also tries to give them a future, a purpose in life. In another popular video from 2015, he for instance explicitly addresses ‘Western and Swedish Young Men’ (The Golden [One, 2015b](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_74)) and asks them to listen to his words. He starts by recognizing their struggle and immediately gives meaning to that struggle. They are struggling because of ‘white guilt’, ‘guilt of being a man’, they are being ‘shamed for being white’ and ‘shamed for being a man’. To all those young guys who recognize themselves in that description, he functions as the bringer of hope, and he does this using two tricolons in a row. In the first tricolon, he addresses the young viewers directly:

> You are important.
> 
> Your life has meaning.
> 
> Your future doesn’t necessarily need to look dark.
> 
> This is also your land.
> 
> (The Golden [One, 2015b](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_74))

The Golden One explicitly addresses these young men individually by using the pronoun ‘you’. The Golden One clearly plays into affect, into feelings young men may have like doubting the meaning of life, but also worrying about the future. Importantly, those feelings are immediately connected to the state of the nations. It is implied that the reason why young men feel dislocated, living meaningless lives, is because their land is taken away from them. The individual is thus immediately portrayed as part of an ‘us’: they 163are also, just like The Golden One himself, owners of ‘their land’. The second tricolon stresses that what The Golden One assumes that these youngsters feel is normal:

> There is nothing strange about honouring your heritage.
> 
> There is nothing strange about not wanting to be a minority in your own country.
> 
> There is nothing strange about being proud about who you are. (…)
> 
> (The Golden [One, 2015b](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_74))

Note here, how through this metapolitical intimacy the classic generic fascist narrative of decline and rebirth ([Griffin, 2008](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_23)) is now individualized. The decline of the nation is visible in the decline of the white young man who is now hopeless and whose future is ‘dark as f\*ck’, to quote The Golden One. The reason for the decline of the nation and white man is found in those ‘extreme left cultural Marxist communist feminists’. The solution? ‘Stop listening to those extreme left cultural Marxist communist feminists, and listen to a guy like me’ (The Golden [One, 2015b](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_74)). Note here that the hope for rebirth is also individualized: it is men like The Golden One who can help young men to find their pride. And their pride is located in their land, their heritage and their willingness to fight for that land and against their minoritization.

When The Golden One gives them hope and perspective. He directly addresses his audience. ‘You are important’, he says, while he looks into the camera making eye contact with the viewer, raises his voice and points in an Uncle Sam kind of way to the audience to recruit them. Such a setting, where the influencer looks directly at the viewer’s eyes, connects the viewer and the participant with each other. It establishes contact between the two, even if it is only on an imaginary level ([Kress & Van Leeuwen, 1996](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_28): 122): it demands the attention of the viewer. The Golden One is directly speaking to his audience, even using both of his index fingers to underline that he is really speaking directly to them. This intimacy is further exploited metapolitically in the personal topics The Golden One talks about. He explicitly stresses that ‘it is perfectly fine to be a man, to be a boy’, of course implying that ‘the left’ doesn’t think that is fine. And he urges his viewers, whenever they see a man who is not confident, to approach him and say that he is important. And again, this outreach is framed within a large societal narrative of decline. Because is it too late now to let good young forces go to waste, we need everyone to be engaged and committed in the battle for the future. The battle against devitalization is thus not only a battle to help the struggling young men, but it is also necessary to save the nation and European white civilization. The self-help narrative is a metapolitical narrative that allows young men not only to become proud but also to become a radical, anti-left, far-right nationalist alpha male. This metamorphosis is a metamorphosis in 164ideology and style. A style that can also be bought in the Legio Gloria webshop in the form of food supplements, coffee and clothing.

This reborn man, the man who is confident, who is willing to fight for his ancestors, his traditions and his civilization, is a man that will be successful. ‘The future can be bright’, says The Golden One, ‘but you have to work for it as well’. To arrive at that future, one has to become a confident warrior, and to become that warrior, one not only has to read, one has to train, go to the gym and learn how to fight. The Golden One presents himself as the role model of a healthy, confident man. He gives training programmes, sells food, gives challenges and allows young men to build a community around him. To become that role model, he uses, like all influencers, his private life in service of gathering eye balls. This influencer practice is commonly understood as ‘networked intimacy’. The concept was initially introduced to try to understand how people use digital media to make friends or to display intimacy in the context of social media ([Miguel, 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_54)). In relation to influencers, it has gotten a slightly different meaning. Networked intimacy has become an instrument to bind audiences to the influencer and create a perception of authenticity. The pictures and videos in which The Golden One introduces his daughter and his wife are all emblematic of the perfect live that he is trying to project: the harmonious marriage where men and women take up ‘their natural gender roles’. His wife is part of that metapolitical business. Together, they project the image of the ideal happy traditional family consisting of a strong man and father, and a caring wife. Emblematic of this traditionalist narrative was the post of his wife on International Women’s Rights Day in 2021. In this post, she shows a picture of The Golden One with their child. On the one side of the image, we read ‘What do you need most in life as a women?’. The answer is provided below the picture ‘A loving family. Congratulations for spoiling this for millions of families since 8 March 1909’. With this post, she confirms the discourse of The Golden One on gender relations and the joys of traditional marriage. A loving family (in her case with The Golden One) is all that a woman needs, she claims. The natural order is thus an order grounded in a dominant patriarch and a submissive feminine woman. The women fighting for women’s rights are portrayed as the ones destroying that traditional family, and thus also as destroying the corner stone of a healthy organic nation. The Golden One and his wife, their individual advice, their use of networked intimacy and their help are all part of a larger metapolitical project. A project that has uptake within the far-right global network.

### The Golden One, the metapolitical legion and algorithmic knowledge

It should go without saying that the metapolitics of The Golden One is dissimilar to the notion of metapolitics forwarded by de Benoist. De Benoist 165not only looked down on the ‘vulgar politics of the politicians’, but he also saw metapolitics as driven by the long-term project to capture hearts and minds ([Bar-On, 2007](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_5): 37). This also meant that GRECE rarely intervened in direct political analysis and that they were not looking for controversies in the mass media. De Benoist recognized that ‘the capture of the cultural realm must be the task of an even smaller, ultra-elitist force fighting against the ‘established order’ ([Bar-On, 2007](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_5): 52). The metapolitics of *La Nouvelle Droite* was, first and foremost, about the production of theory and the distancing oneself from violent activist groups. Second, it was about normalizing those ideas in order to fuel political changes – not by seeking mass media attention or controversy, but by educating the absolute elites. Anyone who has watched the YouTube vlogs of The Golden One knows that his version of metapolitics is not about highbrow intellectual theory or a new theoretical synthesis based on a study of all areas of knowledge published in books and journals in order to propose a coherent worldview ([de Benoist & Champetier, 2000](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_11)). The Golden One is emblematic of this new, 21st-century type of metapolitics, which I coined metapolitics 2.0: a metapolitics which is clearly intertwined with digital infrastructures and digital culture. The Golden One is a metapolitical influencer: he uses digital media and culture to have a voice and to ‘convert’ individuals to the right belief.

Important to understand is that The Golden One does not just reproduce the ideas of others. This would entail that he is a type of neutral intermediary. Anyone who has seen him knows that this is not the case. By using digital media for metapolitical goals, he is producing new ideas, assembling existing ideas in this metapolitical fitness influencer format and repackaging them while communicating them to a new niche. The key to understanding his impact is to analyse his communication in the tradition of social media influencers. Just like most influencers, The Golden One not only produces a clear-cut persona but also mobilizes strategic authenticity and networked intimacy to bind his audience. The difference between traditional influencer intimacy and metapolitical intimacy is that his personal life is used in service of metapolitical goals. After a video was posted where he discussed what it meant to become a father, a whole series followed discussing the war on fatherhood and how to raise daughters. Throughout those seemingly personal videos, he is promoting the traditional values and pan-European worldview that you can also find in a different form in the works of Faye.

### Legio Gloria and the Son of Europe

Like all influencers, The Golden One has crafted his own brand. He has created a very specific public persona – a sort of modern-day pastiche of a Nordic Viking/Bodybuilder – which he uses for metapolitical and economic goals. He combines fitness videos, food advice and training videos with videos explicitly 166dedicated to politics, far-right books and activists. He gets paid to give lectures, and uses Patreon to get monthly funding (586 persons donated each month before Patreon deplatformed him in March 2022). He has his own clothing line, Legio Gloria, which he regularly wears in his YouTube videos. He even has his own nutrition line. The success of The Golden One is clearly not only metapolitical, it is also a small business success. The Golden One’s brand thus finances his metapolitics and vice versa. Through his online presence and his influencer techniques, he manages to inspire far-right activists and youth around the world. It is in this uptake that we can assess the meaning of his work.

One of those viewers and fans is the ‘Son of Europe’. The Son of Europe is a member of the far-right Flemish identitarian movement ‘Schild & Vrienden’ (see Maly, 2019). In a YouTube video with the title ‘How I got red pilled’,

1.  Train at least five days a week,
2.  Stop watching porn or at least masturbating to porn as ‘I want you aggressive and disciplined’. This is non-negotiable if you want to be part of his ‘legionnairies’.
3.  Read an article every day and
4.  Post ‘a glorious picture of yourself’ (…) in the most epic place you know’ and ‘upload it to Instagram with the tag #legiogloria’.

It was through this challenge and especially those posts, said the Son of Europe, that a community was born. This community not only created transnational ties among far-right activists. It also functioned as a learning environment. The Son of Europe claims in his video that it was in this Legio Gloria that he learnt everything about ‘the domination of cultural Marxism’, ‘the domination of certain groups in the banking world’. He even concludes by saying that this ‘formed my ideology as it is up to today’ and even more, he himself started to take up the role of ‘metapolitical influencer’: he started posting English videos and pictures on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube in the genre of The Golden One.

167The Golden One – as an influencer or micro-celebrity within the far-right niche – re-entextualizes Faye’s discourse, fuses it with other traditionalist and identitarian insights, wraps it up in an idiosyncratic format and brings it to a whole new audience. His Legio Gloria challenge shows not only how he creates a group around him, but also how he uses that group to generate interaction on his profile and thus contribute to his own algorithmically sorted visibility. Not only algorithmic knowledge of algorithmic imagination is crucial to generate metapolitical impact in this digital ecology, but understanding and adjusting to the culture of the platform are also at least as important.

The Golden One’s Metapolitics 2.0 is deeply weaved into the new media system ([Maly, 2020a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_43)). The impact and the influence of The Golden One, and thus his role in the distribution of far-right ideology cannot be reduced to his content alone. We have to understand it in relation to his online persona and thus also in relation to the digital and algorithmic environment in which he produces his voice. Not only the management of visibility but also avoiding non-visibility, as Bucher stresses, is a constant worry for all actors in this media system. Making yourself visible and drawing attention are central to all contemporary ideological projects. The Golden One, in his long social media career, has proven to master this game. On top of that, he was able to stay fully integrated into all major digital platforms (YouTube, Twitter, Instagram and Facebook) for almost a decade. He used the affordances of all those platforms and adopted classic influencer techniques to grow an audience, to keep that audience hooked and to build a community around him.

The key to any contemporary metapolitical project is thus to be and stay integrated into the culture of the platform, and more specifically to adjust to its community rules. It is their integration into this new media ecology that allows them to become so influential. Since the end of 2020, we see that The Golden One has struggled to keep integrated. His personal Instagram and Facebook accounts have been deleted, as was his Patreon account. He is now using his existing mainstream accounts to make sure that his audience can move along with him to new platforms like GAB, Telegram and the Odyssee video platform. He has created a new Instagram account (@thegoldenjarl) where he, in less than one year, amassed over 16,8K followers. And in a desperate need to keep himself integrated into YouTube, he has announced to stop posting political videos there. This desperate attempt to reinstate his Instagram account and to maintain his YouTube account shows us just how important mainstream digital media are for this metapolitical project.

## Brittany Pettibone, gender roles and the traditional family

Whereas the Golden One combines purely political content with self-help content to turn beta males into alpha males or even metapolitical warriors, Brittany Pettibone combines political and activist content with conspiracy 168theories and relational advice videos. Both have over 100K followers on YouTube and can thus be seen as curating content for specific niches that are integrated into that new right network. And both metapolitical influencers highlight how important digital knowledge is in a digital metapolitical battle.

Brittany Pettibone became famous within the global new right because of her key role in bringing the #pizzagate conspiracy theory to prominence. She has since built a large following and acquired a prominent status among far-right activists around the world (Maly, 2020). She is working on a transnational scale and has a global following. Pettibone uses the action and meaning-making possibilities of different mainstream digital media like Twitter, Instagram, and YouTube and adopts the practices of influencers to further a metapolitical agenda. With more than 30,500 followers on Instagram, 154,200 followers on Twitter and 137,000 subscribers on YouTube (30 June 2020), Pettibone has created a niched media empire for herself.

### The rise of Brittany Pettibone

In less than one year after her first political tweet, Pettibone had already acquired large visibility – a key value within the attention economy ([García-Rapp & Roca-Cuberes, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_20)). The name ‘Brittany Pettibone’ had become a brand with a substantial audience consisting of alt-right and identitarian activists. In the next months and years, she would capitalize on this position. Since May 2017, Pettibone started to craft her channel around her own personality. The banner ‘Virtue of the West’ was replaced by a professionally crafted intro positioning her name and her own logo.

Since April 2017, we also see that Pettibone more regularly started to use her Instagram account, giving her followers more insight into ‘the back office’ of her political activism and seemingly giving unfiltered access to her private life. This networked intimacy is not only part of the metapolitical goal, it is also very much staged. Whereas in 2016 pictures on Pettibone’s Instagram mostly showed typical family pictures, we see a clear break in 2017. From her invite to Trump’s inauguration, over selfies with Lauren Southern, to her performance at the Free Speech Rally in Berkeley in April 2017: Instagram was now regularly used to give her fans a look behind the scenes of her activist life. With the exception of some old #TBT pictures – showing her travelling with friends, celebrating her dog’s birthday and pictures with her family – most pictures were now carefully staged to contribute to her brand as an ‘important activist’ and create a nostalgic feminine style. The intimacy of these ‘old family’ #TBT photos was re-entextualized in a political context and blended with more glamorous pictures reminiscent of fashion shoots with ‘behind the scenes’ pictures and stories on her political activism. Influencers, Hou ([2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_25): 78–79) argues, try to create an aura of authenticity through the (interactive) representation of the intimate and private self: a practice Hou calls ‘staged authenticity’.

169A good example of how Pettibone uses staged authenticity for metapolitical goals is her wedding. In the weeks and months before her wedding with Martin Sellner – of the pan-European identitarian movement Generation Identity – followers on her Instagram could see her getting her ‘wedding ring sized’, kissing Martin Sellner on a carriage under the caption ‘Du bist die liebe meines lebens’, and pictures of both giving their wedding vows in a church in the Austrian countryside.

All these pictures and captions provide her followers with deeply intimate information. Like all – non-political – influencers, Pettibone mobilizes this aura of authenticity strategically to create a bond with her audience ([Gaden & Dumitrica, 2015](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_19)), giving them the feeling that they really know Pettibone. Important to stress here is how she caters to a specific style and thus functions as a role model or a centre of normativity. The difference with non-political influencers is that networked intimacy and strategic authenticity are now being mobilized in support of metapolitical goals. This metapolitical dimension becomes clear when we see how her Instagram account works in synchrony with her YouTube channel, where Pettibone posted a vlog with the title ‘3 Reasons Marriage Is A Risk (And Why We Still Took It)’ ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_59)a).

The same romantic wedding picture of the couple in traditional clothing is now being used as a thumbnail on YouTube. The title of the video is seemingly unpolitical. The SEO of this video is made for uptake in a very different niche by a potentially very different audience (people who are interested in marriage and maybe have doubts). The video shows the couple on the last day of their honeymoon. First, on a boat in Italy where they make the joke that now that Salvini is out of office, someone has to make sure the waters are safe for illegal immigrants. Later, they film from one of the Italian beaches. Sitting on a beach bed, they address their viewers, with a beer and a café latte in hand (indexing traditional images of men and women), and again with a small joke that the beaches are safe. When they start discussing marriage and why they did it, they are seemingly just rationally talking about all potential problems in marriage. They discuss three questions (1) Is it responsible for right-wing activists to marry and have children considering their precarious financial situation, (2) Is it responsible to set children in this world as right-wing activists and (3) a more general one, should you really bind yourself to one person for the rest of your life.

Throughout the discussion, we see two main frames. The first one is a traditional understanding of marriage and gender roles. In an ideal marriage, the man is the one that goes out working and provides food on the table. The wife is supposed to dedicate her life to the service of the children and the family. These traditional gender roles are constantly flagged throughout the video, and Pettibone explicitly states that she would leave the political life ‘and obviously prioritize motherhood once I have children’ (170[Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_59)a). It is also flagged in the fact that Pettibone decided to adopt ‘Sellner’ as her last name since their marriage.

The second frame explicitly and implicitly constructs a world dominated by the left. All questions related to family and marriage start from the idea that they live as far-right activists in a ‘left-wing’ dominated world. This meta-frame is highlighted in ‘the left’, ‘the globalists’ and ‘Soros funded organizations’ in particular, who they claim are trying to de-platform them, prosecute them and cancel their ‘bank accounts’. This dominance of ‘the left’ is also highlighted in the fact that ‘marriage’ in today’s Western societies is not sacred anymore, that people divorce, and that even polyamorous relationships are promoted. All of this is framed as a consequence of the consumption culture that the left and especially liberals have promoted.

The personal, the networked intimacy and the staged authenticity are deeply political. It is through displaying their personal story – the staged back office of their activist life – that they normalize their political goals, or better, metapoliticize them. This is all the more obvious when Martin Sellner explicitly states that having children is a political act in itself, because not having children ‘is exactly what they – our enemies – want’ ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_59)a: min. 10:17–11:15min), ‘It is a kind of revolutionary act’, it is a kind of ‘in your face against the modern world, all the globalists’ ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_59)a: min. 14:38–11:15min) who don’t want you to marry. Marrying has as a goal to produce children, and thus to reproduce ‘a people’. This framing of marriage and children as revolutionary echoes the great replacement theory where ‘the left’ is ‘replacing’ its people. Within the new right, as we have seen above and broader, the anti-Enlightenment tradition and radical nationalism, ‘the family’ is seen as the cornerstone of the nation, of the community. The prominent trope in new right discourse about the so-called degeneration of society is not only the result of migration and diversity but also of the destruction of the family by individualism and globalism. As Alain de Benoist and Charles Champetier state in their new right manifesto, it is on the local level of ‘the family, the neighbourhood, the village, the city, the professions (…) that one can create a standard of living worthy of human beings, not a fragmented life’ ([de Benoist & Champetier, 2000](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_11)).

The display of intimacy is directly connected to the new right political agenda. The inside view of their honeymoon gives the viewers the feeling of being part of their lives and constructs an image of dedication. Even on their honeymoon, they think about their followers and their political goals. They sacrifice themselves for their cause. The content is also used, just like all other social media content that they produce, to raise money. Most videos they produce not only come with calls to share and to subscribe but also to donate. In some of her videos, Pettibone even explicitly asks and argues why it is important to donate ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_61)c, last 30 minutes). The wedding video is no exception. The issue of de-platforming/demonetizing is raised 171and the video description links to several platforms (PayPal and Stripe in this case) to support their activism and buy her new book. Note also that each video she posts comes with links to all her other channels on mainstream and less mainstream digital channels. In this way, she tries to build an audience on these platforms in the hope of not only having more reach, but also preparing for potential de-platforming.

### Family and relation advice as metapolitics

Since her marriage, the purely political content has become less prominent. The family, marriage, love, happiness, dating, abortion and (white) women and (white) men in general are now key topics on her channel. In the months after her marriage vlog, she posted 17 videos until June 2020 on a wide range of topics: ‘Abortion as a moral good’, ‘The war on men’, ‘What makes Women great’, ‘Why young people are unhappy’, ‘Man Won’t Date “Woke” Women’, ‘Should Women Propose Marriage To Men?’ and ‘Twitter Mob Attacks Mom For Posting Cute Family Photo’. Eleven of these posts deal with relationships and gender-related topics. Even though all these videos seemingly deal with relational topics, they are all deeply (meta)political.

No matter what the topic really is, they all promote a narrative on the so-called dominance of the ‘woke’ and ‘lunatic left’. A world where feminists and anti-racists are willingly destroying the traditional family, marriage and the traditional gender roles of (white) men and women. She describes a world in decay. That decay is visible in the attack on the traditional gender roles, the destruction of the community, and especially the war on men. ‘While feminism may claim to have interest in realizing equality’, Pettibone broadcasts,

> It has shown itself to be far more interested in usurping the traditional male role and that is a war of sort that has been started. Boys and men are not only shamed and belittled for their masculine qualities, their masculinity is deemed toxic, a danger to society even.
> 
> ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_60)b: min: 9:45)

Feminism is framed not as a striving for equality, but as an attack on masculinity and boys, and men in particular. Implicit here is the notion that there is such a thing as ‘pure masculine qualities’ that finds their origins in the biological difference between men and women. Feminism is about the feminization of boys and men, making them into beta males: ‘Meanwhile the feminization of boys and men is upheld, praised and defended. Gone are the days were men valued and respected for their desire to protect and to lead and their societal contributions’ ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_60)b: min: 9:55). We see here how Pettibone supplements the view that also The Golden One is broadcasting: the 172left is destroying traditional families, and especially destroying young men. ‘Not even father-days is safe any longer from the destructive hands of our brave new woke culture’ ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_60)b: min: 09:59).

This ‘left’-wing discourse is presented as the norm in society and thus as all powerful, their discourse is carried by ‘the most powerful institutions: the media, education and entertainment’ ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_61)c: min: 10:27). In contrast to that mass media hysteria, Brittany Sellner portrays herself as the voice of reason or common sense, taking a seemingly middle ground position (see for instance: [Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_61)c: 7:59 [Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_60)b). When she for instance attacks the #metoo movement, she doesn’t do it full frontal, but in a smart, hedged way: ‘I do not claim that society has no need for a movement like the #metoo – movement’, says Pettibone, ‘but if these movements truly do want to accomplish something, they need to be concerned with evidence, fair trials and shining light on all forms of violence, including the violence that affects men’ ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_61)c: 7:30–7:59). Such attacks come with identity effects. She constructs herself as the opposite of the caricature she makes of the #metoo movement. Contrary to them, she positions herself as fair, balanced and only producing evidence-based discourse. This position is reinforced by showing tweets, newspaper and website articles to ‘prove’ her facts. She also includes links to her sources in the bio of the videos. This way of working reminds us of how successful far-right YouTubers like Paul Joseph Watson or Lauren Southern operate. They also carefully construct an aura of ‘evidence based’ discourse to construct their very own idiosyncratic political narrative on the basis of facts, fiction, lies and news taken out of context and re-entextualized in a very different narrative. This type of media literacy enables them to comply with the community standards of YouTube, and thus stay integrated in the digital mainstream and let their metapolitical discourse circulate.

Pettibone’s metapolitical discourse is not new at all but has roots in a two century-old tradition of the anti-Enlightenment. Just like in the anti-Enlightenment tradition in fascist and new right discourse ([Griffin, 2008](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_23); [Sternhell, 2010](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_70)), ‘the Liberals’ and ‘the left’ - Enlightenment, Universalism and Individualism or in short ‘materialism’ – are seen as destroying traditions, the family and the separation of the sexes. This metapolitical work was always done in order to build a new society where traditional values are again put central. ‘We have allowed our society to regress to such a disoriented state, that trying to recover it, would likely take decades and a concerted effort by many many courageous people’ ([Pettibone, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_61)c. min: 10:27). In the conservative revolutionary tradition ([Herf, 1984](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_24); [Sternhell, 2010](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_70); [Mohler, 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_57)), the decline is never accepted, and also today new right metapolitical actors see themselves as the vanguard, the elites who are actively constructing the future ([Faye, 2011](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_17)). And just like all conservative revolutionaries, Pettibone argues that this way forward is found in ‘finding a strong, stable and 173tighten real life community’ ([Pettibone 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_61)c: min: 10:27) built on clear gender roles that celebrate the ‘masculinity’ and ‘femininity’ of men and women.

Brittany Pettibone’s seemingly non-political content is thus deeply (meta)political. It is produced as part of that larger new right metapolitical battle. This political goal cleverly takes the form of self-help content on relations, identity, love and family. The niche that Pettibone is carving out for herself is very similar to the one that people like Mike Cernovish, The Golden One and Jordan Peterson are tapping into. Their success is to a large extent built on a very specific niche of young men and women in search of answers, comfort and self-worth. This niche of ‘Angry White Men’ has over the last decades become a substantial electorate and thus a very powerful and profitable niche ([Kimmel, 2013](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_27)). Pettibone targets this niche and taps or constructs a new one: women and girls who are also struggling in this world. This is the set-up of [Pettibone’s 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_58) book. ‘What Makes Us Girls’ is wrapped in a meta-story of trying to help young girls find their destiny by sharing their personal stories ([Pettibone, 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_58): 4–7). At the same time, it is a metapolitical book. These metapolitical goals are seldom recognized, and the book is sold at major outlets like Amazon and Wordery as a health and lifestyle book. Such a categorization is of course very powerful from a metapolitical point of view: it normalizes the metapolitical goals. The publication of that book, in turn, allowed her to appear on many different YouTube channels, but now as an author dedicated to making young girls happy.

## Metapolitics, trad wives, alpha men and Instagram culture

People do not radicalize in relation to abstract phenomena, but in relation to (a network of) very specific individuals, websites, channels, and discourses, and within a larger socio-economic, political and technological context. The Trump campaign under Steve Bannon succeeded in connecting several of these niches together (the so-called alt-right, incels, #maga-activists, 4channers, anti-feminists, pizzagaters) in one movement ([Maly, 2018a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_34)). Brittany Pettibone and The Golden One are only two of those figures around which a transnational niche came into being. Those niches as we have established are part of a translocal and polycentric network of intellectuals, activists, movements and vloggers dedicated to new right metapolitics ([Maly, 2018a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_34), [2018b](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_35), 2019). They all reproduce key elements of the so-called anti-Enlightenment tradition ([Sternhell, 2010](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_70); [Maly, 2018](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_39)) in its post-WWII new right and identitarian manifestation: organicism, a celebration of inequality, anti-materialism, antifeminism, organic homogeneous groups and anti-leftness (Maly, 2020). But more, they also function as role models, as orders of indexicality: they cater a certain aesthetics, body culture, fashion and style. The influencers are important centres of normativity within the global new right 174niche. It is for instance interesting to note that Dries Van Langenhove, the leader of Schild & Vrienden, not only follows The Golden One and Pettibone, and regularly likes their posts, he himself for instance would stress – echoing The Golden One – that he is against porn and masturbation and stress the importance of body culture for right-wing youth ([De Ceulaer, 2018a](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_12)).

The success of these metapolitical influencers is at least partially due to their knowledge and use of mainstream digital platforms. The programmed connectivity ([van Dijck, 2013](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_79)) and the system of personalization, datafication and vanity metrics help new right influencers to construct a niche, a so-called ‘echo-chamber’, which creates fertile ground for a metapolitical battle. The voice of the metapolitical influencer is produced in a very specific socio-technical context. If they integrate themselves successfully into the socio-technical culture of the platform, they become full members of the attention economy and the platform will contribute to the uptake of their metapolitical battle. Metapolitical influencers are not just ‘using’ these digital media to have an impact and reach. Their integration into the ecology of mainstream digital media contributes to the monetization of the audience labour they activate and gives direction to their digital practices and discourses. This partially explains why known far-right influencers and conspiracy theorists like Paul Joseph Watson, but also The Golden One, Pettibone and Southern, can stay active for so long on YouTube and Twitter. The ‘micro-celebritization’ of metapolitics is a phenomenon that is directly linked to the neoliberal capitalist ideology underpinning the current digital ecology. Their integration and understanding of this ecology at least partially explain their impact. It is the technical construction of digital media and their personalization strategies in relation to influencer practices that shape echo chambers, echo chambers that contribute to the metapolitical project.

It would be wrong, though, to disassociate far-right culture from more mainstream digital cultures. Part of the metapolitical effect is that far-right influencers introduce and appropriate digital cultures, styles and fashions that have clear links to other niches and even the mainstream. We saw it in the appropriation of hip clothing and hairstyles, and we see it in the body culture of The Golden One and the fashion and style of Brittany Pettibone. This focus on culture allows us to at least annotate a classic ‘terrorism’/’radicalization’ studies paradigm, namely that the pathway to radicalization is shaped by the relationship between individual and radical ideologues. This pathway to or process of radicalization is described in the literature as a linear process where individuals move from one stage to the next. It is usually visually represented in a phase funnel model ([De Coensel, 2019](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_13)). Radicalization in this paradigm is about the grievances of a troubled individual who finds a solution or explanation in the ideology of a radical actor. What is blurred out is more mainstream (digital) cultures.

We can illustrate this cultural blind spot through Ebner’s ([2020](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_15)) analysis of trad wives. In her book ‘Going Dark, the secret social lives of extremists’, 175she describes how the trad wives have a strange appeal to her. She explains this appeal in relation to her personal life. Although she does not share the group’s ideology, she uses her breakup with her partner to explain her fascination with the group. Such individual explanations isolate radicalization processes from larger evolutions in society and digital culture. It uses a psychological and personal frame to analyse the impact of radical actors. ‘Everyone’, Ebner says, ‘can be exploitable in moments of weakness, and vulnerability can be a highly temporary concept. The only effective guard is information’ ([Ebner, 2020](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_15): 72).

Radicalization is, as it is so often, presented as a socio-psychological process, where a weakened individual is socialized and radicalized online by far-right actors. This becomes clear when Ebner writes that

> In the end the red pill appears more like a drug that makes its consumer get addicted to the endless chase of an ideal self - whether it’s Red Pill Women desperately trying to be the storybook wife, bending and twisting themselves and suppressing their desires or Red Pill Men attempting to become alpha males, adopting techniques to manipulate and seduce women.
> 
> ([Ebner, 2020](#C_011_c4.xhtml#r4_15): 71)

The drug metaphor implies that ideologues produce drug-like ideologies that get consumers addicted. They sell a bad product that keeps individuals hooked. What the author misses here is that this quest for ‘self-improvement’ fits into a broader and dominant neoliberal culture. Self-care books are - next to cooking books - the most sold non-fiction books. Instagram is full of people helping you become a better version of yourself. These contemporary forms of biopolitics are deeply embedded in mainstream digital culture. Pictures of well-trained alpha males receive thousands of likes on Instagram. The same is true for homemade old school food and pictures of women in feminine clothes. Nostalgia is being sold on a massive scale, and trad wives are occupying only one niche. Trad wives fit within a larger culture, which at least partially explains the success of these groups. For a lot of people, they do not seem all that radical. The metapolitical dimension of far-right influencers is therefore lost (Maly, 2020).

While Ebner’s explanation is of course not necessarily untrue, it is important to stress that radicalization happens in a larger social, economic, political and cultural context. That context is at least as important in understanding how radicalization actually happens. From the moment we include this context in our analysis, the idea of these niches as strange, extremely radical, and very different from ‘the mainstream’ disappears. The boundaries between what is culturally extreme and what is accepted are far more fluid, and that is exactly one of the strengths of contemporary metapolitics: they use existing cultures in order to normalize their ideology and recruit new souls.
