# 5 Data voids, junk news and metapolitics 2.0

DOI: [10.4324/9781003283379-6](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003283379-6)

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

We have established that metapolitics 2.0 and the global new right in general are at least partially defined and enabled by the affordances and interfaces of digital media. The contemporary metapolitical strategies of new right actors are not only crystallizing in the classic metapolitical structures influenced by *La Nouvelle Droite* – think tanks like Spencer’s National Policy Institute, congresses, books, papers and essays – they are fundamentally ingrained in digital cultural practices. The far-right has not only technologically integrated itself, it has also culturally integrated its metapolitical battle in the digital mainstream and even in the hybrid media system in general. The rise of far-right ideas, movements and parties also indicates that this new digital metapolitical battle has uptake and effect on a global scale.

In this chapter, I direct attention towards the role of search engines, data voids and junk news in the metapolitical battle. In order to understand how the far-right tries to metapolitically exploit these data voids and the media ideology that is attached to Google in relation to socio-economic and political contexts, it is relevant to zoom in on three concrete cases. In the first case, I will analyse the so-called Groyper war that was waged against pro-Trump activist Charlie Kirk during Trump’s election campaign. The Groyper war broke loose in 2019 in the slipstream of the Trump campaign and was directed at radicalizing that campaign by targeting Trump’s foot on Campus: Charlie Kirk. Key figures in the fight at the time were Nick Fuentes and Patrick Casey. Fuentes is a far-right revolutionary conservative nationalist that had built a huge following on YouTube. He was also present during the Unite the Right manifestation in Charlottesville and was speaking outside the Capitol building during the riots. Casey on the other hand was the head of the identitarian movement Identity Evrope, 182later renamed the American Identity Movement. The Groypers circulating around Fuentes can be seen as a more localized answer to the alt-right in the glory days of Spencer: they hark back to a radical paleoconservative, Christian nationalist agenda.

In the second case and third, I will show how Covid-19 was used by new right actors and conspiracy theorists to metapolitically mobilize their audiences not only for resistance against the Covid-19 measures, but also to infuse a metapolitical understanding of the current order as being liberal and bad for the people. I start with YouTube conspiracy theory vlogger Paul Watson and look at how he exploits the Covid-19 breaking news data void for his metapolitical agenda at the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic. After that, in the third case, I go deeper into the metapolitics of Covid-19 by zooming out on the relation between Alexander Dugin’s framing of Covid-19 and a more local case: how YouTube channel Kies Dries and Feniks Vlaanderen construct the Corona measures as oppressive.

## Search engines, data voids and metapolitics 2.0

The web can be seen as one giant learning environment and the search engine is emblematic of this. Most people do not realize it anymore, but to ‘surf’ the web in many cases starts by entering something in a search box. This normality is as always, a site of power, or more concretely, it has powerful effects. We search the web to know about movies, entertainment, news or even ‘the truth’. When we open YouTube, we *search* for videos, when we are on Facebook we tap the name of our favourite pages or groups of persons in a *search box*. We navigate the web *through searches*. The search engine in this sense always comes with a media ideology that has the potential to normalize ideas as factual.

### Google and algorithmic agency

Google and YouTube, both part of the Alphabet group, are crucial infrastructures in this learning environment. Since 2015, YouTube has had over 1 billion daily users ([Moore, 2016](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_34): 9). In 2019, 91. 8% of the searches worldwide were done through Google

Google’s discourse about its mission as ‘don’t be evil’ and its claim to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful seems to resonate with users around the globe. If somebody asks a question online, the answer is quite often, ‘Google is your best friend’. This media ideology is also visible in an endless series of memes and GIFs that just order you ‘to Google it’. These are all indications of the cultural impact of the media ideology surrounding Google, an impact that not only guides our online behaviour but also co-constructs how we look at the results that the algorithms of Google present us. Google has become ‘a proxy for quality of information, simply an extension of our collective judgement’ ([Vaidhyanathan, 2011](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_42): 3). Google has reached such dominance that they now have enormous power over what is found and what will remain hidden from the general eye, and thus on what counts as legitimate knowledge and what not. The argument of Thompson ([1990](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_41)) that the commercialization of media is a far bigger threat to the freedom of speech than state control, can be expanded to the digital media of our age. Google leads billions of people towards what they are looking for and in that sense Google functions as their lenses on the world. Google also accompanies us while watching television or scrolling through Reddit, Facebook, YouTube and Twitter. The media ideology, together with the central place that Google occupies in people’s lives, makes it potentially very powerful from a metapolitical perspective. Google is a *de facto* gatekeeper. The company – through its algorithms – determines what will be on the front page of search results. The algorithms running Google are, like all algorithms, not neutral. They are the result of all kinds of decisions on what will be included to define ‘relevance’. Important here, is to stress that it is not just ‘the algorithms as technological artefacts’ that define what will end up on top of the results. To give a desired match, the search engine includes many different signals. The URL of a page, the title and subtitles on a webpage, the general text of that page, metatags, anchors, the links to other articles on that website and the incoming links, are all considered to define its relevance. Note here, that builders of websites have agency here: they can adapt their sites in such a way as to score in Google. The tools are endless: they can focus on building their site in software that allows them to prepare the site for uptake (and thus has a good URL structure, metatags, running on a fast server, …), they can write the texts on the site with search engine optimization in the back of their head and even can use plug-ins (like Yoast SEO) to help them. 184And of course, Google itself provides all kinds of tricks and tools like Google Trends and AdWords to help people to build successful websites. You can even follow courses in the Google Academy on SEO.

Far-right actors are very much aware of this digital ecology and take it very seriously from a metapolitical perspective. Greg Johnson of Counter-Currents, for instance, explains in the context of the educational function of metapolitics, why they list Hitler and Mussolini among the birthdays they commemorate at the Counter-Currents website. The first reason is ideological. Even though the North American new right claims to reject the

> Totalitarianism, terrorism, imperialism and genocide of the old right, they do not reject its political model, its theoretical framework and it’s key figures like Hitler and Mussolini. They claim that they should recognize *their virtues and flaws.*
> 
> ([Johnson, 2013](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_25): 5)

The second reason is found in the fact that those names produce ‘spikes in search engine traffic, which we want to capture’ ([Johnson, 2013](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_25): 6).

Even though Google has become synonymous with search and truth, it is clear that its algorithms direct traffic to many different niches depending on the programming of the algorithms, the search queries and the builders of the websites. Even more, Google has since 2009 embarked on a personalization trajectory. Your results are not necessarily my results. Depending on your own preferences, Google can serve you different lenses in the world. Even though personalization has been highly invested in, depending on who you are and what you have been searching and where you are searching, the result might be very surprising, or worse, discomforting and scary.

A now classic example has been documented by The Guardian. When The Guardian journalist Cadwalladr ([2016](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_7)) typed in the words Jew and Women, the recommendation system of Google suggested search queries as ‘Jews are evil’ and ‘women are evil’. This is not an exception as it can occur on all platforms and is part of a political ideological battle that tries to take advantage of the media ideology associated with Google and increasingly also YouTube. Even though such search engine bombs are well documented, it doesn’t mean that they have become rare. A simple search on ‘Feminism’ on YouTube still gives results that suggest that a lot of anti-feminist content is uploaded and searched for on YouTube. Search recommendations like Feminism vs Logic, Feminism vs men’s rights, feminist cringe or feminist destroyed all assume that feminism is something bad, not rational, cringe and in contradiction with men’s rights. Feminism and feminist are constructed in those automatic suggestions as something we would like to see disappear.

185 

### Metapolitics, algorithmic oppression and data voids

The suggestion of additional phrases in the auto-suggest bar is an attempt by Google to narrow the query and thus give users results that match their interests ([Golebiewski & boyd, 2018](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_22)). But increasingly, we see that many users still seem to stumble onto such biased, racist and sexist autocompletions. Safiya Umoja Noble labels such algorithmic outcomes as algorithmic oppression and points blame almost exclusively to the programmers at Google. She rightfully tries to expose the human biases ingrained in algorithms and stresses that ‘mathematical formulations to drive automated decisions are made by human beings’ ([Noble, 2018](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_35): 1). She highlights that even though algorithms, math and big data all come with the idea of neutrality, objectivity and thus are benign, that is not necessarily the case. As data scientist Cathy O’Neil ([2017](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_36)) also stresses, the algorithms and interfaces reflect the values and ideologies of their makers. These values shape the algorithms, the interfaces and eventually also the effects of them in society. There are plenty of examples of how algorithms and big data enforce racist and sexist stereotypes and deepen inequality in society.

These autocompletions can indeed only be explained when we understand the socio-technical nature of the algorithms behind such search boxes. Important here to stress again is that algorithms only work in relation to data: to human activity. The socio-technical aspect is not limited to the humans doing the programming, we should also focus on what people do in relation to algorithms (see [Bucher, 2018](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_6) for an excellent discussion) in order to explain how the anti-Semitic, racist, anti-feminist, sexist and other far-right content ends up high in search results and auto-completion suggestions in Google and YouTube. A narrow focus on the algorithms and the values of their builders in the back office of digital platforms is too technological deterministic. It erases the responsibility of the users. Algorithms in themselves certainly have effects, but it is equally important to include human agency in trying to use search engines for metapolitical gains. Every professional website, from online shops to news websites, invests in search engine optimization. The dominance of Google is so big that for many sites on the internet, Google is their main source of traffic. Websites are thus built to be found by Google and good editors will apply algorithmic knowledge to make sure that each article is written according to the norms Google installs.

Far-right activists very soon understood the metapolitical potential of the internet and of Google, YouTube and social media in particular. They have invested in using their affordances for metapolitical gains. Individual webmasters have built websites and produced content in such a way that they can be found. More importantly, we see that there is a whole network of far-right websites (see the previous chapters) that link to each other, have social media accounts and have a substantial global uptake through networks of 186social media accounts. YouTube now houses a far-right alternative influence network ([Lewis, 2018](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_27)) where many different vloggers set up collabs to build their audiences. All these actors together form a huge network of sites, movements, individual activists, individual social media accounts, bots and bot networks. Together they are in a position to game the algorithms of YouTube.

Over the years, especially after mainstream media reported dubious results that the search engine produced, Google and YouTube started to invest in creating a more safe environment. Even though Google’s ideology is drenched in ‘freedom of speech’-rhetoric, it has taken measures to suppress hate speech. Like all digital platforms, they moderate while disavowing it ([Gillespie, 2018](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_21): 5). ‘Our products are platforms for free expression’ says Google, ‘but we don’t permit hate speech’ (Google Currents Help, 2021).

As a result of increasing moderation, far-right actors search for new ways to keep themselves technologically and culturally integrated into this mainstream digital ecology. One of their tactics is to exploit data voids. Golebiewski and boyd ([2018](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_22): 1) define data voids as ‘search terms for which the available relevant data is limited, non-existent, or deeply problematic’. Data voids are a result of the way search engines work: they scrape and index existing websites and dig up the most relevant ones for a certain search.

### Metapolitics, junk news and spreadability

The search engine takes a central role within the hybrid media system. To be visible through search is an important aspect of contemporary metapolitics. Another way to become visible is through what Jenkins, Ford and Green ([2013](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_24)) call ‘spreadability’. Spreadability, according to the authors, refers

> To the technical resources that make it easier to circulate some kinds of content than others, the economic structures that support or restrict circulation, the attributes of a media text that might appeal to a community’s 187motivation for sharing material, and the social networks that link people through the exchange of meaningful bites.
> 
> ([Jenkins, Ford & Green, 2013](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_24): 4)

The notion of spreadability directs attention to the socio-technical and cultural assemblage necessary to realize the uptake of a post. Not only do actors need to have access to certain digital media (with their affordances), but they also have to be knowledgeable about the economic, but also political structures that enable but also restrict circulation. From a metapolitical perspective, the cultural aspect is as important: metapolitics 2.0 needs a community that supports metapolitics, and thus actively contributes to its spreadability. This community and the posting actor of course need to stay integrated in the platform. They have to produce content in a form that allows spreading on a certain platform, and they also need to adjust content-wise.

The basic premise of the contemporary attention-driven hybrid media system is grounded in the importance of spreadability, and thus popularity. ‘Friending, following, and trending are not the same functions, but they derive from the same popularity principle underpinning the online economy of social media’ ([van Dijck, 2013](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_43): 13). All these functions are connected not only to the spreadability of content but also to the economic goals of the platforms. Platforms are built around the importance of content circulating and drawing eyeballs; the more users, the more time the users spend online, and the more valuable the platform becomes for advertisers. What is popular will be pushed, and what is unpopular will be algorithmically suppressed. Timing, and thus time and timeliness, are central to spreadability: digital media, and social media platforms in particular, have only increased the importance of breaking news formats, of being first: ‘real-time coverage and hyper-quick publishing have developed in various forms and genres, such as live blogging, push notifications, news alerts and breaking news’. ([Ekström, Ramsälv & Westlund, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_14)). The circulation of ‘fake news’ should be understood in the context of this algorithmically programmed hybrid media system.

Venturini ([2019](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_50)) argues that ‘Viral news’ or ‘Junk news’ is more analytically useful concepts in understanding what is generally called ‘fake news’. He warns that because of its ‘vagueness’, the term easily can become a weapon to discredit opposing sources of information ([Venturini, 2019](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_50): 125). This weaponization of ‘fake news’ is of course essential to the metapolitical practice: what metapolitical actors see as fake is a world that is explained through the globalist paradigm, while the liberal elite sees far-right news as fake, as constructed. That is why Venturini argues that the notion of ‘fake news’ is misleading because it supposes that malicious pieces of news are manufactured, while reliable ones correspond directly to reality, denying the very essence of journalistic mediation in its efforts to select, combine, translate and present different pieces of information in a news story’ ([Venturini, 2019](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_50): 125). This 188is of course not to argue that facts and the truth do not exist, but it is important to understand how actors read/interpret the facts. Failing to understand this is failing to understand how metapolitical actors produce news, not just as fake, but as an alternative reading of the facts, questioning the consensus. This became painfully clear in an interview with Alexander Dugin on BBC ([BBC Newsnight, 2016](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_3)). Dugin starts his answer by arguing that ‘truth’, to him, ‘is relative’ (…). ‘We have our special Russian truth that you need to accept, as something that is maybe not your truth’. The journalist immediately interrupts Dugin, asking ‘Even if it is not true?’. The BBC journalist here chooses not to accept the idea that ‘truth can be relative’, and speaks in terms of absolute truth: something is true or not. In this perspective, Russia is producing ‘fake news’, while the United States is producing truth. From the perspective of the metapolitician, the journalist is reproducing ‘one truth’: the American truth that tries to impose itself as ‘the absolute truth’.

This postmodernist turn started with *La Nouvelle Droite*, and is essential to its ethnopluralist worldview. In this view, truth is connected to certain people, with specific values, norms and traditions. It is this locality that shapes the interpretation of facts, and thus gives ground to several ‘truths’. Important here to realize is that locality, in Dugin’s narrative, is nationalistic, and it is created by the people in power of a nation: the warriors. Or to reframe this in Dugin’s rhetoric: truth is geopolitically constructed. Whereas the United States positions itself as the leader of the world and thus claims the absolute truth, Dugin’s perspective starts from a multipolar world where Russia is also capable of creating its own truth. The difference even goes deeper. The journalist uses a rational orientation towards the truth. Rationality, as a specific orientation to knowledge and truth, is of course intrinsically connected to scientific thinking and especially to Enlightenment (See [Blommaert, 2018b](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_5)). This scientific method is grounded in strictly logical forms of argument, the necessity to have evidence for claims, and is focused on producing ‘absolute truths’. Blommaert contrasts this with reasonability. ‘Being reasonable’, argues Blommaert:

> Is a much less precise orientation to knowledge, and – not to put too fine a point on it – “reasonable” stands for “credible”, something we and our interacting others are ready to accept as true, correct, valid, and to which we are ready to be held accountable.
> 
> ([Blommaert, 2018b](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_5))

Dugin, and with him many new right thinkers, reject the rational method and its outcome. Truth to Dugin is not a matter of the scientific method, but from or of belief ([BBC Newsnight, 2016](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_3)). We could argue that he metapolitically weaponizes ‘reasonability’. And he is not the first anti-Enlightenment intellectual to do this. Within the anti-Enlightenment tradition there was a 189basic hostility towards rationalism, its historicism ‘demolished the concept of a common human nature, of a universal reason that gives rise to a universal natural law, regarding this way of thinking as empty, abstract and above all hypocritical’ ([Sternhell, 2010](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_38): 20). What we thus see in that interview between the journalist and Dugin is a clash between two paradigms: Enlightenment vs anti-Enlightenment, science vs historicism, universalism vs particularism, absolute truth vs relative truth. Dugin’s intervention sees the truth in terms of what is reasonable within a certain context. Or more specifically, the truth is dependent on the soul of the people. In this paradigm, ‘truth’ or ‘knowing’ is the result of the description of the soul of a people ([Maly, 2012](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_29)). It is not the result of a painstakingly, disciplined and detailed methodologically inspired search for the truth, but what is believed by a people. And what is believed by a people is the result of metapolitics, of its culture. This notion of ‘truth’ is also deeply anti-democratic, as the truth is constructed by the elites and not by the common man.

This insight is important, as it underlines why the concept of ‘fake news’ is problematic as an analytical tool in the analysis of the new right. As both the rational and the reasonable approach to truth are grounded in ergoic argumentations, the difference is

> In *how* ergoic patterns can be and are being made, the conditions under which ergoic patterns are being ratified: strict rules of method apply to rational orientations, while such rules are absent (or at least hugely less rigorous) in reasonable orientations.
> 
> ([Blommaert, 2018b](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_5))

‘The reasonable’ approach of anti-Enlightenment thinkers is grounded in the primacy of the organic group. It is the group that determines truth, value and meaning, not science or the scientific method. New right thinkers and activists thus see everything that doesn’t fit their narrative, and metapolitical quest, as ‘fake news’. This framing is not only strategic but also paradigmatic as they do not accept the same notion of what is true and false.

Considering how metapolitics and their conception of truth is connected to digitalization, and thus to the spreadability of discourse, the concept of junk news or viral news is much more productive. It allows us to focus on the *discursive battle for fixing meaning*: on how they try to fix a specific belief in ‘truth’. Junk news allows focussing on the construction of the national or partisan truth or a metapolitical truth that is weaponized to destroy the belief in scientific truths or ‘absolute truth’. This fight is not just a fight for the truth, but a fight for a different world order. Analysing metapolitically weaponized junk news means focussing on its diffusion and uptake of it. ‘It is dangerous’, to quote Venturini ([2019](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_50): 126), ‘not because it is false, but because it saturates public debate’. This saturation not only distracts from more important 190discussions, but it also has potential paradigmatic effects: it makes the rational unreasonable and incredible. It changes how we deal with truth in society, and thus opens a whole can of metapolitical possibilities. This can range from questioning the Corona measures to questioning the whole political and economic system and of course the media themselves. Digital platforms that use deplatforming and delete posts are then not seen as protecting the truth, but as destroying one specific truth in favour of the absolute truth of the globalists. Questioning this ‘absolute truth’, in the words of Dugin, is the start of an awakening ([Dugin, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_12)). This awakening is the result of many different orders of indexicality working on different scales trying to construct a specific ‘truth’. One of these actors is Nick Fuentes, who succeeds in constructing an audience around him and mobilizing them in this battle for meaning.

## Data voids and the Groyper war

Charlie Kirk from Turning Point USA started a Culture War college tour in the fall of 2019. This tour was the first and foremost set up in support of Donald Trump’s re-election. It can easily be seen as a less popular retake of the college tours of Milo Yiannopoulous in 2015 and 2016, who was also set up to get ‘edgy’ support for Trump. By mid-October 2019, Charlie Kirk’s college tour was increasingly haunted by the so-called Groyper and Nicker Groyper Q&A trolls. These offline trolls used the Q&A sessions that were part of the Culture War show format to frame Charlie Kirk as a fake, ‘anti-white’ conservative.

### Charlie Kirk's culture war tour

The 24-year-young Charlie Kirk presented himself as the new cool conservative kid on the block and was hyped as the new conservative wonder-boy ([Guinto, 2019](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_23)). Kirk is the founder of Turning Point USA (TPUSA), a billionaire-funded ‘non-profit’ organization that wants to ‘identify, educate, train, and organize students to promote the principles of freedom, free markets, and limited government’. TPUSA claimed to ‘be the largest and fastest-growing youth organization in America’

In the wake of Trump’s re-election campaign, Charlie Kirk with guests like Rob Smith, Rand Paul and Donald Trump Jr. have embarked on a ‘Culture War’ college tour. The concept of ‘Culture War’ has a long pedigree in the 191United States. Since its rise to prominence, the concept of Culture Wars had a rather negative connotation of radical differences, polarization and, especially in the discourse of Pat Buchanan, it referred to a radical left destroying the nation. Kirk here adopts the concept as a badge of honour to fight for the right for the nation and thus he appropriates an edginess. Kirk adopts a format that Milo adopted four years before and just like Milo’s performances in 2015 and 2016, this college tour was clearly aimed at raising support for Trump by constructing Kirk, Turning Point USA and thus also Trump and his family as edgy and in tune with digital culture. It is also noteworthy that they use nostalgic graphics and superhero-like lighting in the Culture War logo: they are designed to present Kirk as in line with youth culture. In the communication about the tour, Kirk himself is stylized as a fifties kind of reborn Elvis, embodying American nostalgia. The graphic style is reminiscent of an edgy eighties vaporwave neon-light cool, which is also quite common in fashwave art among new right activists and influencers.

It’s not a coincidence that TPUSA was described in mainstream media as making conservativism cool ([Guinto, 2019](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_23)). That was exactly the setup. The whole campaign explicitly positioned itself as an edgy conservative right in the American Culture Wars against ‘the left’. Even more, it took up the same metapolitical understanding of Culture Wars as Milo, Bannon, and Breitbart: as a cultural battle for hegemony ([Maly, 2018a](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_30)). In the words of Kirk: ‘Politics is a by-product of winners and losers of the culture war. To save the culture we must win’. Just like Milo, Kirk was also a regular writer for Breitbart, and his discourse and the tactic of university tours also remind us of the role Milo took up in the 2016 election. But whereas Milo succeeded in unifying the alt-right and alt-light, the Gamergate trolls and 4channers behind Trump, Charlie Kirk struggled to get broad support from the former alt-right and new radical right Christian and America First activists. His legitimacy was explicitly targeted by self-declared Trump fans who questioned his policies on Israel and his betrayal of the heteronormative nuclear family.

### Q&A-trolling Charlie Kirk's Culture War

The Culture War college tour started on 7 October 2019 at the University Of Nevada in Reno, after which the show moved to Grand Canyon University in Phoenix on 21 October, the Colorado State University in Fort Collins and the University of Iowa on 23 and 24 October. The next day, the tour stopped at the University of New Hampshire. During these last stops of the tour, a new phenomenon became visible. More and more new self-declared ‘dissident right’ activists used the opportunity of the Q&A sessions of the show to frame Kirk and what they saw as ‘The Conservative, Inc.’ as imposters and fake conservatives. The old divide and infighting between the alt-right and the alt-light re-emerge but now in a new format, with a network of self-declared 192radical Christian nationalists. These activists go by the name ‘nickers’ – in the sense of fans of extreme-right YouTube personality and host of *America First* Nick Fuentes – or Groypers. Groyper is a meme that first appeared in 2015 on 4chan. It started its life as a version of Pepe the Frog resting his chin on interlinked hands, which then morphed into a figure of its own. Groyper was, again on 4chan, given a new life as a ‘toad, who is friend with Pepe’.

In 2019, the Groypers were a network of young radical Christian conservative activists, shitposters and trolls circling around the Twitter account of @thatgroyper. Many of them used ‘Groyper’ in their profile name. They are white nationalist, deeply conservative, Christian revolutionaries opposing the US alliance with Israel, LGBTQs and the left in general. The Groyper network is known for coordinating targeted harassment against ‘cucks’ and ‘faggots’. The central goal of the Groyper Wars is to mobilize trolls and activists to help push a base of conservatives and Trump supporters in a white nationalist direction (IREHR, 2020). Key figure Nick Fuentes already had a long history within the American radical right and was for instance also present during the infamous ‘Unite the right’ rally in Charlottesville in 2017 and the Capitol Riots in 2020. Another Groyper with history is Patrick Casey of the American Identity Movement (former Identity Evropa).

The Groypers were highly visible on Twitter, even though most of them have a limited number of followers. In mid-October 2019 they went offline and used the Culture War Tour Q&A sessions to launch a far-right ‘Groyper war’ against Charlie Kirk and ‘The Conservative, Inc.’ ([Fuentes, 2019a](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_17)). This phenomenon reached its first climax on 29 October, 2019, when Kirk’s Culture War tour stopped at Ohio State University. As usual, the Culture War rally was live-streamed via Twitter and Facebook. Interestingly, most viewers of the live stream were not watching the stream through TPUSA’s social media accounts but on the DLive channel of rising far new right *America First* vlogger Nick Fuentes. Fuentes used the affordances of Dlive.tv for double screening ([Chadwick, 2017](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_9)) on steroids and broadcasted live comments on top of the remediatization of Kirk’s performance. Interestingly, Fuentes gained far more traction than Kirk: around 4,000 people watched Fuentes commenting on the official TPUSA stream, while only 400 watched TPUSA’s stream.

The reason for this uptake was by then obvious. Nick Fuentes’ audiences – nickers, zoomers and Groypers, as they were called by Fuentes at the time – were hoping that, just like during the Culture War show in Colorado, Groypers would use the Q&A sessions to troll Kirk. According to Fuentes, this first Q&A-troll intervention in Colorado less than a week before started ‘a great crusade by the nickers, the Groypers, by all kinds of right wing people to expose Charlie Kirk (as) a fake conservative, civic nationalist, Conservative Inc.’ ([Fuentes, 2019a](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_17)). Since then, there was a steady escalation of Q&A trolls asking Kirk extreme-right and white nationalist questions. Fuentes’ audience was not let down on 29 October, 2019: 14 people were allowed to 193ask questions after the show, of which 11 were Groypers and nickers. They asked questions aimed at framing Charlie Kirk as pro-Israel, anti-white, anti-American, loyal to a different country, anti-Christian, pro-drag queen and an anal sex-supporting fake conservative. All the interventions in the context of this ‘Groyper war’ were directed towards ‘exposing’ Charlie Kirk as a ‘cuck’ destroying America. This type of activism is quite sophisticated as it makes full use of the affordances of different platforms in the digital ecology. More concretely, the Groypers used Kirk’s show, his live stream and his own social media against him before his own fans. And to add insult to injury, they remediatize it with comments on their own social media where they manage to get even more uptake than Kirk. This sophistication can best be illustrated by zooming in on the Q&A-troll that managed to become the Twitter-talk of the evening on 29 October. For people not in the know, his intervention must have seemed absurd, nonsensical and even a political. This Q&A-troll, just like the one before him, looked like a MAGA kid and even like a supporter of Kirk. He wore an ‘I love ISR’ pin and a ‘socialism sucks’ pin in combination with a red MAGA hat. All indexes of him being a Student for Trump and a supporter of Kirk.

His first words – ‘What a racist question that was’ – also seem supportive of Kirk and his guest on stage, Smith. At first sight, the troll seems to agree with Smith’s qualification of the former Q&A-troll’s question as a racist question, which adds to the interpretation that he is ‘one of them’. That interpretation would soon prove wrong. Let us look at the Q&A session:

*   *Q&A-troll*: I have a quick and fun, light-hearted question for you, Charlie. So, you gave a speech in Jerusalem earlier this year? Were there any awesome fun dancing parties that you guys hit afterwards? Cause I heard that Israelis are some of the best dancers in the world. I mean, if you don’t believe me, Google ‘dancing Israelis’, – it is insane how good their dancing is. Would you agree or disagree with that?’
*   *Charlie Kirk*: Israel is a beautiful country, a great country too’.
*   *Q&A-troll*: ‘It is our greatest ally’.
*   *Charlie Kirk*: ‘Correct’.

This Q&A-troll’s offline intervention was set up, stylized, and formatted as a digital practice. First and foremost, he intervened as a troll using irony to mock the adversary and to make him look like an idiot. Even without considering the digital culture of trolling, the offline intervention cannot fully be understood from an offline perspective. The troll’s performance was clearly produced for digital uptake and addresses not only Charlie Kirk and the audience in the room but all the viewers of the live stream and the multiple re-mediations of that stream. His suggestion to ‘Google dancing Israelis’ directs 194the online audience towards a data void filled with extreme-right anti-Semitic conspiracy theories. This 18-year-old anti-Semitic conspiracy theory is built around the idea that ‘4,000 Israelis’ were absent on 9/11 and 5 were spotted dancing. The Groyper troll here reintroduces this conspiracy theory in the context of a Culture War to highlight that Charlie Kirk’s pro-Israel stance is *against* American interests, and thus to further the America First argument.

This type of message-politics can only be understood and work in the online/offline nexus. The troll not only uses Kirk’s live stream, he uses Google and the accompanied media ideology for a new right metapolitical battle. The Q&A-troll’s intervention uses this media ideology – if you don’t believe me, just Google dancing Israelis – to wrap this anti-Semitic conspiracy theory in an aura of truth. Searching on Google is here used as a synonym for searching for truth.

What may have seemed like an absurd, nonsensical intervention by many of the viewers was met with enormous enthusiasm among the Groypers, nickers and alt-righters on Twitter. The Q&A-troll’s intervention was immediately extracted from the live stream and remediatized within the Groyper network on Twitter. They started to massively tweet the hashtag #dancingisraelis in the hope to get it trending. Googling dancing Israelis after this event (on 30 October 2019) not only directs users to the existing conspiracy theory but also shows several highlighted YouTube clips of the Q&A-troll asking his seemingly nonsensical question. As a result, the Groypers and Fuentes – instead of Kirk – became the ‘talk of the town.’

### Kirk's culture war tour, data voids and metapolitics

Offline Q&A-trolling is thus to be understood within the context of a new kind of activism in a post-digital society, which makes full use of the affordances and media logics of a hybrid media system. Groyper Q&A-trolling amounts to performing a digital practice offline but is clearly not limited to the offline: it carefully hacks the digital communication of its adversary to generate digital uptake. The Groypers’ offline activism ‘hacks’ Kirk’s own media channels to get *their* message circulating. It is Charlie Kirk himself who streams the Q&A-trolling interventions towards his own audiences. ‘Dissident right’ influencers like Nick Fuentes use the affordances of digital media like DLive.tv to take in Kirk’s audience by re-mediatizing his stream and adding live comments. The Groyper network on Twitter, white nationalists, alt-righters, and nickers use Twitter to live comment and to share memes and little extracts of Groypers ‘demolishing’ Kirk’s performances.

This endless remediatization creates buzz around the phenomenon and serves as a recruiting and mobilizing instrument for future Groypers while engaging in Q&A-trolling and other practices. Such networked movements are now quite common metapolitical manifestations. This is not your typical 195old-school hierarchically structured movement, but a movement build around several influencers who function as soft leaders ([Gerbaudo, 2014](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_19)) by hyphening and guiding followers into activism and teaching them how to think and speak (meta)politics. These future interventions will in turn lead to further information flows. And, eventually, they will probably lead to the amplification of their existence and their metapolitical battle’s outreach by the mainstream media, who will feel the need to report on this new type of activism. It is through such seemingly marginal forms of activism that far-right actors seem to succeed in amplifying their message and letting it circulate not only in the margins of the internet but also generate more broad uptake.

Throughout 2019, Fuentes was able to build and mobilize a community of activists around him. He could mobilize this crowd online, not only in the form of trolling actions and crowdfunding but also offline during such Q&A-trolling sessions. In the fall of 2020, he succeeded in mobilizing many of these Groypers or American firsters for different rallies in the Stop the Steal protests and even organizing rallies himself (see the letter of the Select Committee to investigate the January 6th attack on the United States Capitol

## Covid-19, Junk news and metapolitics

Covid-19 is also such a moment of crisis. The pandemic has had an enormous impact on day-to-day politics and far-right metapolitics. It only accelerated the problem of keeping integrated into the mainstream digital media. And this integration was all the more important when offline manifestations became harder and harder to organize. Another issue was that Covid-19 became the dominant news item for months in a row, and thus determined the far-right agenda. The online new right activist had to adjust to this new reality and to a new digital environment. Since the election of Trump in 2016 and the Charlottesville attack in 2017, digital media has become increasingly stricter in their treatment of the far-right online. The libertarian discourse of the mainstream digital media was always accompanied by moderation 196([Gillespie, 2018](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_21)), but since 2016 this moderation was not just focused on what was illegal. More and more platforms developed policies around ‘fake news’, incitement to hatred and the far-right in general. These policies were even intensified after the 2020 elections and the Capitol Riots in the United States when most mainstream digital media platforms designed a strategy of deplatforming and even deplatformization of a substantial part of the far-right ([van Dijck, de Winkel & Schäfer, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_44)).

Covid-19 thus coincided with a new phase in the governance of the digital ecosystem by major platforms like Facebook, Twitter, YouTube and Google. Not just individual users from the fringes, but also massive accounts like the one of Trump were banned (on several platforms at the same time). Even more, the whole movement was the object of de-platformization. This strategy was among other things the result of increasing pressure from the public at large, mass media and politicians on those platforms concerning conspiracy theories, hate speech and racism. When the seriousness hit about Covid-19, we saw an exceptional phase of explicit and visible organization of search results and warnings connected to pages, posts and search results that produced (fake) news about Covid-19.

Considering the lives that were at stake during this pandemic, we for the first time could explicitly see how digital media companies were taking precautions. Several major Western Tech companies – Google, Facebook, Twitter, Linkedin, YouTube and Reddit – declared that they would combat misinformation on the Coronavirus. Tweets and Facebook posts on the Coronavirus came with additional banners from those media with links to reliable sources. On search engines like Google, which had more than enough qualitative news to show, we saw that search results were highly structured. When searching for information on the Coronavirus, Google was very explicit in their interventions: they clearly prioritized official government communication, showing safety tips and local mainstream media news.

### Metapolitics, breaking news data voids and the Coronavirus crisis

New right movements, metapolitical influencers and platforms needed to readjust their discourse and algorithmic strategy in order (1) to keep themselves integrated into the digital mainstream, (2) generate uptake and (3) position themselves vis a vis this new reality. The adjustment to this new socio-technical, political and medical context was not a homogenous process within the global new right ([McNeil-Wilson, 2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_31); [Van Dongen & Leidig, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_45)). This again underlines the importance to understand the globalization of the new right not as a process of homogenization, but as a much more complex, layered, polycentric, transnational and stratified phenomenon. Local movements do not just take over practices and discourses from other movements, but ‘indigenize’ them for local purposes. Thierry Baudet in the 197Netherlands has fully accepted the idea of Covid-19 as a hoax, and part of a large conspiracy ‘the Great Reset’. He aligns, not for the first time, with Alexander Dugin in this case. Also, Pegida in Germany successfully drew the card of Covid-19 as a first step to a totalitarian control and surveillance society ([Volk, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_51)). Other movements have shown themselves more nuanced and restricted (like Schild & Vrienden or Paul Watson who I will discuss here), but they all sought to use Covid-19 for metapolitical purposes, to delegitimize governments and in the end, they used Covid-19 to brand themselves as ‘pro- Freedom’. How they did this completely depended on the chronotope in which they were fighting. Depending on the time and space, we could see movements taking up very different positions. But all of those actors had to take a position and produce content to use Covid-19 for metapolitical goals.

The tired old slogan ‘never waste a good crisis’ has taken on a new dimension in the digital era. Each crisis comes with new search terms and thus new ways in which all kinds of people and organizations try to get their agenda across. The breaking news format has become a central characteristic of the hybrid media system. It of course has its roots in commercial television, where it was used to bring ‘fresh news’ and to report on events that were occurring live. Breaking news as a format was visible in the breaking news banners, live broadcasting and the interruption of the normal schedule broadcasting. ‘Breaking News’ is of course not only an ‘informative format’; it has always been an intrinsic part of a commercialized media landscape. Concretely, it has always functioned as an opportunity for mainstream media to score: to draw in new readers or viewers and to establish themselves as important actors in the media field.

The breaking news format has become increasingly important in an attention-driven hybrid media system. In this new media landscape ‘News organizations have reorganized to prioritize breaking news, understood as crucial in providing the fresh and exciting news feed that online news promise their audience.’ ([Ekström, Ramsälv & Westlund, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_14)). Striving to be the first to bring hot news is at the heart of the battle for virality, and thus also for impact. Especially in cases where breaking news focusses on a rare place or a rare disease for which not many qualitative search results are available, this opens opportunities to drive traffic. Such breaking news data voids also enable actors to optimize their content in order to score top rankings in the search engines of Google, YouTube and other platforms ([Golebiewski & boyd, 2018](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_22)). And even when there is no such data void, or one is not the first to produce content on the hot news, key terms associated with the breaking news still create an opportunity to drive traffic.

Far-right activists, conspiracy thinkers, and right-wing political influencers, as we have seen, have shown to be very skilled and media-literate not only in using breaking news for their political agenda, but also in optimizing 198their content and getting it ready for uptake. The Coronavirus crisis is no exception. The pandemic has been carefully used by these political actors to drive traffic and exploit the public’s attention, to politicize their audience. Counter-Currents ([Costello, 2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_10)), Stefan Molyneux ([2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_33)), Nick Fuentes ([2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_18)) on his America First show, and InfoWars

### Paul Joseph Watson, bat soup and globalism

Paul Joseph Watson was one of those far-right YouTubers trying to metapolitically exploit the Coronavirus from the very start. Watson is a brand of his own. Paul Watson is one of the most successful far-right influencers and conspiracy theorists on YouTube. His videos easily manage to reach several hundred thousand viewers. In 2022 he not only had almost 1, 9 million subscribers, he even succeeded in monetizing his content by getting ad revenue through YouTube. He has been active since 2012 and was deeply involved in the production and reproduction of conspiracy theories on 9/11 and the new world order. In the slipstream, he became active in the pro-Trump camp and was explicitly seen as a central node in the alt-right network by Andrew Anglin of the Daily Stormer ([Anglin, 2016](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_1)). The contribution, said Anglin, of conspiracy theories to the alt-right was questioning mainstream narratives. Richard Spencer, on the other hand, considered Watson as alt-light, as a libertarian individualist in Twitter-fight. If we now consider him as an outsider, as not truly part of the global new right, or not, what matters is that Watson’s discourse produces powerful myths that have a huge uptake. Those myths consistently target globalism, feminism, liberalism, socialism, wokeness and multiculturalism. In other words, his videos are metapolitically contributing to the construction of that new right world order.

The conspiracy theory-producing YouTuber is a master in keeping himself integrated into the digital mainstream. Even though InfoWars and Alex Jones with whom he has been associated for years, have been banned from YouTube, Watson is still very much alive and kicking on the most watched video platform. He is also a master at tapping into existing hypes and driving traffic to his channel. The Coronavirus was thus for him just another 199opportunity to reach a new wide audience and to further a political agenda. One of the reasons for his success is his thorough understanding of search engine optimization on YouTube and the fact that he easily taps into hyped or popular items in the hybrid media system. From the *Joker* movie hype to the bushfires in Australia, Watson seems to have his say on each breaking news item in mainstream media and on YouTube. Paul Joseph Watson is one of those YouTubers that uses each heavily mediatized real-world event to further his political agenda. Already on 24 January 2020, Watson published his first video on the Coronavirus titled ‘bat soup’ ([Watson, 2020a](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_52)). Over 783,000 people have viewed this video so far and more than 16,000 people have commented on it. In the video, Watson manufactures a fearmongering bogus story mixing up facts and fiction. The scientific fact that the Coronavirus was probably transmitted from bats to humans is simplified and reframed in a cultural othering narrative focussing on the ‘habit of Chinese people’ to eat ‘bat soup’. The complex scientific reality of the transition of the virus from bats infecting other animals via their excrement or saliva is completely erased ([Lu et al., 2019](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_28)): the intermediaries transmitting the virus to humans are erased from the picture.

In Watson’s narrative, it is ‘the strange cultural habits of the Chinese’ that are to blame for this pandemic crisis. The combination with the image of a bat in a bowl of soups supports this further. The epidemic is re-entextualized in a, by now, overly familiar discourse attacking the so-called cultural relativism of the left and their moralizations as well as their framing of the right as bigots and racists. The video uses all affordances available to draw in a crowd: it is a short video with a thumbnail that features a scary bat wearing a face mask (indexing the Coronavirus) along with the Chinese flag. Together with the title ‘bat soup’ and the status ‘Eat the bat, bigot!’, the video immediately sparks disgust and fear. Such sensational messages that bring new information, stir controversies and generate instant affective reactions – outrage in this case – perform very well in attention-based digital media like YouTube. Research also shows that ‘Exaggerated, hyper-partisan stories are highly spreadable’ ([Mihailidis & Viotty, 2017](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_32)). Watson is a master at this game. Match this with his timing, and you know how he generates uptake. When most mainstream media were hardly discussing the virus, he already framed it as ‘a globalist disease’.

On 11 March 2019, he posted a second video titled ‘c o r o n a v i r u s’ ([Watson, 2020b](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_53)) accompanied by an emoji with a face mask and the status ‘Thanks, open borders!’ More than 755,000 people viewed the video and it received 77,000 likes and more than 11,500 comments in the first month. This video focuses on the global nature of the Coronavirus and immediately frames it in an existing anti-globalism discourse (Diggit Magazine, 2019). The video makes one point: namely, that any success in the battle against the virus is based on a policy of closed borders. Watson praises Russia, Singapore, 200South Korea and Hong Kong for their swift action in closing their borders and connects this to their success in controlling the virus. All the other measures that these countries have been taking are completely erased. The Coronavirus is used here to stress the deadly effects of globalism and highlight the benefits of closed borders. This frame is one of the dominant frames among far-right movements and organizations in 2020 ([McNeil-Wilson, 2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_31)).

This video by Watson shows the complexity of so-called ‘fake news’. Throughout the video, he uses several mainstream media sources to back his political agenda. Facts are isolated and re-entextualized in a political narrative. As we have seen, Venturini ([2019](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_50): 126) argues that we should understand this type of news not per se as ‘fake’ news but as *viral* news or, better yet, ‘junk news’. Concretely, he argues that we should focus more on ‘diffusion’ than on ‘falsity’. Watson provides a good case for examining these arguments. Watson surfs the waves of breaking news by producing content that simplifies, twists and merges facts with fiction, specifically leaving out certain parts of the truth to make a ‘new’, sensational video like the one in the last example in order to make a metapolitical point: a world without borders is bad for your health. Watson’s content is in the first place ideological (or metapolitical). In order to wage this metapolitical battle, he carefully constructs his content and uses the affordances of the digital ecology to the fullest. The Coronavirus video was not only posted on YouTube, but Watson also used Twitter (and, before his ban, also Facebook), where the video received almost 5,000 retweets. The success of his Twitter account is not only based on his content but also on bots and the bot-like behaviour of his followers. A scan of 2,000 of his followers in Botometer shows that around 20% of his followers are bots or display bot-like behaviour. This type of algorithmic activism boosts interaction, and thus also reach and visibility in this attention-based economy.

Covid-19 was clearly an important topic that drove a lot of viewers to Watson’s channel. Between March and May 2020, Watson published five videos dedicated to Covid-19 and the different government policies. The first videos focused on the origins of the virus and pushed the message that globalism was the real reason that Covid-19 became a pandemic. The following video (Idiots react to Coronavirus, [Watson, 2020c](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_54)) starts with making fun of journalists criticizing Trump’s consistent phrasing of Covid-19 as the Chinese Virus as racist. Not only does Watson make fun of those journalists, he again connects this political correctness narrative to globalism and the refusal to close the borders. In this framing, political correctness becomes the cause of the pandemic and the deaths. Throughout the video, influencers, stars and migrants are portrayed as idiots. This same narrative is produced in the third video (social distancing, [Watson, 2020d](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_55)), where the contradictions between the liberal elites claiming that social distancing is necessary to beat Covid-19, and their own practices and posts asking people to come 201to Chinatown to fight anti-Chinese racism, are highlighted. The main message is exactly the same: political correctness and open borders are bad for your health. It also furthers the meta-narrative that liberals are hypocritical, which is bad for the people. All his claims are accompanied by screenshots of newspaper articles, tweets and clips from TikTok, or get an ironic tone. In essence, his position is carefully drafted to not break the community guidelines of YouTube. Watson doesn’t deny the existence of Covid-19, nor its gravity. On the contrary: in these first videos discussing Covid-19, he blames the liberal, pro-multicultural elites with their political correctness and open border politics for being not strict enough in tackling the pandemic. This narrative is slowly but surely traded in for a new narrative on the ‘control-society’. At the beginning of May 2020, he released a video called ‘Covid-1984’ (Watson, 2020e) hinting at George Orwell’s famous 1984 novel. In that video, he starts again by repeating his position on the hypocrisy of the liberal elites about keeping the borders open for foreigners while pushing for harder measures for the locals. It is by the end that Watson starts criticizing the use of CCTV to monitor social distancing, using anecdotes about the right of the police to stop you from kissing inside of your house, special idea cards to control the freedom of movement and police checkpoints to enforce the quarantine. Whereas Watson in the first videos focused on the lack of policy, he now strongly opposes the surveillance society that he sees emerging (Watson, 2020ge).

## Junk news and the metapolitics of Covid-19: From Dugin to Feniks Vlaanderen

No matter how different new right influencers, politicians, activists and intellectuals frame Covid-19, what they all seem to share is their framing of liberal or left-wing government policies as oppressive. Watson describes it in terms of a big brother society reminiscent of Orwell’s big brother world in his novel 1984. Thierry Baudet frames Covid-19 as part of the Great Reset:

> A transition of the late-capitalist society to a neo-communist one in which climate propaganda as a water melon (green on the outside, red on the inside) controls life and brings it under the control of the state where zero privacy or democracy exists.
> 
> ([Baudet, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_2))

Baudet here follows Dugin who even published a book on Covid-19 as part of the Great Reset. In this book, he tries to theorize two conspiracy theories – the Great Reset and QAnon’s Great Awakening – by recontextualizing them in geopolitical terms. Covid-19 policies are then read as part of the battle of the globalists.

202 

### Covid-19 and the Great Reset as mobilizing myths

Dugin argues that Covid-19 is an excuse to organize ‘mind control (through censorship and manipulation of social media, total surveillance and data collection of everyone) and the introduction of new technologies’ ([Dugin, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_12): 3). Covid-19, says Dugin, is part of the Great Reset. Dugin defines this Great Reset not just as a plan for economic recovery after Covid-19, but as the last stage of (neo)liberal globalization, or globalism. Globalism is all about the destruction of collective identities no matter if they depend on the nation, class or race. This third phase evolves, according to Dugin, around gender and posthumanism ([Dugin, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_12): 12–13), or more concretely around the ‘destruction of Gender as something objective, essential, and irreplaceable’ and the destruction of the human as collective identity ‘that must be overcome, abolished and destroyed’ ([Dugin, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_12): 13). In other words, Covid-19 is part of The Great Reset in the sense that it allows globalists to undo what Trump and the populist wave in Europe have established: the rise of European discontent with mass immigration and gender politics, the Yellow Vest movement, and the election of Trump, who subjected ‘the globalist ideology, practices and goals to hard and direct criticism. And he was supported by about half of Americans’ ([Dugin, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_12): 14). Resistance to the Covid-19 measures is in this sense intrinsically connected to the resistance to the globalist agenda.

We see here again how conspiracy theories function as mobilizing myths. Covid-19 in Dugin’s theory is nothing more than another index of the presence of a globalist elite that tries to destroy its people and is considering becoming totalitarian in order to defend this globalist order. We again, in a different form, are confronted with the interregnum, with the Spenglerian idea that our civilization is in decline and that this decay can be stopped if we hark back to traditional values. Protesting the Covid-19 measures is thus not just a demonstration against specific policies, it is a heroic deed: people are now fighting for their society, for freedom and their identity. They are fighting against totalitarianism. No matter the details of the different new right narratives about the Covid-19 measures, what they all seem to share is that they help construct a Sorelian social myth: it creates a heroic myth that mobilizes the people. If the new right wants to establish this new world order, it has to emotionally touch the masses. As Sorel argued ‘as long as there are no myths accepted by the masses, one may go on talking of revolts indefinitely, without ever provoking any revolutionary movement’ ([Sorel, 2014](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_37): 49)

New right movements around the world have used Covid-19 measures to create such a mobilizing myth. We can see that this critical attitude towards the Corona policies of the different Western governments has paid off for many new right influencers and movements. Not necessarily in the sense of support of a majority who label anti-vaxxers and Corona sceptics 203as dangerous, anti-scientific and undermining the whole Covid-19 approach, but in succeeding to mobilize or at least connect with new audiences who would not see themselves as far-right or even right-wing. Covid-19 allowed new right influencers to reach large new audiences, even if they had to do this from more niched platforms. The Times reported that in 2020, eight of the ten top earners on DLive were far-right commentators, white nationalist extremists or conspiracy theorists in 2020. Nick Fuentes was one of those. It was estimated that he made around $ 1,40,000 through his DLive streams that year ([Bergengruen, 2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_4)). This metapolitical reach led to a large mobilization of power. In different countries around the world, far-right influencers, movements and politicians succeeded in setting up large protest marches against their governments and the Corona policies.

In Belgium, we saw how the far-right political party Flemish Interest tried to surf and make the waves of the anti-Corona protests. N-VA, the radical right party more to the centre than Flemish Interest, also criticized the Corona measures from the federal Belgian government, while they were at the same time deploying them on the Flemish level. Flemish Interest was also actively mobilizing their militants to go to the Corona protests. Dries Van Langenhove, elected for Flemish Interest and president of the identitarian movement Schild & Vrienden, was very vocal in this anti-Covid-19 policy. Even though he was less explicit than Baudet, Dugin or Fuentes, he too zoomed in on the lack of freedom and the devastating surveillance state that Covid-19 gave birth to. Kies Dries is his YouTube channel and the name of one specific format. That format – Dries Van Langehove sitting at a desk in a news anchor pose addressing his audience – echoes the format of Nick Fuentes on his live streaming show. On his channel, Van Langenhove has posted several vlogs, podcasts and episodes of his YouTube show Kies Dries dedicated to Covid-19. On average, those vlogs were watched between 9,000 and 16,000 times, which makes them among his most watched YouTube videos. The videos themselves come with explicit flags that direct the users to more information on Covid-19, but none of his videos, as far as I could see, has been banned, and his account is still up and running. This shows that Van Langenhove succeeds in producing a metapolitical discourse without crossing the norms of the community guidelines.

The central narrative in Van Langenhove’s posts targets ‘the unconstitutional and far-reaching policies’ that the Belgian government has put into practice and the role of politicians and virologists in this. Especially Marc Van Ranst, the Belgian Fauci, is the target ([Van Langenhove, 2021a](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_46)). Van Ranst is an ideal target for the far-right, as he is known not only as a virologist but also as a left-wing, anti-racist and anti-far-right intellectual. Van Langenhove even compared him with Stalin ([Van Langenhove, 2021a](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_46)): an all-powerful dictator. Van Ranst, says Van Langenhove ([2021b](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_47)), has contempt for the people and therefore uses lies to manipulate the people. Contrary to Sweden, 204says Van Langenhove, our elite did not trust its people to behave and didn’t take reasonable measures. In order to further frame Van Ranst as a liar and a manipulator that is not to be trusted, he dug up an old lecture from Van Ranst on crisis communication during pandemics ([Van Langenhove, 2021b](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_47)). In that clip, which was widely circulated online, we see Van Ranst explaining how you can at the start of a pandemic communicate with the media in order to make the people conscious of the danger. Van Langenhove reframes this, by suggesting dark and manipulative behaviour. The effects are clear: The people don’t believe the elites anymore, and trust their own intuition and observation ([Van Langenhove, 2021b](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_47)). Covid-19 is thus framed in a populist logic, where governments and virologists are presented as elites who rule against the voice of the people, who lie and manipulate. Governments and their policies are framed as undemocratic.

Even though Van Langenhove avoids explicit reference to the Great Reset, he does create a very similar narrative about the birth of a totalitarian society. ### Feniks and the Corona protests

Van Langenhove’s metapolitical work around Covid-19 was largely produced in his capacity as a politician for Flemish Interest and on his YouTube channel. Schild & Vrienden was rather absent in the Covid-19 debate, but all of a sudden a new organization took an important role in the Corona protests in Belgium: Feniks. Feniks, represented by Stephan Vanberingen, which is an alias for Sacha Vliegen, was next to Sarah Melis and Ezra Armakye one of the faces of the massive anti-Corona protest march in Brussels on 21 November 2021. Sacha Vliegen was a member of Voorpost, an extreme-right movement in Flanders, the Netherlands and South Africa, and is a member of Schild & Vrienden. This link to Schild & Vrienden is clear in the formatting of the Feniks website. Even though the organization is brand new in 2021, it immediately had a web shop with a sweater and several stickers. The design of the webshop is a duplicate of the Schild & Vrienden webshop. The dominant blue has been replaced with bordeau and the Schild & Vrienden logo has been changed into Feniks, but the overall structure of the webshop is the same.

Feniks presents itself as a ‘metapolitical collective’ that wants to build an ‘antithesis against contemporary globalism’ ([Feniks, 2022](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_15)a). Its motto is ‘Past left and right. Against globalism’. This positioning of Feniks clearly echoes the language of *La Nouvelle Droite*, and especially of Guillaume Faye and Robert Steuckers. That is not coincidental, as Feniks publishes on the Synergon Info blog of Robert Steuckers ([Feniks, 2022](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_15)a, b). Steuckers is a Belgian new right intellectual, a close friend and partner of Guillaume Faye and a former member of *La Nouvelle Droite*’s Studies and Research Secretariat ([Steuckers, 2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_39): 45). Steuckers, just like Faye, fights for European civilization and against Westernization or Americanisation. The new right, according to Faye and Steuckers, was ‘a barrier of resistance to Westernism, Atlanticism and the policies of resignation and submissions that these negative forces led to all around Europe and particularly in Belgium’ ([Steuckers, 2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_39) 45). They stood for ‘serious metapolitics’ and wanted to avoid ‘reckless entryism’. This serious metapolitics was grounded in ideology, an ideology where the state did not only intervene in the economy but also took ‘into account non-economic factors’ ([Steuckers, 2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_39): 66).

This legacy of Steuckers and Faye is clear in the discourse of Feniks. As we can see in the Facebook post below, the intertextuality between Steuckers, Faye and Feniks is explicit: All fight against Atlantism and for European civilization. Feniks published two blogs on their site that were simultaneously published on Synergon Info, a blog by Robert Steuckers in Dutch and translated into German. The first blog was dedicated to the war in Ukraine under the title ‘No more brother wars’ ([Feniks, 2022](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_15)a). The second post focused on identitarianism (and why people claim it would be racist ([Feniks, 2022](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_16)b). This identitarianism is negatively defined by Feniks by referring to migration 206as an identitarian and cultural threat, and positively by referring to the anti-Enlightenment tradition of Herder (which they label counter-Enlightenment or gegen-Aufklaring). The French Revolution, just like with many new right intellectuals, is seen as an attack on the people. Feniks is convinced that this fault line is still very relevant today. On the one hand, you have the Davos – people ([Feniks, 2022](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_16)b), or liberal globalists. These globalists think that their ideals, culture and norms should reign the world and that they should be the basis of a global culture. They refer to a quote of the Flemish Liberal politician Gwendolyn Rutte, who said that ‘Our culture is superior to other cultures and it is fair to say that’. This is read by Feniks ([2022](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_16)b) as ‘A direct reference to the linear view of history and the universal blueprint that should serve for global civilization’.
