Een breuk met het ‘Transatlantische partnerschap’ is noodzakelijk om tot Echte Europese soevereiniteit te komen. || The Sovereignty of Europe remains non-existent as long as it remains subordinate to the United States in its foreign policy. A break with the ‘Transatlantic Partnership’ is necessary to achieve Real European sovereignty. |

*Source:* Facebook page of Feniks.

At the other side of the fault line, Feniks argues, you have the anti-Enlightenment thinkers like Spengler, but also Dugin, who argue ‘That different civilizations can coexist and negotiate on an equal footing.’ Here we see how, with references to Dugin, Herder and Spengler, they introduce a pluralist view of the world where societies are equal but different: ‘Every culture is culturally equivalent according to that principle, even if cultures are at a different stage of their development, or organize themselves according to completely different (eg religious) principles’ ([Feniks, 2022](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_16)b). It is this ethno-pluralism that again allows them to position themselves as the true antiracists, and the globalists as those who herald an imperialist superiority thinking. Not only liberals, they say, but also the left in the form of cultural Marxists has accepted this globalist ideology. What is worse, according to them, is that these globalists and the cultural Marxists destroy collective identities, which in the end will lead to the destruction of European culture and civilization (207[Feniks, 2022](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_16)b). It is thus the identitarian embrace that will save the diversity of the people and humankind.

This identitarian anti-Enlightenment ideology coincides with the Corona protest. The fight against globalism is also a fight against tyranny. The main narrative of Feniks to mobilize against the Corona measures of the Belgian government focusses on freedom. In a Facebook video titled ‘For Freedom, against the System’, posted on their Facebook pages, we see that in the protest march, members of Feniks walked in Feniks sweaters, white masks holding a banner saying ‘No compulsory vaccination, No compulsory masks, no lockdown, no vaccination id’. The following status was posted together with this video:

> Be a free thinker, never accept everything you hear as truth. Be critical and evaluate everything you believe in. The European population has awakened from a psychosis of fear. Globalist politicians like Alexander De Croo and Conner Rousseau are on the losing side. 2022 is the year we take back our freedom!
> 
> (Feniks, Facebook post, 24 January 2022)

Note here how the protest is framed in terms of the ‘European people’ who are awakening. Even though they talk about the Belgian protests, those protests are framed in a European civilizational discourse reminiscent of Steuckers and Faye. And just like Dugin theorizes Qanon and Trump by making use of the InfoWars concept of the ‘Great Awakening’ ([Dugin, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_12): 27), Feniks sees the protests as a process of awakening. Those awakened European people are positioned against ‘Globalist politicians’. Covid-19 measures are thus framed in relation to the globalist ideology, a globalized ideology that is nothing more than tyranny. ‘Today’, Feniks writes in another Facebook post on 23 January, ‘Politicians are taking advantage of a crisis to implement far-reaching control measures for the population. Today we see the consequences of social engineering. Constitutional freedoms should not become conditional’ (Feniks, Facebook post on 23 January). Notice how Covid-19 is not denied, not framed as a hoax, but as a crisis that is used to push a surveillance society.

Feniks thus promotes a discourse quite similar to that of Van Langenhove and Flemish Interest on a local scale, and echoes Steuckers, Dugin’s and Faye’s discourse on Europe, globalism and Atlantism. This discourse tries not only to capture the anger that some people felt during the pandemic, it clearly tries to metapolitically construct and channel that anger away from the concrete anti-Covid measures in the direction of globalism as the main target of resistance. Looking at the uptake of that narrative on their social media, it is clear that it doesn’t resonate with a large mass of people. The maximum amount of likes on posts is around 80 or 100. The massive 208mobilization for the marches in Brussels has thus not been done through the explicit metapolitical discourse of Feniks, but through a more neutral and specific discourse around freedom and criticism of government policy. Feniks did play a crucial role behind the scenes in organizing the marches ([Eeckhaut & Cools, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_13)), including Dries Van Langenhove. Melis was trained by Van Langenhove to communicate with the media. Feniks is thus a metapolitical vehicle of Schild & Vrienden, one that was not known as having far-right sympathies. The massive mobilization is thus the result of a more specific discourse which allows far-right actors to hide behind a respectable front in order to bring together many different niches, and many different channels and local and translocal actors just like the Capitol Riots. They succeeded in merging national and international anti-vaxxers, hipsters on the verge of bankruptcy, holistic believers and extreme-right activists together in a massive march: 35,000 protestors were estimated to join the protests. From a metapolitical perspective of these massive mobilizations as interesting, it allows the organizers to use the populist format and present their discourse as the voice of the people, but it also has the potential of building a larger audience.

The metapolitical move of Feniks backfired from the moment that mass media saw that spokeswoman Sarah Melis wore a Feniks sweater and discovered the links between Feniks and Schild & Vrienden. The eruption of violence after the protests in November ([Cardoen, Decre & Baert, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_8)) also didn’t help, as it became clear that those protests were not ‘just the people’ who were fed up with the Corona policies, but that mass media started to write about how the extreme-right ‘hijacked the protests’ ([Eeckhaut & Cools, 2021](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_13)).

## Junk news, data voids and metapolitics

The massive attention to and communication of mainstream media sources, government and health institution information on the Coronavirus had a double effect. On the one hand, it made it more difficult to ‘stumble across’ junk news. On the other hand, it created suspicion and thus a market for people actively searching for ‘alternative news’ on the virus. Especially people distrusting governments and mainstream media – a public that had been carefully built up in recent years – see these interventions by mainstream digital media as censorship, proof of the Deep State’s existence and even dictatorship. This narrative has shaped a very large niche over the years, which far-right activists have exploited very meticulously during 2020 and 2021, resulting in massive offline demonstrations all over the world. Meticulously meant in this case very careful communication in search of a metapolitical niche that navigates between the enforced discourse on Covid-19 by algorithmic and human moderation, and the quest to use Covid-19 for metapolitical 209goals. But Covid-19 also had a huge impact on new groups of people, and far-right movements and influencers tried to reach those groups and mobilize them, not only for the direct resistance to the Covid-19 policies but also against globalism and the Great Reset.

In all cases analysed, we have seen in detail how far-right activists are integrated into mainstream digital infrastructures and how they mobilize them and the accompanying media ideologies for metapolitical goals. The cases of Paul Joseph Watson, Schild & Vrienden and Feniks illustrate how metapolitical activists use media hypes and global crises to further their metapolitical agenda. It also illustrates how they fully understand the hybrid media logic and exploit it skilfully. Digital media enables activists to reach a large audience by surfing the hype of the moment. Even if social media and mass media are dedicated to weed out ‘fake news’ and conspiracy theories, metapolitical influencers and activists succeed in finding ways to reach their (algorithmic) audiences. The scale social media operate on, and the diversity of platforms, makes controlling metapolitically charged junk news a complex affair. The statements issued by tech companies on hate speech and fake news sound promising, but the point here is that the problem of junk news is a fault of the system. All digital media monetize reach, engagement and even production of content by their users. Junk news is a product of this configuration of the digital ecology and it won’t be fixed with a technological patch. And that is exactly what Big Tech companies rely on. They propose *technological* fixes for combatting this phenomenon of junk news. All too often, this battle against ‘fake news’ focusses on binary logic: whether something is ‘fake’ or not, a producer trustworthy or not. This type of evaluation is not only very hard to make, but it is even harder to programme. In the worst cases, it leads to involuntary blocks ([Koetsier, 2020](#C_012_c5.xhtml#r5_26)) or (shadow) banning of users, but in reality, it often means that non-mainstream media have less reach but also that more subtle types of junk news still circulate. Metapolitical influencers navigate this newly regulated digital ecology carefully and try to stay integrated into the digital mainstream. Watson’s posts, just like the posts of Van Langenhove and Feniks, are still visible on Twitter and on YouTube, reaching ever more people.

Deplatforming in itself is clearly not a silver bullet. Nick Fuentes was for instance banned from YouTube, but he was still very visible on Twitter where he is promoting his different media platforms. And even if DLive suspended his account after Fuentes’ role in the Capital Riots, he has now set up his own streaming platform AmericaFirst.live and his own conference AFPAC. He also managed to have over 10,000 followers on GAB. Important to realize is that while metapolitical actors prefer mainstream digital media, they also prepare for deplatforming by trying to build audiences on new platforms where they are allowed to speak more ‘freely’.

# 6 Metapolitical terrorism and digital media

DOI: [10.4324/9781003283379-7](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003283379-7)

This chapter has been made available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license.

I started this book with words from Brenton Tarrant, the Christchurch terrorist. Fifty years after the founding of GRECE, the metapolitical project seems to have come full circle and ended up not only in the rise of radical right politicians, parties and movements, but also in violence. Dylann Roof in Charleston, Brenton Tarrant in Christchurch, Stephan Balliet in Halle, the Charlottesville car attack, the Capitol Riots, the Buffalo shooting and many smaller violent attacks around the globe illustrate how, in the end, the metapoliticization of the far-right seems to breed violence. Several scholars connect the rise in far-right terrorism to digital media ([Auger, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_2); [Crawford & Keen, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_20); [Weimann & Masri, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_80)). Most attention goes out to the role of conspiracy theories, leaderless resistance and the gamification of terrorism ([Ebner, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_25); [Schlegel, 2021](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_64)a, [2021](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_65)b). A key metaphor in contemporary work on digitalization and far-right terrorism is the idea that far-right terrorism is the effect of ‘a virus of hate’, as Weimann and Masri describe it ([2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_80)). The problem with such a virus metaphor is that (1) it conceptualizes people as helpless and passive creatures (Jenkins, Ford & Green, 2013d), susceptible to ‘the virus of hate’ that some radical right individuals and groups distribute, and (2) the far-right message is portrayed as inherently very powerful.

From an ethnographic perspective, it becomes very clear that radicalization does not happen in a vacuum: it is a layered and complex process. The virus metaphor and also the funnel theory at least partially obfuscate the role of culture and context in general. Radicalization always occurs in specific social, economic, political and technological contexts. In other words, the virus metaphor creates a blind spot for the metapolitical dimension: the fact that metapolitical activists use digital cultures and mainstream cultures in order to normalize their ideas. Understanding the transnationalization of far-right terrorism 214makes studying culture and the meaning-making infrastructures compulsory. The role of digital metapolitics in the so-called fifth wave of terrorism ([Auger, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_2)) and the digital infrastructure of that terrorism has received too little attention. Even more, a lot of those new far-right terrorists have used their killing spree to amplify their voices. This mediatization is a key aspect of that violence. Far-right terrorists carefully prepare the (digital) media uptake of their attack. They build websites, write manifestos, stream their terrorist act or make sure that mass media reports on their violence. They even use their trials to communicate their ideological message to the world. Their terrorism uses hybrid media logics to steer the information flow in the global media system.

In this chapter, I zoom in on the link between that violence and the discourses of *La Nouvelle Droite*, the *identitarian movements* and the American white nationalist media by analysing the manifestos of Dylann Roof and Brenton Tarrant from an intertextuality perspective. The ethno-differentialist discourse of *La Nouvelle Droite* was increasingly drenched in a rhetoric of war, and when such discourse hits the streets, it breeds violence. A discourse analytical approach that focusses on the relation between discourse and violence, and includes a notion of symbolic violence, leads to questioning black and white distinctions between metapolitics and violence, as some scholars seem to assume ([Ravndal, 2021](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_61)). Adopting a cultural perspective makes visible that even though Roof and Tarrant have been socialized in quite different far-right niches operating on different scales within the global new right, they both started from a shared hegemonic notion within the global new right that there is an undeclared war going on. That is why they saw their violence as necessary, not only to defend the ‘white race’, but also to create consciousness about that ongoing war.

Both terrorist acts are emblematic of what I call metapolitical terrorism. Their killing sprees were not only executed to instill fear, but they were also instruments in a cultural war to make ‘white people’ concious about ‘the great replacement’ and to spur them to action. Such metapolitical terrorism of course has a very paradoxical effect. On the one hand, it undermines the traditional metapolitical project by de-normalizing it and highlighting the inherently violent nature of far-right ideologies. On the other hand, within their niche, it normalizes violence by gamifying, praising and framing it as cool and necessary. Andres Breivik, Dylann Roof and Brenton Tarrant are not only central figures in a global far-right culture that celebrate their violence and bravery. They have become edgy memes themselves that are used to normalizing their violence.

## The great replacement and the re-emergence of far-right violence

When de Benoist and *La Nouvelle Droite* introduced metapolitics and ethno-differentialism, it was introduced, as we have seen, as a fundamental renewal of the far-right, a step away from the violent far-right tradition of pre-war 215fascism. This metapolitization of the far-right has been very successful. It met an urgent need of some far-right actors on the margins after the World War II, when even ‘fascism’s more astute activists’ realized ‘that the age of mass armed parties led by charismatic leaders was dead, and that in order to survive at all as an ideology in the absence of a pervasive palingenetic climate, it had to be extensively overhauled’ ([Griffin, 2000](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_32): 165). In the decades after the erection of GRECE, this metapolitization not only inspired far-right intellectuals but also inspired and motivated far-right activists, journalists, political parties and movements to invest in a metapolitical battle. Already in the nineties, we saw that the new, so-called radical right populist parties like the FPÖ in Austria, Vlaams Blok in Belgium and Front National in France, succeeded in translating this metapolitization and especially its ethno- differentialism into electoral capital. Vlaams Blok (Flemish Bloc) as a party had clear connections with the collaboration milieu in Flanders but won election after election with a discourse that combined neo-racism (or a differentialist anti-racism) with an ethnocratic position. Even more, it succeeded in conquering hegemony on concepts such as democracy, culture, integration and migration ([Blommaert, 2007](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_6)). We see an interesting historical parallel here. Differentialism was not an invention *of La Nouvelle Droite*. The first differentialist was probably Joseph Gottfried Herder. In the final analysis of the Herderian multidimensionality, Sternhell argued that Herder’s historical significance was his contribution to the rise of ethnic nationalism ([Sternhell, 2010](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_69): 275–278). It was this cultural nationalism that in the end gave birth to political nationalism and violence.

The story repeats itself at the end of the 20th century: *La Nouvelle Droite’s* cultural battle became a successful political battle. Guillaume Faye was very much aware of this, and argued at the end of the nineties that political parties and activists had an important metapolitical role: they too produced and were able to circulate ideas and could do it on a much larger scale ([Faye, 2010](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_26): 28–30). It was in the wake of that radical right success that Faye argued for a more Gramscian way of understanding metapolitics. This, of course, didn’t include the notion of class, nor did it focus on realizing a communist society or the building of a united front against fascism ([Anderson, 1977](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_1); [Corijn, 2021](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_19)). What Faye meant by ‘adopting of more Gramscian’ understanding of metapolitics was including political parties and movements in the metapolitical strategy, and thus moving beyond purely intellectual metapolitics. The identitarian movement is an example of this new, more activist metapolitical avantgarde ([Maly, 2022b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_51)). Interesting to note, is that this broadening of metapolitics was also accompanied by a more explicit discourse. Not only the concept of decline and the stress on the need for rebirth or renaissance was present, it also came with a more combative discourse. Faye’s ‘Why We Fight’ was drenched in a rhetoric of war. The keywords from the table of contents alone highlight that his discourse immersed people in the idea of civil 216war. Faye talks about enemies, colonization, the dangers of disarmament, the ‘menace of the South’ and the ‘domestic Front’. Faye doesn’t leave room for doubt: Europe, according to him ‘is at war’ but she ‘doesn’t even know it’ ([Faye, 2011](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_27): 29). The role of Faye’s metapolitics is to let people understand their situation as a war-like situation. ‘We Europeans’, he writes,

> Are rapidly and massively being occupied and colonized by peoples from the South and by Islam. (…) Europe is the sick man of the world. It’s obvious in her demographic decline, in her physiological devirilisation, and in the reigning ideology of ethnomasochism, imposed by politically correct censors and the controlled media. We are gnawed at from within and attacked from without.
> 
> ([Faye, 2011](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_27): 29)

This war is a war that threatens the culture, traditions, values and identity of European civilization. If nothing changes, he writes in 2000, ‘in two generations France will no longer have a majority European population, and this for the first time in her history. Germany, Italy, Spain, Belgium, and Holland are on the same catastrophic path, just a few years behind us’. He creates an apocalyptic urgency that needs direct action right now. Faye therefore calls for a reconquest in the name of ‘our people’ and ‘our identity’ ([Faye, 2011](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_27): 264). Nothing is yet lost and pessimism is not an option, according to Faye. He serves his readers a clear dichotomy: ‘In history’, he says, ‘it’s always struggling minorities who make the difference, not the amorphous masses. And it’s no longer a matter of Left or Right either, but whether you’re part of the resistance’ ([Faye, 2011](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_27): 30).

Faye is echoed in the writings of Generation Identity activists. Identitarian Markus Willinger, for instance, starts his book with the following sentences:

> Europe is in a deep crisis (…) it is a crisis of the European spirit. (…) The people of Europe have lost their will to live; they are dying out, because they don’t want to thrive any longer, because they don’t want to have any more children, and because they’ve forgotten what it means to stand up and fight for one’s own.
> 
> ([Willinger, 2013](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_81): 13)

Willinger takes up the narrative of decline, and frames migration, just like Faye, in terms of ‘colonization’ and ‘invasion’ and natality rates and family policies. ‘Never before in human history’, he states, ‘have foreign people invaded to such an extent into a populated region without encountering any resistance from its indigenous residents’ ([Willinger, 2013](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_81): 14). That is why he, and Generation Identity in general, declares war against the 68 ers and the colonizers (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_29); [Willinger, 2013](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_81)). Just like the anti-Enlightenment tradition 217started as a cultural battle and evolved into a political battle grounded in a biological understanding of groups, we see that the cultural and linguistic definition of groups morphs back into (1) a biologically determined view of culture, (2) a political and even a violent battle. The fight for identity in the discourse of Faye and Generation Identity is in the end not only a fight for a ‘biocultural identity’, *but* it is also clearly described as a rhetoric of war, colonization, defending and thus holding the seeds that can grow out in real physical violence.

It is not enough to stop ‘the invaders’, a successful reconquest is also a question of the will and of demographics and family policies. Generation Identity not only takes on board the identity concept of Faye or his narrative on the decline, but they also stress the urgent need for ‘reconquest!’ (Generation [Identity, 2013](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_29): 19). This combination of the motive of decline with the stress on the possibility and necessity of rebirth is what Griffin calls the palingenetic creed ([Griffin, 2008](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_33): 37). He sees this creed as an essential characteristic of generic fascism. This palingenetic creed is also an essential ingredient of the contemporary new right ([Bar-On, 2013](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_4)). The focus of *La Nouvelle Droite* was always, says Bar-On, directed towards the construction of a different modernity. This future society, according to Faye, has to be made by blending the archaic and the new, the modern. And action is needed now. These calls to action cannot be read as metaphors only. ‘Ideas spur people on to action, and even when they are only rationalizations of psychological or social pressures or economic processes, intellectual constructions rapidly acquire a power of their own and become autonomous political forces’ ([Sternhell, 2010](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_69): 30). As we have seen, the ideas of *La Nouvelle Droite* have been taken up by activists and movements around the world, and they have become not only a political force, they also became a source of violence.

One central idea that we find in almost all manifestos of far-right terrorists is the myth of the Great Replacement, also known in slightly different versions as ‘white genocide’ or ‘the colonization of Europe’ ([Crawford & Keen, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_20)). On the website of The Daily Stormer, visitors can see a demographic counter that projects the replacement of whites in the United States. The idea has already escaped the margins. This idea is for instance also promoted in books of far-right political parties like Flemish Interest in Belgium ([Van Grieken, 2017](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_76)a; [Maly, 2020b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_50)), but also in the discourse of more centre-right politicians of the Christian Democrat party. This theory, according to Ebner ([2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_25): 236) combines ‘all four features of a violence-inciting ideology, so-called ‘crisis narratives’: conspiracy, dystopia, impurity and existential threat’. In what follows, I want to discuss two cases of white terrorism that are motivated by the idea that they should help save the white race and make people conscious: (1) The shooting of Dylann Roof and (2) the murderous killing spree of Brenton Tarrant. I will discuss both cases not only as examples of metapolitical terrorism but also as reflecting the integration of those actors in different far-right niches within the global new right culture. 218Dylann Roof will be analysed as an American white nationalist terrorist operating on a more local scale. I will show how he is socialized online in relation to white nationalist sites such as American Renaissance, the Council for Conservative Citizens and The Daily Stormer, but also in relation to more traditional neo-Nazi sites such as Stormfront. Those sites form communities and learning environments on an American scale. Even though most far-right sites and organizations denounced his murderous riot, his discourse and to a lesser extent even his terrorism eventually generated global uptake. Not only did he became memefied, his manifesto was framed as a product of ‘truth-seeking’ and even more other white nationalist terrorists followed in his footsteps. As a result of this ‘audience labour’, his localism became globalized.

Brenton Tarrant referred briefly to Roof, but he clearly was influenced by far more sophisticated discourses and terrorist practices. He operated on a higher scale of cultural globalization. Even though he is an Australian, he travelled the world, sought contact with far-right movements in different countries and was socialized in new right communities that operate on a more globalized scale. His discourse is deeply influenced by identitarianism and far-right meme and streaming culture on 8Chan. If Dylann Roof speaks like an old school racist and American white supremacist, Brenton Tarrant represents the *metapolitization* of far-right terrorism. Interesting, though, is that both terrorists see their act not only as part of that ongoing war against invaders; they also see it as part of the culture war.

## Data voids and Dylann Roof's metapolitical terrorism

17 June 2015. Dylann Roof enters the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston. From the anti-slavery movement, over the 1968 civil rights movement until today, this 200-year-old church – one of the oldest ‘black’ churches in the United States – has had a strong commitment to the civil rights movement in the United States. That commitment was targeted by Roof, shooting ten and killing nine of the believers that day. Roof imagined himself a warrior in a centuries-old civil war. His killing spree was planned and executed not only to generate fear but also as part of a larger metapolitical goal. Roof wanted to spark up a new civil/racial war and the first step to achieve that was to make whites racially conscious. Seen from the perspective of an attention-based media system, his murderous riot can also be read as a way to generate attention for his manifesto.

### Dylann Roof, metapolitics and white nationalist terrorism

The central problem of today, said Roof, is that white people are not racially conscious anymore. In his opinion, modern history classes, media and rules 219make whites racially unconscious (Roof, 2015: 2). ‘Black people are racially aware almost from birth, but white people on average dont (sic) think about race in their daily lives. And this is our problem. We need to and have to’ (Roof, 2015: 2). Race, in Roof’s mind, is what organizes society on its most fundamental level. Society, in his case America, should be a *white* America. Even though Roof sees himself as an American patriot, and honours the soldiers who fought for the country, he hates ‘the sight of the American flag. Modern American patriotism is an absolute joke. People pretending like they have something to be proud of while White people are being murdered daily in the streets’ (Roof, 2015: 5). On several pictures on his website, we see Roof burning the American flag and waving the confederate flag with pride. Good American patriotism equals white nationalism, and that is why he prefers the confederate flag. The confederate flag is used as a symbol of white nationalism, it stands for a nostalgic history where whites were still in charge. The America that was worth fighting for, was the America before the desegregation and civil rights movement:

> I myself would have rather lived in 1940’s American (sic) than Nazi Germany, and no this is not ignorance speaking, it is just my opinion. So I dont (sic) blame the veterans of any wars up until after (sic) Vietnam, because at least they had an American (sic) to be proud of and fight for.
> 
> (Roof, 2015: 5)

Roof clearly argues here in favour of American blood-and-soil nationalism for European people. Only when a nation is racially homogenous it can be a good society. Diversity within one nation is seen by Roof as an essential treat. From this racist ideological perspective, the problem is that whites, because they, contrary to blacks, are not race conscious, are blind to the problems of a diverse society. The threat of diversity is defined by Roof in racial terms. It is for instance because he defines Jews as white that he doesn’t see their presence as a problem:

> Unlike many White naitonalists (sic), I am of the opinion that the majority of American and European jews (sic) are White. In my opinion the issues with jews (sic) is (sic) not their blood, but their identity. I think that if we could somehow destroy the jewish (sic) identity, then they wouldn’t (sic) cause much of a problem.
> 
> (Roof, 2015: 4)

His racism is *old school*, and race is the fundamental diacritic. Culture follows from the idea of biological races. In his manifesto, Roof describes several ‘races’ (Black, Jewish, Asian and Hispanic people), allocates different 220cultural characteristics to each group and describes the relations whites should have with those races. Note the complete absence of Muslims and Islam as a diversity problem: it is first and foremost the ‘black race’ which occupies Roof. Black people are a danger to whites and that danger is in essence racially defined. ‘Niggers’ says Roof, ‘are stupid and violent. At the same time, they have the capacity to be very slick.’ \[…\] ‘Negroes have lower Iqs (sic), lower impulse control, and higher testosterone levels in generals (sic). These three things alone are a recipe for violent behavior’. (Roof, 2015: 3). It is thus the biological nature of races that is framed by Roof as the cause of ‘black violence’ against whites. His racism is based on a reproduction of the old biological racial discourses where each race is seen to have ‘a biologically determined capacity for cultural development’ ([Miles, 1993](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_55): 28). Roof ranks the races and discusses their cultures just like colonial discourse from superior to inferior, from cultured and civilized to barbaric ([Corbey, 1989](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_18)) and he is very explicit about the superiority of the white race (Roof, 2015: 2).

This vintage ‘scientific racist’ discourse is very much present on websites where Roof was active as a reader or poster like American Renaissance, the Council for Conservative Citizens, Stormfront and The Daily Stormer ([Philip, 2015](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_58)). His racism indexes the context in which Roof lives and writes. It not only reflects the racist history in the United States or the fact that Obama was president, or the sites he visits, but it also reflects the Americanization of *La Nouvelle Droite’*s metapolitics. Whereas *La Nouvelle Droite* thinkers such as Alain de Benoist focus their attention on recent migration or Islam, in the case of Faye, and use culture and identity as the explicit diacritics, the North American new right is still grounded in explicit biological racism. In his book New Right vs. Old Right, Greg Johnson from Counter-Current argues that contrary to *La Nouvelle Droite*, the American new right, ‘because of the blending of European stocks and breakdown of more compact European national identities in North America’, is ‘forced to stress the deeper roots of common European identity, including racial identity’ ([Johnson, 2013](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_36): 2). This is probably also the reason why Faye and not de Benoist was so influential among American new right actors. Roof’s discourse echoes this American racist tradition, and this is nowhere more obvious than in the complete absence of attention to Islam or Muslims (Roof, 2015: 2). We also see it in his white supremacist discourse explicitly claiming white superiority. Roof, contrary to *La Nouvelle Droite’s* differentialism, adopts a hierarchical differentialism. His discourse blends modern-day racism with a discourse that echoes the long history of structural and biologically determined anti-black racism in the United States that has roots in the racism of the plant owners from the 19th century, the KKK and the southern racial conservatists.

221 

### Synchronizing the history of segregation

Roof’s manifesto contains an abundance of orientations to different chronotopic histories. The American civil war, colonial racism, Hitler’s Nazism, the black civil rights movement, neo-Nazi skinheads, the KKK and even Hollywood movies are all invoked to make his point. Contemporary conservative discourse on minorities is mixed with biologically determined racism from the colonial era, new right discourse on Jews and the Council of Conservative Citizen’s discourse on apartheid and black-on-white crime. Roof’s discourse is not just a ‘local’ discourse, it obviously has transnational roots, but it is primarily used for local ends: it is made meaningful in the local life of Roof. In this life, black people are seemingly his biggest occupation. It is also not an individual discourse, it has a long and complex, transnational social and political history. The synchronization of these historicities speaks very clearly to us in his use of different concepts to categorize blacks: he uses the words niggers, negroes, blacks and black people interchangeably to describe ‘the dangerous other’. All these concepts have a different chronotopic history that sticks to them. It also indexes his integration into those different traditions. It is through a careful analysis of his language use that we can determine that he speaks as a member of a specific ‘community of racists among which there exists bonds of imitation’ ([Balibar, 1991](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_3): 18). This community is not a homogenous community, but exists as a network of different nodes that each function as centres of normativity. It is Roof’s individual integration in this specific configuration of niches that shapes his discourse. That networked community of racists is polycentric: it is oriented around different online places that co-construct Roof’s discourse. His discourse on race wars as a civil war has clear intertextual links with discourses one can find on sites like the Council of Conservative Citizens, American Renaissance and The Daily Stormer. The manifesto is thus best read not as an individual product, but as the result of a dialogue with others. When he for instance claims that ‘Jews are white’ and that many disagree with that, he is in dialogue with the forum members on neo-Nazi sites like The Daily Stormer or Stormfront ([Philip, 2015](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_58)). And he enters that dialogue by appropriating the voice of the American Renaissance that sees Jewish citizens as potential allies ([Taylor, 2006](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_71)). In other words, his specific idiosyncratic discourse shows his integration into a very specific American polycentric white nationalist niche.

Roof’s voice synchronizes many different historical events, ideological positions and his own biography into a new voice. This voice indexes the very specific position and a very specific time in history from which he speaks ([Blommaert, 2005](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_5): 142). He not only speaks as a white male, a white supremacist, a ‘real American’ or a Southerner. He also speaks from a self-proclaimed underdog position: Roof talks (and obviously writes) as a white 222drop-out from a southern state in the multicultural America of the 21st century under Obama, a black president. It is this very specific class position, which intersects with racial fault lines in the United States, that not only makes him influenceable by far-right racism, but it also shapes his discourse. His own biography, his own experiences become a metonym of the state-of-affairs of the United States. He speaks in the name of ‘the white race’ and ‘white culture’ that in his eyes has lost its dominance in America, and even in Europe ‘the homeland of whites’ (Roof, 2015: 3). The different historical events, experiences and relations are blended in one text with the explicit goal of convincing the reader. This synchronization of historicities with his biography is an act of power in the margins.

The most dominant centre of normativity in Roof’s discourse is the Council of Conservative Citizens. It is also the only organization that he explicitly names in his manifesto. According to their Statement of Principle, the Council adheres to the idea that

> America is a Christian country and that its people are a Christian people \[…\] We therefore oppose the massive immigration of Non-European and non-Western people \[…\] We oppose all efforts to mix the races of mankind, to promote non-white races over the European-American people through so-called ‘affirmative action’ \[…\] We support the cultural and national heritage of the United States and the race and civilization of which it is part.
> 
> (Council of Conservative Citizens, 2015)

The Council of Conservative Citizens, just like Roof, defines the real America as a ‘European-America’ and thus a white America. Note here the differentialist dimension that is added to this more traditional biological racist discourse: the focus is on resisting the mix. What the Council of Conservative Citizens means with ‘the race and civilization of which it is part’, becomes obvious quite quickly. A short look at their magazines and articles reveals that they side with the apartheid regime in South Africa and Rhodesia. This focus on the former apartheid countries explains why Roof is so occupied with those countries that he even wears their flags on his vest. ‘Race integrity’ is high on the Council of Conservative Citizen’s agenda. The fact that Roof mentions the site explicitly in his manifesto shows that he aligns himself with their agenda, he shares their ideas on white nationalism, racism and supremacy, and wants to promote them. His battle and their battle are one: Creating racial consciousness and fighting for a white America.

The Council of Conservative Citizens was founded in 1985, but its history dates back to the so-called Citizen’s Councils. Those councils were the mass social movement arm of the white nationalist anti-desegregation Dixiecrat revolt. These old councils were known as actors of massive popular grassroots resistance ([Lowndes, 2008](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_40): 39–41). After a very successful period of 223mass mobilization, they lost impact in the 1970s but found new life in the eighties as the Council of Conservative Citizens. Among the spokespeople of those new councils was Jared Taylor. Taylor is an influential classic white nationalist and paleoconservative who also runs American Renaissance and is known for his stress on the importance of race. Taylor not only played an important role in facilitating racist discourse, he also is an outspoken fan and friend of Guillaume Faye ([Steuckers, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_70)). The intertextuality between Roof’s discourse and that of the Council of Conservative Citizens and the American Renaissance becomes very explicit when he takes on board the notion that the basis of all problems of violence and criminality is in the end a problem of ‘race relations’. Roof here echoes the classic discourse of ‘race realists’ like Jared Taylor on the assumed correlation between race and criminality (see for instance, [Taylor, 2007](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_72)). As a result of this discourse on diversity and criminality, he sees segregation as the only viable option. He followed the argument that

> Segregation was not a bad thing. It was a defensive measure. Segregation did not exist to hold back negroes. It existed to protect us from them. And I mean that in multiple ways. Not only did it protect us from having to interact with them, and from being physically harmed by them, but it protected us from being brought down to their level. Integration has done nothing but bring Whites down to level of brute animals.
> 
> (Roof, 2015: 2)

Roof’s plea for segregation is grounded in his old school racism that stresses that social behaviour is biologically determined. Roof’s apartheid is also grounded in a hierarchical differentialism that sees blacks as closer to nature, more violent and animal-like. It is this racial conception of blacks that (1) grounds his plea for segregation and (2) drives him to take action. ‘I believe,’ Roof says ‘that even if we made up only 30 percent of the population we could take it back completely. But by no means should we wait any longer to take drastic action’. Whites, according to him, need to take back control and segregate. That is the only way forward. His pleas for apartheid are again indexes of his socialization in relation to the Council of Conservative Citizens. A lot of their publications were dedicated to the struggle of the Boers in South Africa and they explicitly praised the necessity of apartheid to protect whites. Roof was not known as a good student, but this far-right ecology proved very productive for him.

Echoing the discourse of the Council, he sees contemporary South Africa after apartheid as proof that it will only get worse. ‘If anyone thinks that think (sic) will eventually just change for the better, consider how in South Africa they have affirmative action for the black population that makes up 80 percent of the population’ (Roof, 2015: 3). It is from this perspective that he feels that 224drastic action is needed. That drastic action cannot be limited to the internet, it needs to go offline.

> ‘To take a saying from a film, ‘I see all this stuff going on, and I dont see anyone doing anything about it. And it pisses me off’. To take a saying from my favourite film, ‘Even if my life is worth less than a speck of dirt, I want to use it for the good of society’. ‘I have no choice. I am not in the position to, alone, go into the ghetto and fight. I chose Charleston because it is most historic city in my state, and at one time had the highest ratio of blacks to Whites in the country. We have no skinheads, no real KKK, no one doing anything but talking on the internet. Well someone has to have the bravery to take it to the real world, and I guess that has to be me.’ (Roof, 2015: 6).

### Racial consciousness, metapolitics and violence

Roof’s murderous riot served two interconnected goals: (1) awakening the racial consciousness of the ‘white race’ and (2) engaging those ‘race realists’ in a racial war that he hoped would enflame by his murderous riot. The killing spree was a way to draw eyeballs to his manifesto and his site in the hope of fixating on the meaning of his terrorist act and enflaming a race war. Making white people racially conscious is Roof’s fundamental goal, as it is only when they are conscious of the racial fundaments of contemporary problems that they will realize that segregation is the only solution and take the necessary steps. In order to achieve that racial consciousness, he set up, several months before his riot, a website which he called The Last Rhodesian

The idea behind *The Last Rhodesian* is emblematic of Roof’s idea of white people being under attack and losing the racial war between white and black in the United States of the 21st century. The Last Rhodesian is a metaphor for the last white man fighting for power over ‘its rightful nation’. That message was 225multimodally constructed on the home page (see [Figure 6.1](#C_013_c6.xhtml#f6_1)). On the black background, and below the title The Last Rhodesian in contrasting white, visitors saw a still from the Australian cult movie ‘Romper Stomper’ picturing the dying neo-Nazi named Hando after being stabbed in the neck with a *Hitlerjugend* knife. Hando wears several neo-Nazi identity emblems himself: Shaven hair, SS skulls and a Swastika pin on his jacket and even a tattoo on his neck reading Skinhead. The picture is recontextualized, and as a consequence, it acquires a whole new meaning ([Silverstein & Urban, 1996](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_67)). Whereas in the movie, Hando is stabbed by his neo-Nazi buddy, this context disappears on the website. In combination with the title, Hando becomes ‘The Last Rhodesian’: that is, the last white nationalist, a victim of the centuries-old civil racial war that Roof envisions to be still shaping the contemporary world. The homepage multimodally states that it is urgent for white people to act if they don’t want to get extinct. White genocide is near. Note that Roof does not use a hipster identitarian as the central picture: the last white man is a neo-Nazi, with explicit identity emblems.

Figure 6.1 Homepage The Last Rhodesian. [Return to text.⏎](#C_013_c6.xhtml#f6_1b) ¶ *Source:* [www.lastrhodesian.com](http://www.lastrhodesian.com).

![Figure 6.2 Google trends for the search term ‘council of conservative citizens’. ¶ Data Source: Google Trends (https://www.google.com/trends).](images/Figure0226-01.jpg)

Figure 6.2 Google trends for the search term ‘council of conservative citizens’. ¶ *Data Source:* Google Trends ([https://www.google.com/trends](https://www.google.com/trends)).

Roof’s manifesto, his website and violence all contribute to getting his message out. And from this perspective, we see how his murderous riot is continuous with the metapolitical battle that the Council of Conservative Citizens is waging. The Council sees the internet as a metapolitical tool to communicate, to educate and to fight for their goals, and it is Roof’s killing spree that generated massive attention for their site. According to Google Trends, an all-time high number of people searched for the Council of Conservative Citizens on the day Roof entered the Charleston church. In other words, he drove a massive amount of traffic to their site.

226 

### Data voids and terrorism as metapolitics

Roof’s manifesto was not only a deeply racist legitimation of his murders or a truthful account of his radicalization, it was also a metapolitical manifesto in its own right. Roof may not have been very knowledgeable about using social media, or sites that are built to be found, but he did understand mass media logic. He understood that his murderous riot would produce endless headlines and make journalists and regular users search for his manifesto. Even more, Roof was very conscious about the role that online search can play in becoming racially aware, as he himself claims to have been radicalized through Google. In his manifesto, he not only explains his deeds and goals but also explains how he became racially aware:

> The event that truly awakened me was the Trayvon Martin case. I kept hearing and seeing his name, and eventually I decided to look him up. I read the Wikipedia article and right away I was unable to understand what the big deal was. It was obvious that Zimmerman was in the right. But more importantly this prompted me to type in the words ‘black on White crime’ into Google, and I have never been the same since that day. The first website I came to was the Council of Conservative Citizens. There were pages upon pages of these brutal black on White murders. I was in disbelief. At this moment I realized that something was very wrong. How could the news be blowing up the Trayvon Martin case while hundreds of these black on White murders got ignored?
> 
> (Roof, 2015: 1)

Golebiewski and boyd give the case of Dylann Roof as a concrete example of radicalization through a data void. According to them ([Golebiewski & boyd, 2018](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_31): 4) the search query ‘black on white crime’ is a ‘classic example of a data void’ that is weaponized by far-right actors. In this analysis, Roof’s manifesto is read as a truthful self-reporting of his own radicalization process. What is missed is the metapolitical dimension of Roof’s terrorist act. 227Roof wanted to make white people racially aware (Roof, 2015: 1). The passage that Golebiewski and boyd ([2018](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_31): 4) see as evidence of Dylann Roof’s radicalization through a data void is at the very least also a performative and metapolitical act. Even if he really searched Google for ‘black on White crime’ after reading the Wikipedia article, it is most likely an index of his pre-existing ideological convictions. There is little in the Wikipedia article that will lead somebody to type in those words in that order, let alone that he would capitalize white and not black. Roof’s murderous riot is not just ‘taking the online battle offline’ as he claims, it was also very much about generating attention for the cause, and thus using the offline to direct people to online echo chambers. It was no coincidence that he mentioned the Council of Conservative Citizens, and we shouldn’t read this manifesto as a pure testimony without metapolitical goals. His mentioning of the search queries is certainly also an invitation to the reader to Google black-on-white crime. His riot and his conviction generated a massive peak in search queries for black-on-white crime. A peak that was only topped during the murder of George Floyd in 2022.

![Figure 6.3 Google trends for the search term: black-on-white crime in the United States 2015–2020. ¶ Data Source: Google Trends (https://www.google.com/trends).](images/Figure0227-01.jpg)

Figure 6.3 Google trends for the search term: black-on-white crime in the United States 2015–2020. ¶ *Data Source:* Google Trends ([https://www.google.com/trends](https://www.google.com/trends)).

Personal testimonials are a common metapolitical practice among far-right influencers. As Lewis ([2018](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_39): 24) shows, the transformation from left to right, or here from so-proclaimed non-racist to racially aware, is a popular testimonial trope that is weaponized to amplify support. These testimonies are often framed as awakenings. Roof’s ‘personal awakening’ is an invitation for people reading his testimony to do the same, to read Wikipedia, to Google black-on-white crime and to go to the website of the Council of Conservative Citizens. And that is exactly what people did after Roof’s racial murder: they typed in ‘black on White crime’ and when they did that, they found the entrance to a new world.

It is not a coincidence that the results I got when searching black-on-white crime in Google on the day of his terrorist attack was a link to the site of the 228Council for Conservative Citizens. The second result was a link to the FBI with stats that seemingly support this white nationalist trope. This was accompanied by a collection of memes that was highlighted by Google images on the search page. If you click on images you would find that all the images and memes Google provided to people searching these words, supported the narrative of Roof. Roof directed an enormous amount of people – the most in the last five years – to a data void filled with far-right content. This data void is an intertextual bubble: all links and images support the same discourse. The point here is that the informational ecosystem that Roof directs his audience was an information environment created by far-right activists in relation to the algorithms of Google.

### Roof, hybrid media salience and (failed) metapolitics

Reading Roof’s testimonial, not as a personal explanation of his killing spree, but as a metapolitical act to make people racially aware, allows us to see much more. Like Laqueur ([1977](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_38): 112) already established, the success of a terrorist operation is almost fully dependent on the publicity it generates. Seen from this perspective, Roof’s murderous riot was a huge success. It was his act that drove traffic to his manifesto, to the site of the Council of Conservative Citizens and into the black-on-white crime data void. Roof uses his murderous act and a very rudimentary website to ‘set the agenda’. The agenda-setting theory, and especially the concept of salience, highlights how media attention for certain issues is not just a reflection of reality but also shapes reality. In a hybrid media system ([Chadwick, 2017](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_17)), we see that legacy media are not the only actors anymore capable of setting the agenda. Roof’s killing spree can thus be seen as a form of ‘hybrid salience’ ([Maniou & Bantimaroudis, 2018](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_53)), the notion that the attention to his deed has now been fragmented over different media, actors and niches, and with that hybridization comes new interpretations of the event. This polycentric salience also means different ways of uptake.

Roof’s act was mass-mediated and he enjoyed horizontal (social media) and vertical (mainstream media) salience. The uptake and understanding of his act and discourse were different depending on the niches in which the uptake took place. In the legacy media, his murderous riot and his white nationalist and racist discourse completely undermined the potential for uptake of his discourse. Even without taking the massacre into account, his white nationalist and deeply racist message was out of touch with the spirit of the time ([Silverstein, 2003](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_66)). It did not align with the dominant ideologies, and in that sense, it was devoid of key characteristics of metapolitical discourse that were always designed to at least aspire to normality and avoid all racist, extremist or radical connotations. Only a small niche of 229far-right extremists would subscribe to Roof’s discourse. The reason that got him the attention he wanted is the same reason his message can only be read as mad, psychotic, deeply racist, horrible, sick and so on, from a mainstream perspective. Even the extreme-right white nationalist website that inspired Roof, the Council of Conservative Citizens, not exactly a moderate voice, had to distance itself from his monstrous act. At the same time, we see that they had done it in such a way so as not to alienate their ideological base. Looking from the mainstream or the left, the statement of the president of the Council of Conservative Citizens published on the white nationalist website American Renaissance (Holt [III, 2015](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_34)) is very remarkable:

> It has been brought to the attention of the Council of Conservative Citizens that Dylann Roof–the alleged perpetrator of mass murder in Charleston this week–credits the CofCC website for his knowledge of black-on-white violent crime. This is not surprising: The CofCC is one of perhaps three websites in the world that accurately and honestly reports black-on-white violent crime, and in particular, the seemingly endless incidents involving black-on-white murder. \[…\] The CofCC is hardly responsible for the actions of this deranged individual merely because he gleaned accurate information from our website.

Holt’s words show that mainstream or legacy media are still dominant in a hybrid media system. They still set the agenda and the accepted ways of thinking about certain events or thoughts. The whole message reflects this position of the mass media and the pressure they can put on far-right organizations to position themselves *vis à vis* radical and violent acts. Holt cannot but denounce the violence and keep Roof at a distance. On the other hand, the CofCC’s president is also addressing another part of the population integrated into a very different media environment where people think differently – maybe not so much about the act itself, but at least about the discourse that Roof has positioned in the hybrid media system. With this one speech act, Holt has to address two very different audiences with different normativities at the same time: ‘the general public’ who is shocked by the massacre, and his radical base who may or may not disapprove of the act, but certainly supports the discourse of Roof. That is why he calls Roof deranged and denies any responsibility while at the same time soothes his base by emphasizing ‘the accurate information’ the Council of Conservative Citizens is providing. In this attempt to please both audiences merged together through Roof, he tries to further his ideological agenda and explicitly states that the organization stands by ‘the honest and accurate facts’ that Roof has written down. The effect of his communication has two consequences. First of all, we see that all politicians, mostly Republicans, that 230have accepted money from the organization or spoke at their events, tried to distance themselves publicly from the organization. Most of them even sent their money back. Roof and the mass media attention for his metapolitical terrorism created a serious backlash for the organization. Secondly, we see that the white nationalist supporters were satisfied with this response. More than 200 people reacted on the site of the American Renaissance (Holt [III, 2015](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_34)), most of them praising Holt for his ‘rational tone’. In these reactions, we see explicit intertextual links with the discourse of Roof and the Council for Conservative Citizens. Pleasing their audience thus meant further marginalizing the organization.

Roof failed from an old school metapolitical perspective and he has clearly also failed to start a racial war. His terrorism and his explicit discourse made him into a racist lunatic that the Council for Conservative Citizens could not support publicly. At the same time, his act did make his manifesto salient. And if we assess his act from a more niched perspective, we see different things. The blog *The Alternative Right*, which at the time was not yet known as a key centre of the so-called alt-right, jumped in to defend ‘the white men’s burden’, gun possession and the inevitability of racism. Racism will keep rising, the blog argued, because ‘There is an iron law that ensures that the more multicultural a society becomes, the more racist it inevitably becomes’ (2015, 25 June). The alternative right re-entextualized Roof’s terrorism and his discourse in a neo-racist and differentialist new right discourse. Racism, in this logic, is the natural reaction to a multicultural society. The Alternative Right, by re-entextualizing Roof’s discourse, tries to normalize his black-on-white discourse and uses it to stop the banning of guns: ‘Banning guns in America is simply not doable. This is because gun ownership is embedded in American culture and society, and the continuing threat from Black and Hispanic dysfunction will mean that Whites will continue to support it’ (The Alternative [Right, 2015](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_73), 19 June).

Counter-Currents on the other hand even called for a crowd-sourced operation to thicken the manifesto of Roof and back it up with proof, with facts. Following this crowdsourcing, Counter-Currents published *Dylann Roof’s manifesto (Annotated)* with Dylann Roof as author and known alt-right and Arktos editor James O’ Meara as editor. The annotated text appeared on 30 June 2015 on the site with many footnotes ‘supporting’ Dylann Roof’s world view’. The text came with a disclaimer that stated that

> The purpose of this project is to show that Roof’s worldview was not based on ‘ignorance’ or ‘prejudice’ but on verifiable facts. Of course, none of these facts necessitated Roof’s decision to go on a shooting spree, which was an error of moral and practical reasoning, not of matters of fact.
> 
> ([Roof, 2015b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_63))

231Roof’s metapolitics may have failed in a public sphere dominated by legacy media, but it clearly had uptake and impact within a niched sphere. Brenton Tarrant was only one of his readers.

### Bowl patrol, memes and white terrorist culture

Roof’s killing spree was metapolitical in nature: he was killing to realize cultural change: only when white people became racially aware and understood that the civil war was already in full swing, they would be able to start fighting for a different future. Roof’s terrorism shouldn’t be understood as the act of a loner but as a reflection of a certain culture. The idea that Dylann Roof was a lone wolf may be correct if one looks at it through the terrorism studies lens as ‘an attack carried out by a single individual without any operational ties to a terror organisation’ ([Boaz Ganor, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_13)). From a cultural studies perspective, it is without a doubt that there is nothing ‘lone’ about his behaviour. Roof’s actions reflect a very specific and identifiable albeit complex, layered and polycentric culture. Within that network of sites, he became somebody. He not only learned to think about race relations in relation to texts on those sites, but he also interacted with others ([Philip, 2015](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_58)). In doing so, he acquired very specific templates of thoughts and rationalized far-right thoughts and modes of action. His act and his manifesto show us how the affordances of online infrastructures allow for the production and normalization of such very specific, culturally organized logics of action ([Blommaert, 2017b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_9)).

The act in itself was not only the effect of such a far-right-niched culture, but it was also the start of vibrant cultural production. His discourse not only became the centre of attention, but it was also debated in mainstream news. President Obama’s multiple interventions may have been very powerful in producing a negative message and denouncing his racist view for the majority of the audiences, but the matter still remains that he has generated uptake for his discourse. As a result of this mass mediatization, Roof has become a (ironic) ‘cult-hero’ among certain extreme-right activists. His bowl haircut became the raw material for massive amounts of ‘memes’ that functioned as convivial devices in far-right online communities. Such convivial devices facilitate ‘the production of a social-structuring level of engagement in loose, temporal, and elastic collectives operating in social media environments’ ([Varis & Blommaert, 2014](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_78)). On Discord, for instance, there was a Bowl Patrol server. The meme below ([Figure 6.4](#C_013_c6.xhtml#f6_4)) was shared on that server and shows a bowl cut take on the classic ‘That’s where you’re wrong kiddo’ meme. The bowl cut here not only indexes Roof but also the fact that he was able to truly hit ‘the other side’. It functions within that context not only as an ironic attribution of coolness to Roof’s hairstyle but also as phatic communication: it creates conviviality or groupness. This groupness is 232also indexed by the bowl cut patrol logo on the meme. This logo is made by superimposing Roof’s bowl cut on a shield that resembles the divisional insignia of the Waffen SS. Members of that Discord server read as a who’s who of the alt-right and neo-Nazi scene in the United States. They include key figures from Vanguard America, The Right Stuff network and The Daily Stormer. ![Figure 6.4 Bowl cut meme ‘That's where you're wrong’ kiddo with the bowl cut patrol logo. Return to text.⏎ ¶ Source: https://discordleaks.unicornriot.ninja/discord/server/30.](images/Figure0232-01.jpg)

Figure 6.4 Bowl cut meme ‘That's where you're wrong’ kiddo with the bowl cut patrol logo. [Return to text.⏎](#C_013_c6.xhtml#f6_4b) ¶ *Source:* [https://discordleaks.unicornriot.ninja/discord/server/30](https://discordleaks.unicornriot.ninja/discord/server/30).

The reason why he is being labelled a Saint, or a chad (see below), is because he has been successful in his attack. Success here is measured in terms of victims. In the meme below ([Figure 6.5](#C_013_c6.xhtml#f6_5)), we see a gaming logic introduced in the discourse. Roof is being framed as a winner because he succeeded in killing so many churchgoers. Gamification of terrorism has become a central focal point in far-right terrorist research after the attack of Brenton Tarrant in Christchurch ([Ebner, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_25); [Schlegel, 2021](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_64)a, [2021](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_65)b). The attack of Tarrant, but also of the far-right gunmen in Halle in Germany, Poway in California, El Paso, Texas in the United States and Baerum in Norway followed a similar format in which 233not only ideology, or integration in far-right hubs like 4chan and 8kun, it also showed their integration into gaming contexts. GamerGate was a well-known recruiting base for the alt-right in 2014 and 2015 ([Yiannopoulos, 2017](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_82)). Not only gaming culture and gamified language were appropriated, but we also saw that they used the gaming infrastructures. The riot in Charlottesville was organized on the gaming server Discord, and Schild & Vrienden also used Discord to organize themselves ([Maly, 2019a](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_47)). With the use of these infrastructures and cultures came the gamification of terrorism. On the one hand, we see how far-right terrorists in Christchurch, Halle and El Paso have adopted the Let’s Play video format and live streamed their attacks. Such a live stream gamifies the attacker’s and the viewers’ experience of the event (Schlegel, 2021: 6).

![Figure 6.5 Gamification of terrorism. Return to text.⏎ ¶ Source: https://discordleaks.unicornriot.ninja/discord/server/30.](images/Figure0233-01.jpg)

Figure 6.5 Gamification of terrorism. [Return to text.⏎](#C_013_c6.xhtml#f6_5b) ¶ *Source:* [https://discordleaks.unicornriot.ninja/discord/server/30](https://discordleaks.unicornriot.ninja/discord/server/30).

On the other hand, we see how gamification introduces new frames to understand the terrorist act. The gamification of terrorism also has a 234metapolitical dimension: game discourses and practices are now being used to change the frame in which members of their community understand the terrorist act. In the meme above, Roof is not a loser or a terrorist: he is a chad, a saint who successfully fought for his people. As a result of this success in game terms, the bowl cut – usually an index of the prototypical losers – can become an index of success and coolness (see [Figure 6.6](#C_013_c6.xhtml#f6_6)).

![Figure 6.6 Bowl cut chad meme. Return to text.⏎ ¶ Source: https://discordleaks.unicornriot.ninja/discord/server/30.](images/Figure0234-01.jpg)
