The group created a group identity around Dylann Roof’s killing spree. In this small extremist community, the bowl cut functions as an index of being enlightened and even becomes the stuff that is seen as ‘chad-like’. In the meme ([Figure 6.6](#C_013_c6.xhtml#f6_6)) above, we not only see an alpha male represented in ‘the classic chad meme’, but the chad now also has a bowl cut and is awarded with traditional neo-Nazi sign tattoos. All conversations in those Discord groups combine very explicit neo-Nazi racist discourse with genocidal edgy jokes and memes with a celebrative but also deeply ironic discourse on the actions of Roof and his haircut. These interactions among far-right neo-Nazis are not metapolitical from a mainstream perspective. They weren’t produced for uptake by broad audiences, they were part of intimate and ludic but also very shocking interactions that normalize racist violence among ‘friends’. In this group, this discourse has a clear cultural dimension and normalizes outsider behaviour.

Blommaert (2017) uses Raymond Williams’ concept of ‘structures of feeling’ to show how such interactions gradually become ‘structured’ by ideological framings provided by similar feelings articulated by others in the group. It is ‘through such ludic forms of practice’, Blommaert argues, that ‘this sharedness is experienced as important and formative’. In other words, the memes, the racist discourse, the praise for Roof and the group emblems, all contribute to the normalization of violence. It is through such interactions in very specific, for outsiders incomprehensibe, language full of references to the 235bowl cut such as ‘The Final Bowlution’, or ‘TheBowlfather’, that new radical logics of action are normalized. In the specific meme culture of this group, not only the martyr-ship of Roof is celebrated, but his actions are presented as welcome actions that should be expanded. The memification of Roof is thus an index of a far-right terrorist culture. According to Unicorn Riot and the Antidefamation League references to Dylann Roof and the ‘bowl cut’ or ‘bowl’ have turned up in at least five recent criminal cases.

## Metapolitics 2.0 and Brenton Tarrant's reconquest

Brenton Tarrant, the perpetrator of the terrorist attack in a New Zealand Mosque taking 49 innocent lives, defines himself in his manifesto as a crusader for the white race, a terrorist even and an eco-fascist. And he does it with pride. He sees himself, just like Breivik and Roof, as a future hero, as a soldier fighting for the survival of the white race. Contrary to Roof who was emblematic of a radical American manifestation of the global new right, Tarrant was deeply integrated into the digital culture of the global far-right on a global scale. He was active on 8chan, travelled the world and searched for contact with far-right activists and terrorists in different countries. The attack of Tarrant was also far more sophisticated than the one of Roof. And that 236sophistication wasn’t limited to the execution of the riot; it became especially clear in his discourse and how he prepared the uptake of that discourse in the hybrid media system.

### The great replacement and reconquest

The title of Tarrant’s manifesto is the first indication of his integration into global new right. The Great Replacement is a classic trope among the identitarian movements in Europe. It is commonly seen as referring to the work of Renaud Camus, who, in two French books published in 2010 and 2011 and one English book published in 2020, defined what he called ‘Le grand remplacement’ or the Great Replacement. This replacement according to him is about ‘the brutal change of population which has been taking place in France (and in Europe) since the beginning of the last quarter of the last century and which has been gaining momentum ever since’ (Camus, 2020: 19). Camus describes this replacement in terms of a new colonialism that is executed by invaders or so-called ‘replacees mostly from Africa and very often Muslims’ (Camus, 2020: 21) and facilitated by the ‘replacists, who want the change of people and civilization, which they are prone to call multiculturalism, or ‘vivre ensemble’ (Camus, 2020: 20). The replacists is a collective name for the mainstream politicians, journalists and media in general.

Camus’ diagnosis of replacement relies on ‘an ethnic or racial “common sense” of belonging’ ([Bracke & Aguilar, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_15)). Replacement, or colonialization in his discourse, doesn’t rely on taking over the political power of a foreign country; it refers to the visual changing of society. In his 2020 book, we can see this ‘common sense’ notion of belonging in how he answers his own question of what it means to be French: ‘Not asking (oneself) the question (to oneself). Not Wondering about it’ ([Camus, 2018](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_16): 12). France and French-ness should be felt as natural, something that is hegemonic and is just there in all little villages and streets. The mere presence of ‘the Other’ destroys that common sense in Camus’ logic. It is this visual and common sense destruction that makes him rephrase multiculturalism and integration paradigms as ‘replacement vehicles’. The replacement or colonialization equals the destruction of a nostalgic common sense that becomes visible in the streets through ‘turbans and Djellaba’s’. Important to stress here, is that in the end, culture is racially determined for Camus and race thus takes a central role in this thesis. ‘When all is said and done’, Camus says ([2018](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_16): 66), ‘we are a European people of white race’. Not only does Camus define the French as a race, replacement is defined as a *replacement of races*.

Camus’s theory is grounded in a racial blood-and-soil organicism that especially resembles the work of Guillaume Faye. Already in 2000 did Faye write his book ‘The Colonisation of Europe’, in which he makes the exact same claim as Camus. He, too, reframes immigration in terms of ‘a massive 237colonization settlement of the West’, predicts ‘an ethnic civil war’ and sounds ‘the call to reconquering’ ([Faye, 2016](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_28): xii). Both Camus and Faye are key intellectuals of the European identitarian movement. Camus may denounce that he is an identitarian ([Camus, 2018](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_16): 12), his ideas on the Great Replacement have found fertile soil among identitarian activists who pushed that idea to fame. The uptake of this far-right conspiracy theory is substantial and was increasing on a monthly basis before the Christchurch attack. Before that attack, researchers found ‘1.5 million tweets referencing the Great Replacement theory between April 2012 and April 2019 in English, French and German language’ ([Davey & Ebner, 2019](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_24)). The identitarians have been a crucial factor in the uptake of this far-right theory. Martin Sellner ([Traditional Britain Group, 2017](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_75)), when delivering his speech during a Traditional Britain conference in 2017, not only refers to this replacement theory, but he also explains it in similar terms as Camus. People, he said,

> cannot withstand a complete replacement. Today we see a rupture, we see people on the streets, when I was walking from London, there are all these Arabic Scriptures on the shop, saw the face of those people and I knew, those people are not British, they do not feel British, they have a completely different identity.

The replacement or colonizing is described in relation to the presence of ‘non-whites’, and the visibility of their cultures and languages in the streets.

This same ‘eye witness’ discourse framing ‘diversity in one country’ as colonization and migrants as invaders is also present in the discourse of Tarrant when he describes his visit to France. Seeing the diversity in the French streets was for him the final straw that pushed him into action.

> The final push was witnessing the state of French cities and towns. For many years I had been hearing and reading of the invasion of France by non-whites, many of these rumours and stories I believed to be exaggerations, created to push a political narrative. But once I arrived in France, I found the stories to not only be true, but profoundly understated. In every French (sic) city, in every french (sic) town the invaders were there. No matter where I travelled, no matter how small or rural the community I visited, the invaders were there.

This paragraph echoes the words of Camus and Sellner; he also presents the visible changes in the streets as ‘proof’ of replacement. Notice also how Camus, Sellner, Tarrant and Roof use a testimonial narrative in order to convince the reader. Just like Roof claimed not to be raised as a racist, Tarrant claims to not have believed the theories on replacement, but then – the epiphany moment arrived when he saw it with his own eyes. Varis ([2019](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_77)) points out that such ‘ideology of seeing is believing’ attributes authority to the visual as ‘evidence’. 238In a similar vein, Blommaert (2019) describes the position of the ‘eye witness’ as an argumentative device in strategies of persuasion, articulating a particularly compelling ‘veridictional’ epistemic stance. It is this *my eyes don’t lie* strategy that is used to give authority to what in the public debate had already been framed as a far-right conspiracy theory during and after the Unite the Right Tiki Torch march when protestors would chant ‘you will not replace us’.

Another intertextual connection with Faye and the Identarian movement that Tarrant stresses is the importance of differences in birth rates.

> If there is one thing I want you to remember from these writings, its (sic) that the birth-rates must change. Even if we were to deport all Non-Europeans from our lands tomorrow, the European people would still be spiraling into decay and eventual death. Every day we become fewer in number, we grow older, we grow weaker. In the end we must return to replacement fertility levels, or it will kill us.

Or in other words, just like Faye, Camus and Willinger, he is tremendously concerned with family policies and the survival of the white race. Note here too, that he does not only refer the reader to several Wikipedia links with numbers to ‘prove’ his point, but also relies on the ‘Seeing is believing’ ideology. He claims that he could see the decline in birth rates in the people on the streets in France.

> The french (sic) people were often in a minority themselves, and the French that were in the streets were often alone, childless or of advanced age. Whilst the immigrants were young, energized and with large families and many children.

Images of diversity, and especially the dichotomy between young migrants and old white people, are seen as emblematic of the death of the white race. The replacement is described and felt as acute: replacement is understood as white genocide and the death of white civilization. This replacement is not only seen by the right in the declining birth rates or the presence of migrants and Muslims in particular, but also in Islamic terrorism now and historic wars. Tarrant tries to legitimize his killing spree as ‘revenge on the invaders for the hundreds of thousands of deaths caused by foreign invaders in European lands throughout history’. He sees himself as a warrior or knight that, just like ‘Traini, Anders Breivik, Dylan Roof, Anton Lundin *Pettersson, Darren Osbourne’*, takes a stand against ethnic and cultural genocide. Tarrant frames his terrorist act completely within this theory of replacement. It is this theory that normalizes his logic of action. Important to stress here, again, is that this terrorism is not only executed to instil fear but serves metapolitical goals. Tarrant, just like Breivik and Roof, searches for an audience for his message.

239 

### Securing uptake for his manifesto

Tarrant was methodical not only in the execution of his terrorist attack but also in making sure that he generated uptake. Before he entered the Masjid an-Nur in Christchurch, he posted a message on his Facebook page ‘with links to seven different file sharing websites that contained copies of a manifesto he had written explaining his motivation for the terrorist attack he was about to carry out’.

His media literacy also speaks from his post on 8chan. This bulletin board is not only dedicated to sensational stuff, but it is also known for its radical audience which favours ‘edgy content’ and is a meme-making factory. If we analyse the announcement of his raid on 8chan, it becomes obvious that he saw himself as ‘amongst friends’ whom he addressed as people he has spent a lot of shared time with. His use of the 8chan lingo and the meme that accompanies his post all index that he was indeed a long-time and fully integrated member of this online anonymous community. This post was not only a message to friends but also first and foremost a call to action. It was posted two minutes after his Facebook post and was thus clearly part of his well-planned strategy to secure uptake of his killing spree. The post contains links to his Facebook Livestream and to the different sharing platforms.

Four minutes later, after messaging family members, he sent out a mail to the Office of the Prime Minister, the leader of the Opposition and many media organizations. In that mail with the subject line ‘On the attack in New Zealand Today’, he uses emotionless and formal language: ‘I was the partisan that committed the assault. I have attached my writings to explain my actions and beliefs as well as provided links to webpages to download the documents below’. Notice also how he manages to mobilize different genres. Whereas his post on 8chan was trollish and indexed his integration into that niched culture, his mail to the officials and mass media was written in formal, passionless rhetoric. These genres are clearly mobilized to produce uptake within the groups he is addressing.

Just like Breivik was very much concerned about the uptake of his compendium ([Ravndal, 2013](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_60)), Tarrant invested a lot in getting that manifesto out. Tarrant, contrary to his role model Breivik, did not invest in acquiring the e-mails of thousands of far-right sympathizers to get the message out; 240he made efficient use of the mass media logic and the social media logics to guarantee massive uptake throughout the whole hybrid media system. He announced it on 8chan, and he also set up a Facebook account and a Twitter account on 12 March and mailed it to important political people and journalists. Just like Dylann Roof and Breivik’s terrorism, Tarrant’s terrorism had a substantial metapolitical dimension. Tarrant, just like Breivik, even interviewed himself at great length in his manifesto, thus preformulating the news and providing answers to questions. In a hybrid media system ([Chadwick, 2017](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_17)), white terrorists use digital media and offline action to draw attention to their cause. And attracting eyeballs was exactly what he did. His killing spree made interest in the Great Replacement theory spike. It became the talk of the town on a global scale. Even if the Great Replacement theory was already gaining massive traction in the months before the attack, his killing spree caused unseen search engine activity.

![Figure 6.8 Google trends for the search term: The great replacement between 2004 and 2020. ¶ Data Source: Google Trends (https://google.com/trends).](images/Figure0240-01.jpg)

Figure 6.8 Google trends for the search term: The great replacement between 2004 and 2020. ¶ *Data Source:* Google Trends ([https://google.com/trends](https://google.com/trends)).

Even more important than spreading the news, his manifesto and the live stream, he urged the 8chan anons to repackage his manifesto in memes. In memes and meme culture, he saw a far more effective way of spreading his message. In the manifesto, he urged his followers to ‘Be creative, be expressive, be emotional and above all be passionate. (…) Paint, write, sing, dance, recite poetry. Hell, even meme. Create memes, post memes, and spread memes. Memes have done more for the ethno-nationalist movement than any manifesto’. The importance of this far-right trolling and meme culture in the contemporary far-right pro-violence culture cannot be underestimated ([Maly, 2018a](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_41)). Tarrant himself was clearly a product of that culture and he did all he could to please them. Not only did he post the announcement with the live stream, but he also made a soundtrack from extreme-right video memes. This soundtrack was beat to his live stream of the mosque shootings – a soundtrack that was heavily discussed on 8chan during his livestream by anons who got the references.

He thus explicitly produced raw material for the production of memes in the hope that they would catch on, go viral and spread the message. Even more, 241he gave them the assignment to do so. As a member of such a community, he not only understood their role in the continuity of the distribution of his manifesto and stream, he also knew the cultural potential of that community in normalizing far-right violence. As we have seen, those memes not only contribute to the normalization of a certain logic of action, they also contribute to a specific terrorist culture. This culturalization of Tarrant is now a fact, not only in New Zealand but also around the world.

In the spring of 2021, I was asked by Telefacts, a news show on VTM, a commercial television channel in Belgium, to analyse data they had gathered on far-right radicalization. In those data, I encountered a new young Flemish identitarian group that operated on Instagram under the name Volksverbond (People’s Union). On their public page, they would post metapolitical slideshows to ‘inform’ the people about the colonization of Belgium by migrants. In their private chats, they not only celebrated Brenton Tarrant’s terrorism or shared memes about him, but they also normalized having guns and learning to use them. In a meme posted in their chatbox, the members of the group not only presented him as Jesus and thus not only as a saint but also as a saviour; they also claimed that his music was on their playlists and that watching his video is the best indoctrination video in the world. Here you see that (1) the live streaming is aimed at ‘the highest degree of publicity possible’ ([Schlegel, 2021b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_65): 7), (2) live watching generates not only live watching but also extended watching. It becomes a resource around which a culture can grow. This culture is again not a local affair, but potentially a global one. It uses the gaming format and its associated normality to normalize terrorism. In those memes, just as we have seen in the terrorist culture around Roof, we witness the reframing of the act of Tarrant. In the gaming format, Tarrant has become the hero of the narrative: he is the winner of the game, the saint. As a direct result, you see a normalization of violence and a culture of guns. Considering the Belgian context, where guns and their use are strictly regulated and where no mainstream gun culture exists, it shows how Tarrant’s terrorist attack produced a culture that was deglobalized and resulted in further radicalization. The irony of the meme facilitated a culture where far-right violence was celebrated. Gamified language, and thus also gamified far-right terrorist culture, shouldn’t be just disregarded as unimportant, a mere by-product. Language as we know is performative ([Pocock, 1973](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_59)): it is through language that we acquire a perspective on reality. Gaming cultural resources are potentially powerful in shifting the perspective on violent terrorism by normalizing it. It is through the logic of the action frame of the game that Terrant and Roof became seen as Saints, heroes or chads. Even if the members celebrating those perpetrators make those comments in an ironic way, they still contribute to the distribution and normalization of his violent actions and his far-right ideology. Or in other words, it contributes to the social relatedness of the group ([Schlegel, 2021b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_65): 7).

242The fact that Tarrant’s manifesto, his stream and his playlist have generated such substantial uptake means that they contributed to white terrorist culture. This not only indexes his knowledge of those niches but also how powerful they can be. Scholars refer in this context to the recruitment effect of the gamification of terrorism. The introduction and appropriation of gaming culture in far-right terrorism generates further uptake and thus visibility of the act in the hybrid attention economy. It is through his live stream that Tarrant generates massive visibility. Tarrant and the gaming culture of white terrorism have provided a format for far-right attacks. This format not only has the potential to normalize, but it is also made for uptake within the whole hybrid media system. The power effects become clear when new far-right terrorists step into his footsteps. John Timothy Earnest, who stormed a synagogue in Poway, California, and opened fire on the Jewish congregation, said he was inspired by Tarrant, and also the man who murdered 22 people in El Paso claimed to be a supporter of the Christchurch shooter ([Daerden, 2019c](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_23)). In Norway, a man followed Tarrant’s example. Not only did they all write manifestos and claim to be inspired by Tarrant’s manifesto, but they also posted on bulletin boards to announce their attacks ([Daerden, 2019b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_22)). The usual label of copycats or lone wolfs obscures the cultural and social aspects of these logics of action.

## White terrorist culture and metapolitics 2.0

Both terrorist attacks of Roof and Tarrant can, from a cultural perspective, be understood as part of a dialogue. A dialogue with very specific niched communities within the global new right. Roof’s manifesto oriented itself to American nodes in that global network, whereas Tarrant was in a clear dialogue with his ‘lads’ on 8chan. Tarrant was also with the identitarian movement in Europe whom he had financially supported by donating over 2,500 British pounds ([Daerden, 2019a](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_21)). Tarrant especially was very much integrated into the global new right, and white terrorist culture in particular. He knew the theories of the global new right and had, or at least claimed to have, studied the practices and manifestos of previous far-right terrorists and used ready-made formats, including the gamification of his killing spree, which was already an existing format.

Tarrant himself stresses the social dimension of his attack when he frames himself and his actions as part of a group of ‘soldiers’. The categorization of ‘lone wolf’ presupposes an old hierarchical form of organization with clear leaders. In a post-digital era, with its gamification and ‘leaderless’ resistance ([Crawford & Keen, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_20): 3), this is an anachronism. Instead, the concept of leaderless far-right resistance is adopted by the American Klansman Louis Beam ([Crawford & Keen, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_20)). The problem with this concept is that it obfuscates more than it illuminates. The seemingly leaderless resistance is not so 243much leaderless as it is networked. Offline (and online) mobilization is more and more the result of so-called reluctant leaders or soft leaders ([Gerbaudo, 2014](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_30)). These leaders lead by example, by posting things online, setting up pages or administering groups. It is through the network effect and the affordances of digital media, and its facilitation of networked individualism ([Miller, 2011](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_56)) and digital cultures, that the coherence of the fifth wave of terrorism, in terms of discourse and logics of action, are shaped. Roof, Tarrant and the Buffalo Shooter are not just terrorists, they also act as leaders within those niches. They hoped to make people aware and to lead by example. In his manifesto, Tarrant explicitly wanted to persuade other white men to become soldiers. And of course the same is true for their own behaviour: they themselves were influenced by others who led by example. If we take on board one of the fundamental insights of symbolic interactionism, namely that ‘(...) social interaction is a process that forms human conduct instead of being merely a means or a setting for the expression or release of human conduct’ ([Blumer, 1969](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_12): 8), we understand how the ‘lone wolf categorization’ doesn’t work to describe and understand the acts of Roof and Tarrant. Their behaviour is not only individual behaviour, it is also social and cultural behaviour. The fifth wave of terrorism is rooted within the global new right. It is the result of a cultural synchronization of far-right ideologies and myths like the Great Replacement theory, digital culture in general and the cultural gamification of terrorism. The result of this polycentric culture is visible in specific logics of actions: the announcement of the act, the search for media uptake through the use of mass and hybrid media logics, the appropriation of gaming culture and infrastructures for massive effect, and the publication of a manifesto for metapolitical goals. The Buffalo Shooter is an excellent example of this type of terrorism. He was adopting the logics of action of Brenton Tarrant: he used his killing spree to generate attention for his manifesto, which was also clearly inspired by Tarrant. Just like Tarrant, he metapragmatically preformulated the news by interviewing himself. The manifesto also echoes Dylann Roof’s manifesto, as he, just like Roof, describes the different races. What is more, there is again that link to a whole series of nodes within the global new right: from /pol /to The Daily Stormer and Breitbart. His discourses are mainstream within the global new right, and his killing spree is a tool to generate attention, to let people search for the Great Replacement.

If we take Tarrant as an example, we see that he is socialized, or formed as you wish, in relation to many different centres of normativity operating on different scales. Tarrant’s manifesto, in form and content, shows a remarkable resemblance to the manifest of Breivik. And Tarrant himself explicitly praised ‘knight justiciar Anders Behring Breivik’ as a model from which he took inspiration. And this normativity of Breivik becomes clear in the main motifs that echo Breivik’s manifesto. Tarrant constructs himself, just 244like Breivik, through gamified language as a knight: a crusader. Moreover, he even claims, probably falsely, to have contacted Breivik and ‘receiving a blessing for my mission after contacting his brother knights’. Brenton Tarrant thus not only looks at Breivik, he imagines himself as a member of the reborn Knights Templar, a crusader against ‘cultural genocide’ fighting for ‘Millions of European and other ethno-nationalist peoples that wish to live in peace amongst their own people, living in their own lands, practicing their own traditions and deciding the future of their own kind’. This reference to ‘millions’ supporting his cause is also a direct intertextual link connecting Tarrant’s and Breivik’s manifestos, and a constant theme in Breivikian circles.

If we further analyse the discourse in that manifesto, we see next to the link with the identitarians Camus and Faye, which I already discussed, that his discourse also orients to contemporary alt-right discourses on white nationalism and white genocide as expressed by people like Richard Spencer, YouTube channels like Red Ice, or extreme-right sites and publishers like Counter- Currents. He, for instance, frames himself as ‘an Ethno-nationalist Eco-fascist’ fighting for ‘ethnic autonomy for all peoples with a focus on the preservation of nature, and the natural order’. Such eco-fascist rhetoric was also to be found in Richard Spencer’s infamous Charlottesville Manifesto where he defined man as having ‘the potential to become nature’s steward or its destroyer’ ([Spencer, 2017a](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_68)). The terrorist act is legitimated in the manifesto by taking refuge in existing new right discourse. The result of his killing spree and the launched manifesto is that it creates echo-chamber uptakes, for instance in an article on Counter-Currents that ‘explains’ his killing spree from the same assumptions and discourses that Tarrant mobilizes to explain his deed ([Johnson, 2019b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_37)): ‘We obviously don’t know all the facts yet, but based on the manifesto attributed to Tarrant entitled “The Great Replacement”, Tarrant believes that whites are being replaced in our homelands by fast-breeding non-whites, including Muslims. This is absolutely correct’. Johnson of course distances himself from this killing spree and claims that it is against white interests, but at the same time, he uses this act to stress this could ‘not have happened in a homogeneously white society’. Ergo, if you want to avoid racial violence, you should not stop the racists or far-right terrorists, but the mixing of races.

8chan was clearly one centre to which Tarrant oriented. The fact that he speaks the language and understood the rules of online practices show the degree to which he was a member of this group (See also [Ebner, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_25)). He not only knew the group culturally, but he also knew their language and ways of doing. His post on 8chan indexed to his 8chan peers that he was one of them. He treated the anons as ‘fellow crusaders’ in a battle to save the white nations of the world. He did see a clear distinction between ‘their cultural war’ and his killing spree. He saw it as their duty to start spreading memes and engage in shitposting to spread his message further. He thus did everything he could to not only please them but also to activate them. Again, we see how through his acts and discourse a lot of other people’s voices are reproduced.

245What looks like an individualist action offline has clear social-cultural and political online dimensions ([Veranoudi, Lu, Molnar, & Liza Tóth-Szöllős, 2019](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_79)). He not only acted offline as an individual who made the choice by himself, but also imagined himself online as a Knights Templar warrior and a member of several polycentric and transnational white nationalist networks. And importantly, he not only imagined himself as part of a group with a goal, his followers and the followers of Roof took on board the same mission. Even though Tarrant explicitly states that he is not a member of any nationalist or political group or organization, we should be careful to label Tarrant a ‘lone wolf’. Legally speaking, he probably acted alone. The Norwegian judges passing judgement on Breivik concluded that too. But if we analyse the roots and formats and discourses of those perpetrators we see that this labelling is inadequate to understand white terrorism as a contemporary phenomenon. The concept of a ‘lone wolf’ comes with associations of individuals radicalizing themselves while being isolated in society. It immediately triggers the frame of ‘the freak’ with mental issues. This individualist ‘freak’ frame has an offline bias and uses an anachronistic model of political and activist organization, which makes us blind to the social, cultural, and political dimensions of these types of radicalization. The thing is, his offline behaviour had an enormous online shadow.

Dissociating the individual act from the broader social, cultural, political and technological context in which his voice is produced causes us to miss the broader picture of white terrorism. It is a socio-cultural and technological fact. It is constructed in collaboration with other people from different corners of the world and different timeframes in niched online spaces. In digital culture studies, scholars have now been arguing for several years that digital media are spaces where new types of social groups emerge. These groups are light communities ([Blommaert, 2016](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_7)), micro-populations ([Maly & Varis, 2016](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_52)), networked ([boyd, 2001](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_14)) or affective publics ([Papacharissi, 2015](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_57)). They do not necessarily share the same location, nor do they know each other’s name, but they do function as social groups. They produce norms and normality, and engage in structured and formatted modes of practice ([Blommaert, 2017b](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_9)) and logics of action. Note that these social groups are in themselves also polycentric. Roof oriented himself towards largely American-based hubs in the global network, whereas Tarrant operated on a more global scale. Many more different configurations are possible. One example is the Hanau terrorist who combined Great Replacement rhetoric with even more marginal conspiracy theories ([Crawford & Keen, 2020](#C_013_c6.xhtml#r6_20)).

White terrorist culture is thus in itself a polycentric social group that occurs as a network of different nodes that come together with an individual or a series of individuals. Important is that we cannot understand white terrorism without looking at the emergence of contemporary new right metapolitics. It is this ideological dimension, embedded in YouTube channels, fora, journals, books, think tanks, Discord servers, memes and manifestos that 246explain an essential part of the rationale of the terrorist and the cultural material informing his acts. White terrorists cannot be understood if we detach their individual acts from the social and online dimensions that shaped them and generated audiences for them.

To conclude this chapter, I want to zoom out again and try to understand the effects of far-right terrorist culture within the global new right. As I see it now, far-right terrorism and violence always have four effects. First, violence always comes with a spike in attention not only to the violence, but also to the ideological project of the perpetrators. Secondly, it usually comes with a surge in the digital media the perpetrators were using to announce their act. Thirdly, we see a break-up of the groups after the attack. Some seem to laud the violent action, others clearly want to walk a more metapolitical path. Fourthly, new media are used to further the metapolitical goals, or even more, new alt-tech media is set up, or one tries to re-integrate that media in the digital mainstream. This results in many more niched groups that again can start to grow, to create their own metapolitics and logics of action. Important to realize is that fragmentation in niche groups, from a meta-perspective, doesn’t harm the metapolitics, it only redistributes the actors who can recruit in their own niches. Even more, those niches are from an ideological perspective still connected, and nothing prevents them from coming together again when certain situations call for it.
